papers.abstract: Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.
authors: Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
bullets: Targets the challenge of converting visually plausible layouts into simulation-ready, spatially grounded 3D environments.
Uses hierarchical diffusion sampling to arrange furniture within functional room zones.
Compiles proposals by extracting spatial relations, fitting geometry, and locally correcting object poses.
Across five room types, it achieves the highest reported visual quality and physical stability, with no detected collisions or out-of-bounds objects.
Navigation policies trained in SceneBloom scenes outperform those trained on an equal number of real scans when evaluated on held-out real scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Framework overview. SceneBloom decouples visual layout sampling from 3D scene compilation. Given a room description and retrieved exemplars, a vision–language model (VLM) produces a zone plan with a prompt qj for each zone, and a diffusion model conditioned on qj and asset LoRAs Λj samples zone visual proposals Ij . 3D perception models lift the proposals into zone layouts Lj , and a VLM extracts relation contracts Cj from the proposal images. Guided by these relation contracts, the geometric compiler applies hierarchical layout fitting and relational refinement to produce the compiled furniture layout. Wall and surface objects are then added, yielding the simulation-ready scene shown in room and agent views.

Figure 1: Overview of SceneBloom. SceneBloom compiles visual proposals of functional zones into a simulation-ready 3D scene, and resampling the same prompt yields different layouts. Its scenes are more physically plausible than those of prior generators and train a better objectnavigation policy than an equal number of real scans.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. For each method and room type, we show the scene whose score is the median of its ten scenes. Enlarged regions illustrate functional organization and physical placement across methods, each retaining its native asset source. Aggregate results are in Table 1.

Figure 3: Effect of contract-guided compilation. All rows start from the same lifted scene, and each adds one step; the enlarged views show relation groups from the contract. Raw lifted layout: objects keep their lifted poses, and lifting errors break relations such as chairs facing their table. Geometry-only compilation: fitting assembles a collision-free room but leaves these relations broken. Contract-guided compilation: fitting under the contract, followed by relational refinement, restores these relations while the layout stays collision-free.
Figure 6: Training from scratch. SR (%) on the 36 real HM3D validation homes. Points average three training seeds. Shading marks our margin over the best other source.
Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparisons on offices and bathrooms.
Figure 5: Ablation of proposal source and contract guidance. Results on 50 furniture-only scenes with shared inventories, assets, and sizes. Appendix D lists the exact values.

Table 7: Generation wall clock per scene. Measured from each run’s own artifacts, one scene at a time, over the baseline pools of Table 1 and a 50-scene run of our pipeline. The span is layout generation for every system: rendering and physical settling are excluded. Each job generates one scene on one H100-class GPU, except SceneWeaver, which runs on 8 CPU cores. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 2: Policy fine-tuning and generalization. SR and SPL (%) on 100 seen-goal and 107 unseengoal held-out generated scenes and on the 36 scanned scenes of the HM3D-OVON subset. Finetuned rows average three training seeds. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 3: Real-environment transfer with occluders. SR and SPL (%).
Table 9: Language-model usage and cost per scene. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 8: Our layout-generation time breakdown. Mean wall clock over a 50-scene production run with the same scene requests as Table 1. Components differ from the total by 0.2 seconds due to uninstrumented orchestration and rounding.

Table 12: Navigation-mesh connectivity. Our layouts and the two controls are measured on their fine-tuning pools of Section 4.2.2, the baselines on their pools of Table 1. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 15: Search difficulty of navigation episodes. Share of episodes (%) whose goal stays hidden after a full turn at the start position or is hidden at the start heading, measured with one camera for every set.
Table 14: Real-environment transfer on cleaned episodes. SR and SPL (%) on the 631 HM3D-OVON episodes without annotation errors.
Table 4: Relations a zone contract can hold. The VLM selects relations; the compiler checks them geometrically and performs all pose changes.

Table 5: Physical stability under the REST3D protocol (Ma et al., 2026). Stab. is the percentage of movable objects within the translation and rotation thresholds, and the last three columns measure motion severity. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 11: Ablation of proposal source and contract guidance. Values plotted in Figure 5. Viol. is the percentage of relations in the extracted contract that the compiled layout violates. Bold/underline mark best/second-best.

Table 10: Retrieval ablation. Results on 50 scenes, ten per room type; LDD uses the 30 bedroom, dining-room, and living-room scenes. Zones is the mean number of functional zones per scene, and the visual quality of both rows is judged in a single run, so the with-retrieval row rescores the scenes of Table 1 and differs from it by at most 0.02. Bold marks the better value.

Table 13: Training from scratch. SR and SPL (%) on the 36 real HM3D validation homes for 40, 80, and 120 training houses. Trained rows average three training seeds. Bold/underline mark best/second-best at each house count.

papers.selection_reason: Generates realistic 3D indoor environments for embodied agent training; fits embodied learning and 3D scene generation.
papers.title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
papers.tldr: SceneBloom generates realistic, diverse, and physically valid indoor 3D scenes by combining diffusion-based layout sampling with contract-guided geometric compilation.

papers.abstract: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.
authors: Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Addresses fragmented action-labeled data caused by action-specific world models.
Maps discrete action identities and continuous spatiotemporal coordinates into a pretrained video model’s positional space.
Uses cardinality-calibrated attention to reduce bias from different action representation granularities.
Evaluated on force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose conditioning.
The jointly trained unified model improves action following and surpasses action-specific experts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UniAction. Diverse action forms are represented as sparse action elements: semantic identities index tokens in a shared codebook (Sec. 3.1), spatiotemporal positions use the backbone’s native positional encoding (Sec. 3.2), and action and video tokens interact via cardinality-calibrated attention (Sec. 3.3).
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across four action forms. UniAction follows the input actions more faithfully than other conditioning mechanisms. Overlays indicate the input action.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with action-specific experts. Compared with separate training, the jointly trained UniAction follows the input actions more faithfully and produces more plausible dynamics and visual appearance. Overlays indicate the input action.
Figure 5: Generalization. Both models are trained only on force data, with all forces applied at t = 0; columns show test-time forces at different t. Trajectories are colored by frame.

Figure 1: One world model for heterogeneous actions. Instead of training a separate model per action type (left), UniAction conditions a single world model (middle) on heterogeneous actions and outperforms the action-specific experts across all four action forms (right).
Figure 10: Temporal generalization on balls.
Figure 9: Temporal generalization on dominoes.

Figure 11 shows 24 generations from the jointly trained UniAction. Except for the second row in the left column of (c) and the upper-left example in (d), whose initial frames come from the test set, all initial frames were generated by GPT Image 2 and were unseen during training. Each strip shows the initial frame and two later frames; paired left and right strips use matching frame indices.
Figure 11: Scene and appearance generalization across four action forms. All six variants in (c) share the same hand-pose input. Arrows and highlighted keys indicate the input actions.
Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparisons. Overlays indicate input conditions.

Figure 12 shows three long videos generated by the jointly trained UniAction. Each training sample contains only one action form. Since all actions share the same representation and conditioning pathway, tokens from different action forms can be directly concatenated into a single sequence at inference time without additional training. These results combine force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose, with both simultaneous actions and transitions between actions over time. The initial frames were generated by GPT Image 2.

Figure 12: Generalization to unseen action compositions. Each block (a)–(c) shows one video in three rows of six selected frames, read from left to right and then from top to bottom. Arrows, pose overlays, and highlighted keys indicate the input actions.
Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparisons. Overlays indicate input conditions.

Table 1: Comparison with visual-based (VACE (Jiang et al., 2025)) and token-based (CrossAttn (NVIDIA, 2026b)) conditioning mechanisms across four action forms. Best and second-best results are bold and underlined.
Table 3: Ablations of spatiotemporal grounding and cardinality calibration. Each variant changes one component (A→B: A replaced by B). Best in bold, second-best underlined.
Table 4: Construction of the test set.

papers.selection_reason: Unifies heterogeneous action conditioning for action-conditioned video world models, directly addressing interactive world-model learning.
papers.title: UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
papers.tldr: UniAction unifies heterogeneous action conditioning in one world model by encoding actions as sparse semantic elements with spatiotemporal coordinates.

papers.abstract: To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .
authors: Philipp Lindenberger, Paul-Edouard Sarlin, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–robustness trade-off between sparse keypoint and dense pixel matching.
Takes image pairs and points from the first image, then predicts corresponding coordinates in the second image.
Searches a limited set of dense-pixel correspondences to provide dense-matching accuracy at sparse-matching speed.
Simultaneously rejects unrelated or visually ambiguous image pairs, improving correspondence reliability.
Experiments report improved Pareto performance for relative pose estimation and strong gains in SfM and visual localization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of FlexGlue. Each of the two images is encoded by a CNN backbone. The resulting dense tokens are fused by a Transformer that outputs context-augmented tokens. These tokens are decoded into overlap heatmaps and classify whether the image pair is unmatchable, in which case the inference stops. Otherwise, a query point in one image is turned into a sub-pixel coordinate in the other by interpolation of its feature, dense correlation, and match refinement.

Figure 3: Visual disambiguation examples. Left: Images overlaid with PCA of learned features. Center: Estimated correspondences pre-filtering. Right: We report the covisibility score after 3 and 9 layers in the top-left. Top: Our method correctly identifies a covisible pair. Bottom: We correctly identify challenging doppelgangers from various domains early and stop matching.

Figure 5: Run-time on different keypoint budgets and layer ablations. RoMav2’s (Edstedt et al., 2026) run time is independent of the number of keypoints, but has a large overhead. LoMa (Nordström et al., 2026) is very efficient but scales quadratically, while our method is fairly efficient and scales linearly (left). Our method learns strong matching and disambiguation early on, while the run time grows linearly with the number of layers (right, black line).

Figure 10: Scene clustering on IMC2025. Image graphs recovered by our method with visual disambiguation only. Colors denote the predicted clusters and edges the retained image pairs. Top: landmarks are separated into clean clusters. Bottom: a single wrong pair (red) passes our filter.

Figure 13: Visual disambiguation examples. We show some visual disambiguation examples from the test sets of DG (Cai et al., 2023), ViSym-F (Xiangli et al., 2025), and LaMAR-DG (Sarlin et al., 2022). Top left is the GT label, right our covisibility score. Our method effectively distinguishes hard covisible pairs, but sometimes mislabels under extreme appearance or viewpoint changes, or when context is missing (middle row failure, wrong facade).

Figure 9: PCA of the aggregated tokens. For each image pair, we show the two views and the first three principal components of their tokens at 9 layers as RGB. Our method learns structural priors such as horizontal and vertical lines, perspective, and planarity, and clearly highlights covisible areas.

Figure 14: Qualitative matches. Correspondences of LoMa-G, SP+RoMav2, and SP+Ours on two pairs per dataset, colored by their reprojection error. We report the number of matches N and the precision at 3 px. LoMa gets 2048 keypoints, and RoMav2 and our method get 1024 keypoints for fair comparison.

Figure 6: Detailed results on LaMAR-DG. AUROC and AP of FlexGlue and DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) per scene (a), difficulty (b), time (c), and device (d). Difficulty bins are tertiles of MegaLoc similarity per label, i.e., hard negatives are highly similar and hard positives dissimilar. FlexGlue remains robust on hard, cross-day, and cross-device pairs, where DG++ degrades strongly.

Figure 14: Qualitative matches (continued). Bottom: failure cases on TartanAir, Hypersim, and MegaDepth. All methods fail under extreme rotation of a repetitive ceiling (top) and on a strongly self-similar scene (middle). On the repetitive facade (bottom), our method matches the wrong instance of a repeated element, while RoMav2 succeeds.

Figure 12: Dense matching across layers. Unfiltered dense correspondences of FlexGlue after 3, 6, and 9 layers, colored by their error from green (<1 px) to red (≥5 px), with the PCK@1px per image. Despite being supervised only at sparse queries, FlexGlue yields fairly accurate dense correspondences. Deeper layers mostly refine matches and fix errors close to depth discontinuities.

Figure 11: Dense matching. Dense correspondences of FlexGlue, colored by their error from green (<1 px) to red (≥5 px), with the PCK@1px per image, from the coarse readout, with our refinement, and with the RoMav2 (Edstedt et al., 2026) refiner. The coarse matching has weaknesses near depth discontinuities, which the refiners address.

Figure 8: Comparison of matching modes. Left: Point-to-point correspondences estimated by our model, colored by epipolar error (green < 1 px). Center: Keypoints colored by being matchable sparse-to-sparse (green), and keypoints only matchable sparse-to-dense (blue), highlighting the repeatability issue. Right: Sparse-to-dense correspondences. Especially under large scale changes and on low-texture areas, sparse-to-dense matching yields many more, accurate correspondences.

Figure 4: Hard negatives of our LaMAR doppelganger benchmark. From left to right: different floors (CAB), indoor (HGE), outdoor (HGE), and cross-device (LIN) pairs. None of the pairs overlap, despite a high retrieval similarity (sim) from MegaLoc; ∆xy and ∆z denote the horizontal and vertical distance between the two cameras.

Figure 7: Corrected ViSym test labels. Each pair shows the original ViSym label (Orig.) and our label (New). The original labels miss covisible pairs under strong viewpoint changes and mark some pairs of distinct but similar facades as covisible.

Table 8: Doppelgangers ablation. AUROC on ViSym-F and LaMAR Disambiguation. Our model learns disambiguation early, and guidance from match supervision improves generalization. Even without labelled data our model achieves high accuracy. Training in-domain increases accuracy. Right: Qualitative examples with GT, DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) and our disambiguation score.
Table 2: Two-view matching in additional domains. FlexGlue exhibits the highest matching accuracy over multiple datasets from different domains. A higher resolution further improves results.
Table 11: Training datasets. Number of training scenes and relative sampling weight of each dataset. Doppelgangers is only mixed in during fine-tuning with negatives.

Table 4: Uncalibrated end-to-end SfM. On ETH3D, FlexGlue exhibits a higher matching accuracy than existing approaches, resulting in more accurate poses. Disambiguation further increases pose accuracy by preventing collapse of reconstructions.

Table 5: SfM with distractors. On IMC2025, FlexGlue yields better reconstructions thanks to its disambiguation. Using 10k keypoints instead of 4k further improves, but makes LoMa timeout on Kaggle (OOT).
Table 9: Keypoint detectors. FlexGlue works with any detector. RaCo yields the most accurate reconstructions, while all detectors perform similarly on two-view matching.
Table 10: ViSym test relabelling. We manually clean GPS-annotated labels of ViSym by hand. Most corrections turn negatives into positives. The last row counts the pairs kept in our balanced subset.

Table 3: Detection of Doppelgangers. We report AUROC and AP on DG (in-distribution), ViSym and LaMAR, as well as the matching time. FlexGlue achieves the highest disambiguation accuracy across all datasets when trained on the same labelled data (DG), especially +10 AUROC points on the LaMAR benchmark, at much higher throughput.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse-to-dense feature matching with pair disambiguation directly supports 3D vision tasks such as Structure-from-Motion and visual localization.
papers.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
papers.tldr: FlexGlue combines sparse-to-dense matching with pairwise disambiguation to achieve efficient, accurate, and reliable visual correspondence estimation.

papers.abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
authors: Xi Chen, Fengqi Hu, Zeyu Shen, Jiaying Xu, Shangding Gu, Pan Xu, Anqi Liu, Laixi Shi
bullets: Addresses limited reusability and unclear empirical boundaries in robust RL.
Integrates 17 representative online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under one interface.
Provides evaluations across real-world shifts, humanoid tasks, and vision-language-action tasks.
Analyzes 273 perturbation configurations to map where robust RL methods succeed or fail.
Offers an open-source, reproducible, and extensible platform for research and application.

papers.abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.
authors: Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting high-quality dexterous manipulation data with many finger joints.
Uses the same hand hardware for data collection and deployment, avoiding a hand-embodiment gap.
Operators control wrist motion with a hand-held device and select or adjust skills for coordinated finger movements.
Records commanded joint targets and measured states; behavior cloning trains visuomotor policies without skill labels.

papers.abstract: Semantic misinformation can arise when an authentic image is paired with a caption that changes or distorts its narrative. Because the image itself may contain no visible signs of manipulation, methods designed to detect pixel-level artifacts can miss these misleading image-caption pairs. We study this problem using DGM4+, a dataset designed to evaluate the detection of global scene and semantic inconsistencies. We propose a multimodal model that combines image-text representations from SigLIP with visual scene features from DINOv2 through a projection MLP, and adapts Qwen2-VL-7B using LoRA. The model jointly predicts whether an image-caption pair is authentic, identifies the manipulation type, and grounds the misleading caption tokens. On the DGM4+ validation split, the model achieves an F1 score of $0.9679$ for binary authenticity classification. These results suggest that parameter-efficient adaptation of vision-language models is promising for detecting semantic inconsistencies, while also motivating further work on precise token-level grounding.
authors: Tarunya Prasad, Bharatesh Chakravarthi

Uses LoRA to adapt Qwen2-VL-7B for joint authenticity classification, manipulation-type prediction, and token grounding.
Achieves an F1 score of 0.9679 for binary authenticity classification on the DGM4+ validation split.
Token-level grounding remains an area for further improvement.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

papers.abstract: In medical robotics, data-driven soft-tissue shape control requires deforming tissue toward desired morphologies through sequential physical interactions. This challenge is particularly important in microscale manipulation, where localized deformation is difficult to observe, represent, and control, while physics-based models can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to realistic environments. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, but target-conditioned control requires effective representations of both observed and desired tissue states. In this work, we introduce an OCT-guided data-driven framework for tissue shape control, learned from user-guided demonstrations and executed with closed-loop OCT feedback. We study full-volume, tissue-masked sparse-volume, and voxelized point-cloud representations, with or without residual conditioning, using deterministic (Explicit) and generative diffusion (Diffusion) policies. Across 12 configurations and 576 phantom rollouts on 3-DoF depth and 6-DoF directional tasks, OCT-derived 3D representations support both Explicit and Diffusion policies, with performance depending on representation and residual conditioning. Residual conditioning reduces directional Shape RMSE from 0.748 to 0.555 mm for full-volume Diffusion, while voxelized point-cloud Explicit with residuals achieves 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control, with comparable accuracy at intermediate unseen targets and consistent performance across deployments. We further evaluate the framework in 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts, extending to biological tissue with final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations. These results establish volumetric OCT as current and goal representations for learned closed-loop tissue shape control across deterministic and generative action models.
authors: Chaoyu Zhang, Guangshen Ma, Mark Draelos
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of observing, representing, and controlling localized soft-tissue deformation, especially at microscale.

Across 576 phantom rollouts, residual conditioning and representation choice improved control accuracy; the best reported errors were 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control.
An additional 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts achieved final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations, supporting transfer beyond phantoms.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

bullets: Implementation differences between inference and training can make nominally on-policy RL updates effectively off-policy and destabilize training.

papers.abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
authors: Dianye Huang, Jiamei Guo, Yue Zhou, Mingde Li, Yi Xiong, Wei Wang, Nassir Navab, Zhongliang Jiang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between continuous measurements and discrete token-based numerical prediction.
Uses a shared vision-language backbone with autoregressive text generation, visual prompt tuning, and diffusion-based prediction of caliper coordinates and measurement length.
Adds coordinate-length consistency and ensemble post-processing to refine estimates.
On four echocardiographic tasks, it reduces measurement errors by 21.4–37.6% versus a Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline and preserves medical question-answering performance.
Also improves X-ray vertebral measurement error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels; evaluation is limited to the reported ultrasound, question-answering, and X-ray tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.
authors: Thomas Landeg, Thierry Tambe
bullets: Targets brittleness when robot actions enter states poorly covered by training data.
Trains a small failure-prediction head on outcome-labeled rollouts using the frozen VLA’s internal representations.
When failure risk crosses a threshold, it pauses control, backtracks the arm, and returns control to the unchanged policy.
Adds only 0.48–0.88% to model parameter counts.
On LIBERO-Long, reduces failure rates by 19–48% and improves success by up to 7.4 percentage points; gains are smaller on easier suites, while all tested MetaWorld configurations improve.

papers.abstract: Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance.
authors: Pietro Di Nicco, Lucio La Cava, Andrea Tagarelli
bullets: Addresses BPE’s fixed whitespace boundaries, which split meaningful multiword expressions and formal-language structures.
Uses adaptive frequent-pattern mining with thresholds conditioned on candidate length and whether patterns are general-language or formal-language.
Allocates vocabulary capacity more effectively to underrepresented notations such as LaTeX.
Evaluated on five LaTeX and natural-language datasets, with gains in encoding efficiency and domain-specific language-model performance while preserving general-language performance.

papers.abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq
authors: Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
bullets: Addresses the failure of ordinary logical equivalence, which can incorrectly accept unrelated statements when a powerful prover proves each independently.
Judges Lean-checked proof terms against allowed transformations such as logical rearrangement and library-equation rewriting.

SemantEq-ProofAudit filters language-model proofs, accepting none of 104 non-equivalent pairs and increasing recall from 65.4% to 81.1% on 407 equivalent pairs under the best prompt.
The approach separates proof generation from acceptance, allowing stronger provers to improve recall without changing the acceptance criterion.

papers.abstract: HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.

papers.abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.
authors: Panagiotis Koromilas, Eleanna Vali, Diogenis Antonopoulos, Eleni Saka, Dimitris Christofis, Nikolaos Ioannis Bountos, Konstantin Klemmer, Ioannis Papoutsis, Yannis Panagakis, Mihalis A. Nicolaou
bullets: Standard Lipschitz location encoders have intrinsic dimension at most 2, causing low-rank embeddings and preventing optimal contrastive alignment.
Frozen image encoders act as covariance regularizers, but multimodal settings require targets that are both cross-modal aligned and high-rank.
LoCA first jointly aligns Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders, then trains location and tabular metadata adapters with multi-view contrastive learning.
Across 17 geospatial, environmental, socioeconomic, biodiversity, and climate tasks, LoCA records the most task wins and wins 68.8% of per-task comparisons.
The approach is evaluated within the scope of the five compared state-of-the-art encoders and the listed downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.
authors: Sadra Emami, Benjamin Weigell, Mohammad Reza Mousavi, Gunel Jahangirova, Hugo Araujo, Bernhard Bauer
bullets: The study evaluates 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on 1,000 EffiBench problems with hardware-level energy monitoring.
Optimization inference consumes 0.79–8.68 MJ per model-configuration pair; limiting output length reduces this energy by up to 69%.
42 of 44 configurations generate code that uses more energy per execution than canonical human solutions, with overheads from 4% to 886%.
The two energy-saving configurations require roughly 10^6–10^7 executions to offset optimization energy costs.
Mixture-of-Experts models use less inference energy than similarly sized dense models without sacrificing correctness.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of LLM inference and generated-code energy use; directly informs energy-efficient AI deployment and decoding choices.
papers.title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
papers.tldr: LLM-driven code optimization often reduces runtime at the cost of substantially higher energy use, including during both inference and execution.

papers.abstract: While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $\Delta^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.
authors: Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
bullets: The modality gap persists in shared embedding spaces learned by models such as CLIP and CLAP.
The method replaces unit-sphere embeddings with probability-simplex representations.
Softmax adapters and Total Variation similarity provide a shared, calibrated coordinate system for both modalities.
Across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks, the centroid ℓ₂ gap is reduced by 97–99%.
Retrieval performance matches or exceeds that of standard unconstrained models.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the modality gap in multimodal models by using simplex-constrained representations and geometric priors, improving cross-modal alignment and retrieval.
papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.tldr: Constraining multimodal embeddings to the probability simplex with lightweight adapters substantially closes the modality gap while preserving strong retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Obaidullah Zaland, Monowar Bhuyan
bullets: Human corrections vary in modality, urgency, behavioral scope, and privacy sensitivity across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments.
Naively shared updates may improve mean performance while suppressing rare safety interventions or causing unsafe behavior on other robots.
Corrections should retain their context and uncertainty when determining what to share.
Each candidate update should be evaluated in the receiving robot’s closed loop before deployment.
The paper proposes counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda; it reports no experimental results.

papers.selection_reason: Federated adaptation of VLA policies and safety across embodiments is directly relevant to embodied AI and VLA.
papers.title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
papers.tldr: Federated sharing of human corrections for VLA robots requires context-aware, closed-loop safety checks and privacy evaluation rather than optimizing average task success alone.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.
authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey, Jangseon Park, Jason Kong, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing
bullets: RL post-training rollout generation can dominate training cost, while existing speculative decoding methods face memory, policy-alignment, or repetition-exploitation limitations.
NgramRL builds bounded n-gram caches from recent rollouts, requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident state.
Target-model verification preserves the original rollout distribution; uncovered speculative outcomes safely fall back to sequential lookup.
Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward, reaching up to 1.99× SuffixDecoding and 7.0× prompt-lookup decoding.
An adaptive fan-out prefetcher improves measured Spider rollout throughput by 1.38× over synchronous NgramRL and covers 96.6% of outcomes at a candidate budget of 16.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates RL post-training for LLMs using rollout-aware n-gram speculative decoding, improving the efficiency of reasoning capabilities in large language models.
papers.title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: NgramRL accelerates RL post-training rollouts by using recent per-prompt n-grams as a self-updating speculative drafter, with adaptive prefetching to reduce lookup overhead.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.
authors: Yi Qin, Marawan Elbatel, Shanshan Song, Taoran Huang, Jiarong Guo, Ningshu Li, Lehan Wang, Chenxu Zhao, Jiexin He, Machteld J. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a medically grounded multimodal vision-language model with comprehensive clinical reasoning, directly fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
papers.tldr: EchoChat is a multimodal generative AI model that provides broad, evidence-grounded echocardiographic interpretation and improves report quality and diagnostic performance.

papers.abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io
authors: Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Groezinger, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Pierpaolo Mori, Nael Fasfous, Alexander Frickenstein, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: Addresses inaccurate global rank allocation and rank collapse in Fisher-based SVD compression.
LEMS models layer-wise local/global importance and error propagation, then allocates ranks using an ILP.
KFAC-SVD uses token-wise statistics to mitigate rank deficiency during decomposition.
Evaluated on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 families, with gains extending to models up to 70B parameters.
Reports up to 4.8 percentage-point zero-shot accuracy gains from LEMS and a 15% average perplexity improvement from KFAC-SVD.

papers.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search

papers.abstract: In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs
authors: Anouar Imel, Jin Qi
bullets: Across three small open models, reports for a claim and its complement systematically summed to more than one.
The inconsistency appeared in network simulations, real fact-checking claims, and controlled two-outcome worlds.
It exceeded same-meaning paraphrase effects and persisted across sampling, peer-group sizes, and report strengths.
Complementary initial populations diverged over repeated rounds rather than remaining mirror images.
Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction, but improved final-round Brier loss for only one model.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the consistency of complement probabilities in LLM-agent opinion simulations, providing empirical analysis of LLM behavior in agent-based reasoning tasks.
papers.title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
papers.tldr: LLM-agent opinion simulations often violate complement consistency, so simulated probabilities should be tested for wording symmetry before being interpreted as beliefs.

papers.abstract: Latent communication requires both an effective continuous reasoning process and an interface through which an external model can leverage its intermediate computation. We present J-Comm, a framework comprising two core components. First, a training-free Geometric Agreement for Latent Reasoning (GEAR) reweights token candidates over existing model embeddings, which monotonically optimizes geometric consensus among candidate tokens in embedding space at each step. Second, we introduce an H+J (Hidden-and-Jacobian) communication interface that gives the Receiver two complementary views of the Sender's reasoning. The H channel supplies continuous inputs derived from feedback distributions, while the J channel conveys intermediate-state cues in vocabulary-indexed Jacobian-lens coordinates. Intuitively, H provides inputs for the Receiver to reason from, while J offers additional guidance within its computation. The Receiver reconstructs these cues using its own dictionary and injects them into intermediate layers during prefill, enabling communication without sharing key-value caches or requiring identical model widths. In Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-4B communication, J-Comm achieves the highest mean score across seven benchmarks, including 94.80% on MATH500, 54.55% on GPQA-Diamond, 73.33% on AIME2024+2025, and 62.93% success on ALFWorld. Compared with TextMAS, it improves performance by 1.29-8.59 percentage points and reduces generated text tokens by 19.2-74.8%.
authors: Xiangwei Wang, Wei Wang, Sachith Seneviratne, Ken Chen, Yu Xia, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
bullets: Addresses latent communication without sharing key-value caches or requiring identical model widths.
GEAR is a training-free method that reweights token candidates to improve geometric consensus in embedding space.
The H+J interface sends continuous feedback-derived inputs plus vocabulary-indexed Jacobian-lens guidance from Sender to Receiver.
The Receiver reconstructs and injects these signals into intermediate layers during prefill.
For Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-4B communication, it reports the highest mean score across seven benchmarks, with fewer generated text tokens than TextMAS.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a five-level organization of message formation and understanding within thinking and activity in which ASI participates. Its central thesis is that a language model's context is fundamentally incapable of presenting the foundations of utterance formation for examination and verification. These foundations are established in advance by acquired schemas, systemic representations of the world of activity, and connections accepted as true within them. Neither context nor trained LLM weights, in themselves, attest to the presence of deliberately constructed systemic representations. The five levels distinguish systemic representations of the world of activity, a particular situation cut out from those representations, its narrative description, the full sense of a message, and text. A situation's schema-model is not identical to a story about it. A recipient reconstructs the full sense from an abbreviated text through jointly constructed and agreed-upon representations and joint activity. Reverse work proceeds from the full sense through an extended description and the situation's schema-model to the reconstruction of systemic foundations. The theoretical foundations draw on the systems methodology of G. P. Shchedrovitskiy, the structural differential of A. Korzybski, and the Meaning-Text theory of I. A. Mel'chuk. The contribution is a specific systemic-activity organization of content for examining and adjusting message foundations and controlling the consequences of their transformation. Further research concerns large graphical models of activity on reconstructible systemic foundations, distinct from text generation from context.
authors: Maxim Osovsky (Adam University, Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan)
bullets: Argues that context and trained LLM weights alone cannot reveal or verify the schemas and world representations underlying utterances.
Distinguishes five levels: systemic activity representations, a selected situation, its narrative description, full message sense, and surface text.
Models communication as reconstruction: recipients infer full sense from abbreviated text through shared representations and joint activity.
Draws on systems methodology, Korzybski’s structural differential, and Meaning–Text theory.
Proposes a foundation for examining and controlling transformations of message meaning; future work targets reconstructible graphical activity models rather than context-only text generation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a theoretical five-level communication architecture for strong language-based ASI, focusing on systemic representations and message formation, relevant to future LLM architectures.
papers.title: From Deliberately Constructed Systemic Representations of the World of Activity to Dialogue: A Five-Level Communication Architecture for Strong Language-Based ASI
papers.tldr: The paper proposes a five-level communication architecture to make the systemic foundations behind language-based ASI messages explicit, examinable, and adjustable.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.
authors: Marek Masiak, Andrzej Szablewski, Nicola Cancedda, Constantin Venhoff
bullets: Targets backdoors introduced by poisoned fine-tuning data, which can be difficult to localise and remove.
Activates only the k largest adapter latents per token and trains solely with downstream loss.
Produces sparse, functionally causal circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than dense LoRA circuits.
In sleeper-agent model organisms based on Gemma and Qwen models, identified circuits were necessary and sufficient for the backdoor.
Ablating these circuits removed the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance; scope is demonstrated through backdoor case studies.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse interpretable LoRA with k-active latents offers a transferable efficiency and interpretability technique for LLM fine-tuning and circuit analysis.
papers.title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
papers.tldr: TopKLoRA makes LoRA fine-tuning sparse and interpretable, enabling faithful identification and surgical removal of backdoor circuits while preserving normal instruction following.

papers.abstract: Longitudinal causal effect estimation is complicated by time-varying confounding and treatment-confounder feedback loops. Existing methods generally require data-specific nuisance-model fitting, and many are tailored to prespecified treatment sequences or prediction horizons, leading to time-consuming computation at deployment. We introduce *Policy In-Context Longitudinal causal Effect estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks* (**PICLE-PFN**), the first foundation model for longitudinal causal effect estimation that supports *dynamic* treatment policies. PICLE-PFN represents target policies through in-context history-decision demonstrations, providing a unified interface for a broad class of treatment policies. Pretrained over synthetic data sampled from longitudinal structural causal models, PICLE-PFN amortizes causal effect estimation across datasets, policies, and horizons. Given a new observational dataset and target policy, it directly predicts conditional average potential outcomes (CAPOs) in one forward pass without task-specific training or hyperparameter tuning. Across synthetic and semi-synthetic longitudinal benchmarks, PICLE-PFN achieves competitive RMSE and substantially improved uncertainty calibration with a fraction of deployment runtime, compared to state-of-the-art conventional estimators trained and tuned separately for each dataset.
authors: Wenxin Chen, Kyra Gan, Mingyu Lu, Zilin Jing, Fei Wang, Hoifung Poon, Tristan Naumann, Peniel Argaw
bullets: Addresses time-varying confounding and treatment–confounder feedback in longitudinal causal estimation.
Encodes dynamic policies as in-context history–decision demonstrations.
Pretrains on synthetic longitudinal structural causal models to amortize estimation across datasets, policies, and horizons.
Predicts conditional average potential outcomes directly for a new observational dataset and policy.
Shows competitive RMSE, substantially better uncertainty calibration, and lower deployment runtime on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks.

Figure 1: PICLE-PFN Architecture. Feature pooling encodes longitudinal covariates and treatments into embeddings processed by a shared backbone with causal temporal attention and rowattention. Window-specific readouts combine window indices, initial policy demonstrations, and factual outcomes (masked for queries). They cross-attend to trajectory-specific backbone representations under window-specific masks: query readouts access only pre-intervention history, while context readouts access factual data through e and additionally attend to target policy demonstrations. Row-attention uses only context keys and values and operates separately within each readout window. Query readouts yield CAPO predictions across admissible windows in one forward pass.

papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) offer strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities, but their high pretraining cost raises a practical sustainability question: does this upfront investment pay off over a full deployment lifecycle, compared to supervised standalone models that must be periodically retrained? We model the cumulative carbon cost of different approaches across a realistic industrial scenario: Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments, but a classical model remains cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried ones. For cases where reducing the TSFM's own cost matters, we show that removing a single encoder block (7.9% of parameters) via a gradient-free pruning criterion yields a consistent 6 to 9% reduction in FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency, at essentially no cost to zero-shot forecasting performance across a 25-task benchmark.
authors: C\'ecile Luc, Nathana\"el Lemonnier, Ievgen Redko
bullets: Frames TSFM sustainability as a lifecycle comparison between upfront pretraining and recurring retraining.
Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining carbon cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments.
Classical standalone models remain cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried deployments.
Removing one encoder block (7.9% of parameters) cuts FLOPs, emissions, and latency by 6–9%.
Pruning preserves essentially unchanged zero-shot forecasting performance across 25 tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses sustainability and efficiency in Time Series Foundation Models by proposing a gradient-free pruning criterion to reduce FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency.
papers.title: Sustainability of TSFM Deployment and Pretraining: From Carbon Footprint Analysis to Mitigation via Pruning

papers.abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) has provable robustness guarantees that should ease the transfer of policies from simulation to robots, known as sim-to-real. Yet, weakly regularised algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) remain the de facto choice in sim-to-real pipelines, while the practical benefits of regularisation for transfer remain poorly characterised. In this work, we study the sim-to-real performance of commonly used RL algorithms, with the aim of characterising the effects of regularisation on robotic performance. To that end, we derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a novel regularised RL algorithm based on the soft mellowmax value function, which carries strong robustness guarantees. On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, SMM-AC is competitive with baselines like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). On real robots, SMM-AC achieves higher return, while exhibiting greater robustness to perturbations in observations, the environment, and dynamics than baselines. Together, these results demonstrate that regularised RL improves real-world policy deployment through better robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and changing real-world conditions.
authors: Danilo Vucetic, Mohamad H. Danesh, Florence Clerc, Hsiu-Chin Lin, Jonathan Tremblay
bullets: Sim-to-real transfer is difficult because simulation and deployment conditions differ.
The study characterises how regularisation affects robotic policy transfer.
It introduces Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a regularised RL algorithm with robustness guarantees.
SMM-AC is competitive with SAC on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks.
On real robots, it achieves higher return and greater robustness to observation, environment, and dynamics perturbations.
