papers.abstract: Enterprises are deploying agentic AI across the software development lifecycle, and they need the behavioral logic of the systems they act on, not stakeholder documentation. A seven-agent reverse-engineering pipeline recovered this logic, processing 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts describing scope, journeys, rules and acceptance criteria. Recovery does not confer usability. Entities like offer, eligibility, and activation recur across services under a shared vocabulary, related in name but operationally distinct, so one end-to-end journey implicates over a thousand near-identical rules that must not be conflated. Flat vector retrieval fails, returning an identical rule from the wrong service at high similarity with no signal of error. Content-level ontology, the traditional remedy, did not exist, and relating every occurrence of recurring entities would have cost more than the engagement and not survived a release cycle. We place the ontology at the artifact level. In this machine-generated corpus, each artifact retains its producer, component, service, domain and type, provenance that disambiguates before content is read. We present a knowledge layer that organizes before retrieving: a self-describing catalog, a sparse metadata registry, and a navigation hypergraph defined over artifacts rather than extracted entities. Queries resolve to artifact identifiers that constrain vector search, so the competing rule from another service is absent rather than outranked, making disambiguation structural, not statistical. Built in under a week and admitting new services by convention, the layer serves SDLC agents, developers, quality engineers and analysts. It supported root-cause analysis and resolution of 100+ production defects with developer verification and attributed 35 release regression failures to specific rules and services.
authors: Garima Agrawal, Prasun Das, Akshay Sarvade, Priyanka L, Minisha N, Sravani Joshna, Hemath Manivannan, Lavanya Korada, Sambhrit Pattanayak, Srashti Gupta, Siddu R, Prasad Kalyanasundaram
bullets: Enterprise agents need behavioral logic from software systems, but recovered rules across services are difficult to disambiguate.
A seven-agent pipeline processed 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts covering scopes, journeys, rules, and acceptance criteria.
The proposed layer combines a self-describing catalog, sparse metadata registry, and artifact-level navigation hypergraph.
Queries first resolve to artifact identifiers, structurally excluding similarly named rules from unrelated services before vector search.
The layer supported root-cause analysis for 100+ production defects and linked 35 release regressions to specific rules and services.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a knowledge layer for RAG in multi-agent systems, focusing on organizing and retrieving information, which is a core memory mechanism for LLMs.

papers.tldr: An artifact-level knowledge layer improves enterprise RAG for multi-agent systems by organizing provenance and scope before vector retrieval, preventing cross-service rule confusion.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model-tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies, and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence, and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82\% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54\% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43\% to 85.71\% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93\% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91\% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52\% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.
authors: Yuhua Jiang, Chang Xu, Feifei Gao, Li Zhao
bullets: Targets harnesses that unnecessarily re-invoke reasoning after tool feedback has already determined the next action.
Uses recursive self-improvement to refine harness configurations, with validation selecting the deployment configuration while keeping actor weights fixed.
Stores exact actions and dependencies in Executable Decision Graphs; guarded reuse and certified callback substitution replace eligible reasoning callbacks.
On HumanEval, preserves 90.82% success while reducing tokens per task by 29.54%; on DeepSeek Harness, raises success to 85.71% and cuts tokens by 87.93%.
MBPP ablations report lower cost than single-use graphs and retained callbacks, though reuse is bypassed for novel decisions, unsupported evidence, or selector abstention.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method for improving token efficiency in LLM agent harnesses through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement, directly addressing token management and efficiency.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation aligns teacher feedback with a student's current behavior, yet acquiring useful supervision for multi-turn agents requires identifying both where guidance is needed and whether the student can sustain the interaction afterward. We introduce Frontier-OPD, which addresses this problem through the student's learning frontier: decision situations that remain challenging but admit useful autonomous continuation after brief teacher guidance. To operationalize this frontier, Frontier-OPD organizes on-policy experience into a shared-state trajectory graph, where trajectory-balanced aggregation of teacher-student disagreement identifies distinct intervention candidates while preserving the histories needed for replay. Short teacher bridges are then assessed by comparing agreement over the bridge and the ensuing student continuation with an equally long segment of the original trajectory, providing a behavioral proxy for guidance that the current student can build on. Accepted teacher responses augment ordinary distillation data, and fresh rollouts renew the frontier estimate as the policy changes. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld report higher mean autonomous performance than the compared distillation baselines across the evaluated student scales and teacher configurations, with ablations indicating complementary effects of candidate selection and guidance filtering. In one ALFWorld timing setting, the additional collection cost is offset by a shorter time to a target success rate.
authors: Zheng Jiang, Yiming Chen, Houde Qian, Ling Li, Chaoyang Li, Lifeng Sun
bullets: Targets the learning frontier: situations that remain challenging but are likely to benefit from brief teacher guidance.
Builds a shared-state trajectory graph and uses trajectory-balanced teacher–student disagreement to identify intervention candidates while preserving replay histories.
Filters short teacher bridges by comparing bridge and subsequent student behavior against the original trajectory as a proxy for useful, sustainable guidance.
Adds accepted teacher responses to distillation data and continually refreshes frontier estimates through new rollouts.
Outperforms compared distillation baselines in mean autonomous performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld; candidate selection and guidance filtering have complementary effects.

papers.abstract: Real-world 3D reconstruction pipelines often rely on multi-view images degraded by lossy compression. While compression artifacts have been extensively studied in single-image or video restoration, their impact on multi-view geometry remains largely overlooked. In this work, we identify compression-induced cross-view geometric inconsistency as a critical failure mode, where view-dependent artifacts disrupt feature matching, dense correspondence, camera parameter estimation, and downstream 3D reconstruction tasks such as novel view synthesis. To address this problem, we propose CompMVR, a compression-aware multi-view diffusion restoration framework that jointly refines compressed views while preserving cross-view consistency, and construct compressed datasets for systematic evaluation. Unlike conventional restoration methods that optimize each image independently for 2D perceptual quality, CompMVR leverages learned compression priors and cross-view correspondence to recover visual details while improving geometric reliability across views. Experiments across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels demonstrate gains in restoration quality and downstream 3D tasks, including novel-view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching. These results establish compressed multi-view restoration as a distinct problem and highlight its importance for 3D reconstruction under lossy compression. Code and data for this paper are available at https://mchaewon.github.io/CompMVR-project-page/.
authors: Dong-hwi Kim, Chaewon Moon, Hojun Song, Dongbeom Kim, Junyeong Jang, Aro Kim, Gahyeon Kim, Heejung Choi, Jehee Kim, Gianella Cravioto, Sohyun Lee, Gyeongjin Choi, EunHye Jeong, Soo Ye Kim, Jaehyup Lee, Sang-hyo Park
bullets: Lossy compression disrupts cross-view geometry, harming feature matching, correspondence, camera estimation, and novel-view synthesis.
CompMVR jointly restores compressed views while preserving geometric consistency across views.
The framework combines learned compression priors with cross-view correspondence rather than restoring images independently.
Compressed datasets enable evaluation across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels.
Experiments report improved restoration quality and downstream performance in novel-view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our proposed CompMVR. (a) In Stage 1, we learn a compression-aware latent representation by training a compression prior embedder. The latent is optimized through image reconstruction and supervision of coding parameters (codec type and QP). The latent is injected via cross-attention and fused with the UNet input, while a compression artifact estimator (CAE) predicts spatially varying residual maps for degradation-aware restoration. To enforce cross-view geometric consistency, we further apply a cross-view correspondence loss during training.

papers.abstract: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication
authors: Arundhati S. Shanbhag, Brian B. Moser, Federico Raue, Tobias C. Nauen, Andreas Dengel
bullets: Targets the computational overhead of repeatedly updating replay buffers under fixed memory budgets.
Constructs buffers without optimizing or using training signals from the continual learner.
Uses geometric coverage of a frozen pretrained feature space, weighted by class and sample density.
Evaluated on balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy online class- and task-incremental streams.
On Tiny-ImageNet, it is 2.3–8.8× faster than coreset-based selectors and improves the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance.

papers.selection_reason: Replay exemplar selection for continual learning directly matches the continual/online learning topic.
papers.title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: CARES efficiently selects replay exemplars using class-aware, density-weighted coverage in a frozen feature space, delivering strong continual-learning performance with substantially lower selection cost.

papers.abstract: Split inference partitions a Vision Transformer between a resource-constrained edge device and a server. However, transmitting intermediate tokens across the communication channel is costly. Deploying fine-tuned backbones to every endpoint becomes expensive as well. We study token reduction for split inference under a frozen backbone, where only a small adapter is shipped. We observe that the CLS token plays a dual role: it acts as the global summary the receiver needs for classification, and it serves as a signal on which patches to keep. We propose Consomm\'e, a method utilizing both characteristics. There, an information bottleneck compresses the CLS token into a compact latent which is transmitted in place of the full CLS token and conditions a learned patch gate merging patches into exactly $k$ tokens via soft assignment. It reaches any budget in a single step, thus escaping the per-layer cap of bipartite matching (BPM). On DeiT-S/T, it leads all methods at aggressive token budgets and remains operable at shallow splits where BPM cannot operate, while matching fine-tuned methods at gentle budgets at a fraction of their deployment cost.
authors: Man Ngo, Jan S. Rellermeyer
bullets: Targets split inference with a frozen backbone, avoiding deployment of separately fine-tuned backbones.
Uses an information bottleneck to transmit a compact CLS representation instead of the full CLS token.
Conditions a learned patch gate on this representation to softly merge patches into any desired token budget in one step.
On DeiT-S/T, performs best at aggressive budgets, works at shallow splits where BPM cannot, and matches fine-tuned methods at gentler budgets with lower deployment cost.

papers.title: Consomm\'e: Conditioned Token Merging for Split Inference
papers.tldr: Consommé reduces communication in split-inference Vision Transformers by compressing the CLS token and conditionally merging patches into exactly k tokens using only a small adapter.

papers.abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $\alpha=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $\alpha/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $\alpha_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.
authors: Dario Bocchi, Matteo Negri, Flavio Nicoletti, Francesco D'Amico
bullets: Models token prediction as a teacher–student linear classifier over sequences of embedded tokens, with one matrix per position.
For continuous spherical embeddings, the problem reduces to noiseless regression when labels fix the teacher-output direction.
Exact teacher recovery occurs above the example load α_rec = d²/(d−1); spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at high inverse temperature.
Random-association storage capacity scales as d² for margins of order 1/√d.
For finite vocabularies, labels identify Voronoi cells, and the Bayes-optimal learner first learns directions where the vocabulary has greatest variance, even for an isotropic teacher.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Memorization capacity of random associations. (Left) Critical load per degree of freedom αc/d 2 for standard alignment, Eq. (35). The curve shows the Gardner prediction in Eq. (35). Markers show simulations at d = 1, 2, 3, 4 with N = 1000. (Right) Critical load per degree of freedom for vector alignment, Eq. (38). Theoretical curves for d = 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 64 (continuous lines) and the d → ∞ limit of eq. (39) (dashed curve) are shown together with numerical simulations for d = 2, 3, 4 of finite systems of size N = 1000.

Figure 1. Schematic representation of the learning problem with continuous (top) and vocabulary (bottom) token embeddings. In both settings, the token perceptron maps the input sequence ξ = (ξ1, . . . , ξN ) to the field uW (ξ) = (Nd)−1/2 ∑N i=1 Wiξi. (Top) continuous embeddings, with input vectors on the unit sphere Sd−1 and prediction ŷ(ξ) = uW (ξ)/∥uW (ξ)∥. (Bottom) vocabulary embeddings, with each input vector drawn from a fixed vocabulary {z1, . . . ,zD} ⊂ Sd−1. The prediction is the vocabulary vector with maximal overlap with uW (ξ).

Figure 2. Using the rescaled load, the generalization error ϵg curves converges for large embeding dimension. We compare analytical predictions (solid lines) to numerical results (dots) for the generalization error ϵg of the spherical cross-entropy loss with λ̃ = λ/d = 1 versus the rescaled load α̃ for different values of the embedding dimensions d.

Figure 4. For d > 1, generalization error decreases as λ̃ increases and eventually reaches zero for λ̃ → ∞ for α̃ > d d−1 = α̃rec(d). Generalization error ϵg versus λ̃ = λ/d at α̃ = 0.5 (left) and α̃ = 5 (right). At low load, all curves retain a positive error. At high load, cross-entropy recovers the teacher for every d > 1, differently from the d = 1 case where error stays finite.

Figure 3. Spherical cross-entropy learning curves at infinite λ̃. Generalization error ϵg versus α̃ = P/(Nd) for different embedding dimensions, obtained by minimizing cross-entropy at finite λ and then taking λ̃ → ∞. Vertical dashed lines mark the exact-recovery thresholds α̃rec = d/(d− 1) for d > 1, Eq. (30). The black dashed curve shows the d → ∞ limit, with threshold α̃rec = 1.

Figure 8. The optimal strategy is to learn high variance vocabulary embeddings direction first, then weaker directions as more data is available. (top left) case d = 8, D = 128, (top right) case d = 16, D = 128, (bottom left) case d = 8, D = 16, (bottom right) case d = 16, D = 16. In all cases we observe that the normalized overlap q∗m increase monotonically with the corresponding λm. Therefore, even if the task is isotropic (learning an isotropic spherical teacher), the anisotropy of the vocabulary affects the geometry of the inference. Saddle-point from replica computation defines implicitly the relations q∗m(λm) that control how learning happens in each spectral direction m.

Figure 6. Learning curves of generalization error for vocabulary classification task. We compare the approximate Bayes-optimal analytical learning curves derived with the spectral anisotropic replica computation with real students trained minimizing cross-entropy loss without constraints on weights norm. The two minimization procedures are different in principle, but the fact that they are close imply that cross-entropy is able to find a solution with ϵg close to the optimal, similarly to [23, 41]. Both results are explicitly dependent on the extracted vocabulary Z, and therefore we generate 16 different random spherical vocabularies for each d,D couple and we obtain prediction and numerical curves by averaging the error over the same 16 vocabularies. A numerical simulation with increasing number of variables N would have the Bayes-optimal predictions increasingly becoming lower bounds for ϵg. We note that when d < D numerical results have higher ϵg then predictions as expected, while instead when d ≥ D some of the numerical points have lower ϵg. This is compatible with the fact that our computation is an approximation of the full d× d problem, that we expect to work best in the regime d < D.

Figure 7. Learning curves scale correctly by normalizing amount of data via α̃. (Left) D=16 case; we note that here d = 32 > D and in that case rZ saturates and the curves do not shift anymore when plotted against α, as occurs in Fig. 6. (Right) D=128; in this case all curves have d < D and therefore the problem remains full rank. We observe that, even if the curves are rescaled correctly, there is still a dependence on d,D due to the term HZ that depends explicitly on the vocabulary.

Figure 9. Schematic representation of the minimization of the potential. We show how the square distance to points (z, t̄) is minimised under the different constraints of SA and VA storage. Left panel: the minimisation for SA storage. For different points (full dots) in the z, t̄ half-plane, we show the projections (crosses) on the satisfability half-plane z > √ dκ, indicated in green, corresponding to the points h∗, t∗ that minimise the potential on the constraint set C = {h ∈ R, t ≥ 0 : h ≥ √ dκ}. Right panel: the minimisation for VA storage. Again, points in the z, t̄ plane (full symbols) are associated to the corresponding points h∗, t∗ that minimise the potential on the constraint set C = {h ∈ R, t ≥ 0 : h ≥ κefft} (crosses). In the blue region C = {h ∈ R, t ≥ 0 : − t κeff ≤ h ≤ κefft}, to minimise the potential each point is projected onto the line z = κefft. In the orange region (z < − t̄ κeff ), all points are projected to the origin.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of token embedding and vocabulary geometry relevant to LLM token prediction.
papers.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
papers.tldr: The token perceptron’s generalization depends strongly on embedding geometry: continuous embeddings permit exact teacher recovery, while finite vocabularies turn learning into inequality-based classification that prioritizes high-variance directions.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video-MemComp, a training-free and sensitivity-aware context management framework for memory-constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer-wise structural sensitivity via a first-order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre-RoPE safe zone with an attention-conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer-wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high-sensitivity layers. Video-MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full-cache and state-of-the-art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.
authors: Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
bullets: Targets memory bottlenecks and error accumulation in long-context streaming video understanding.
Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to separate local approximation error from layer-wise structural sensitivity.
Aggregates tokens in a pre-RoPE safe zone with attention-conserving logit bias to reduce geometric distortion.
Dynamically allocates KV-cache budgets using offline gradient priors and online context entropy.
Matches or exceeds full-cache and existing compression methods on MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema; Qwen2.5-VL-3B rises from 62.3% to 64.1% with over 90% KV-memory savings.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of our Video-MemComp Framework. Guided by Taylor expansion (top), we split global memory compression into two objectives. 1) Minimizing Local Approximation Error El (middle): Pre-RoPE Aggregation merges redundant tokens based on inter-frame filtering and intra-frame merging. Intra-layer KV Pruning selects key-value pairs using a dialogue-aware Proxy Query Qproxy. 2) Managing Structural Sensitivity Sl (bottom): A Tri-Hybrid Budget Allocation dynamically assigns the total memory budget Btotal using offline structural sensitivity, online information density, and uniform regularization to protect critical layers from aggressive pruning.

Figure 1 Our architecture. While standard Video-LLM models suffer from linear O(T ) memory growth, VideoMemComp maintains strictly O(1) memory via a Taylor-expansion-guided hybrid strategy, enabling efficient streaming video understanding. Specifically, we decompose the error via Taylor expansion into local approximation error El and layer-wise structural sensitivity Sl. To minimize El, we adopt Attention-Preserved Pre-RoPE Aggregation and Intralayer Sparsity-based KV pruning. Meanwhile, Sl is used to guide layer-wise budget allocation.

Figure 2 Performance on MLVU with Qwen2-VL-7B. Our method outperforms strong baselines across all memory budgets, and even surpasses the Full KV baseline at 6K, 12K, and 24K KV budgets, showing that Video-MemComp removes redundancy while preserving key semantics. See Section E.1 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 5 Accuracy-Memory trade-offs on Qwen2.5-VL-3B (VideoMME Long Video). Token Compression (Blue) excels in high-budget regimes, notably surpassing the dense baseline by mitigating attention dilution. Conversely, KV Compression (Orange) demonstrates robustness under strict memory constraints. Our Hybrid Method (Green) achieves the optimal Pareto frontier across all budgets, balancing redundancy removal with attention preservation. See E.4 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 6 Hyperparameter landscape of budget allocation. OVO-Bench accuracy is shown as a contour over uniform prior (λu) and structural sensitivity (λs); λe = 1 − λu − λs represents the dynamic entropy weight. The global optimum(star), revealing that a dominant structural prior combined with subtle dynamic adjustment yields superior performance compared to uniform allocation. See F.3 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 7 Joint Impact of Spatio-Temporal Compression Thresholds. The heatmap plots accuracy across varying Inter-frame (θinter) and Intra-frame (θintra) similarity thresholds. The landscape reveals a convex optimization zone, where the peak represents the optimal trade-off between aggressive redundancy filtering and semantic preservation. Notably, overly aggressive temporal pruning (low θinter) causes irreversible performance degradation. See F.4 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 4 Statistical Visualization on Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Layer-wise budget allocation (stacked bars) is shown under an average budget of 500 KV tokens per layer. Gradient Norm (Sl), Entropy (H), and Feature Magnitude (∥V ∥) are normalized for comparison. The strategy effectively assigns higher budgets to shallow layers, while more aggressively pruning deeper layers. See Appendix E.3 for details.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses streaming-video KV-cache and token compression for efficient MLLM inference.
papers.title: Video-MemComp: Taylor-Guided Sensitivity-Aware Memory Management for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Video-MemComp is a training-free method that compresses streaming-video KV memory by modeling sensitivity and approximation error, achieving over 90% memory savings with improved accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

papers.abstract: Hospitals regularly buy software that clinicians and patients depend on. Because these purchases are costly, hard to reverse and can affect patient care, buyers look for evidence of which peer institutions already use a product and which systems it connects to. This evidence is public but scattered across vendor websites, press releases and third-party pages. Language-model agents can now collect it at low cost, but the correctness of the extracted claims is difficult to establish, and a wrongly listed customer can mislead buyers and misrepresent an organisation. We present a pipeline that builds a knowledge graph of customer and integration relations from the open web under one rule: every edge must be supported by a verbatim quote from its source page. Pages come from a deterministic crawl of each vendor's site and a budgeted ReAct agent that searches the rest of the web. A permissive extractor proposes relations with quotes, and a layered grounding stage decides which to keep, using a referent step that reads the whole page when a quote names only one side, deterministic checks, and a panel of five model calls voting on nine criteria. On 61 vendors, the pipeline reaches 0.94 precision and 0.71 recall against a page-level key covering the 6,428 candidate relations proposed by its extractor, whose verdicts were drafted by one model and re-checked with a second. Against the golden reference, the marketplace's own curated list, it scores lower, but 89% of the relations it keeps that the reference lacks are stated on a page. A confidence score built from the panel's votes keeps more correct relations than the fixed rule at the same precision, and reaches 0.90 precision at 0.90 recall. We also discuss how narrow, bounded model calls, string-matched evidence and voting address long-context degradation and run-to-run variance.
authors: Juan Felipe Duran, Arthur Tobler, Martin Valli\`eres
bullets: Addresses the risk of misleading buyers when software customer and integration claims are extracted from scattered public web sources.
Uses deterministic vendor-site crawling plus a budgeted ReAct web-search agent to find pages and a permissive extractor to propose quoted relations.
A layered grounding process verifies quotes with whole-page referent checks, deterministic rules, and five-model voting across nine criteria.
Across 61 vendors, the fixed rule achieves 0.94 precision and 0.71 recall against a page-level reference; a confidence score reaches 0.90 precision at 0.90 recall.
The approach is scoped to open-web evidence and discusses bounded model calls, string-matched quotes, and voting as safeguards against context and variance issues.

papers.selection_reason: Uses language-model agents to build a quote-grounded knowledge graph, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Every Edge Needs a Quote: Building a Quote-Grounded Knowledge Graph of Healthcare Software Adoption with Language-Model Agents
papers.tldr: A quote-grounded language-model pipeline builds a healthcare software adoption and integration graph, achieving high precision by retaining only relations supported by source-page evidence.

papers.abstract: AI representation is emerging in digital democracy, assisting in voter emulation and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) behave differently depending on the model, the prompt context, and the voter information they receive, representing some groups more accurately than others and potentially making the emulation unfair to certain groups. We investigate demographic biases in LLM-emulated electorates: how accurately LLMs represent individual votes, whether some voter groups are represented more accurately than others, and whether AI alignment can reduce these disparities without sacrificing overall accuracy. Using three U.S. presidential elections, we compare a closed-source and an open-source LLM across voters' demographic features and test AI alignment strategies toward fairer voter representation. Removing gender from the voter profile reduces the largest group error of the models by 22-42%, and removing education reduces it by 64%, whereas removing self-reported race increases the mean group error by over 40%, all without lowering accuracy. Common alignment strategies, such as repeated queries or fairness instructions, do not reduce these errors and can double them.
authors: Yi Qi, Srijoni Majumdar, Evangelos Pournaras
bullets: The study examines whether LLMs accurately emulate individual votes and whether accuracy differs across demographic groups.
It compares one closed-source and one open-source LLM across three U.S. presidential elections.
Removing gender or education from voter profiles reduces the largest group errors, while removing self-reported race increases mean group error.
These attribute-removal strategies do not lower overall accuracy.
Repeated queries and fairness instructions fail to reduce errors and can substantially increase them.

papers.abstract: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.

papers.abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.
authors: Yves Delley, John Coller, Zachary Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun W. Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi B. Seshadri, Tanner Clary, Sandy Klemm, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic, Annalisa Pawlosky

papers.abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.
authors: Navyansh Mahla, Sashank Vandrangi
bullets: Targets fragmented or conflated entities and retrieval errors caused by relying on initial similarity scores alone.
Uses cautious indexing with type-label reconciliation and tiered entity resolution.
Combines entity/triple retrieval with a bounded local graph and query-conditioned, receiver-normalized diffusion.
Preserves direct evidence while recovering missed connections through seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization.
On MemoryAgentBench, reaches 55.1 average accuracy—5.4 points above the strongest retrieval-based baseline—with sub-$0.001 mean synthesis cost on four reported columns.

papers.abstract: We study strongly adaptive regret for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, a setting that evaluates a learner's performance over arbitrary sub-intervals. This framework captures complex sequential decision-making problems where both the environment and the cost of switching decisions fluctuate over time. We propose a novel algorithm which, for any interval $[a,b] \subseteq [T]$, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(\|g_t\|^2+\lambda_t\|g_t\|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $\lambda_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round $t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of this development, we further establish the first strongly-adaptive guarantees under delayed feedback. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.
authors: Andrew Jacobsen, Emmanuel Esposito, Hao Qiu, Mengxiao Zhang
bullets: Addresses interval-wise performance in OCO when switching costs vary over time.

papers.abstract: Generating editable 3D urban scenes from a single image requires detailed building assets with a coherent spatial arrangement. Occlusion and perspective ambiguity make it difficult to infer complete building geometry together with consistent relative scales and positions. We present CityLift, a framework that generates individual textured building meshes from an urban image by coupling scene-level spatial modeling with building-level synthesis. CityLift first learns building shape and placement jointly through coupled scene and instance streams, producing coarse sparse structures in a common coordinate system. We then introduce generative spatial inheritance, which maps each building's coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned 3D feature field into a local volume to guide a flow model that generates finer structure. The same coordinate mapping places the generated meshes back into the scene, preserving their spatial relationship to the scaffold. To address the scarcity of urban data pairing scene images with individual 3D buildings, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic scenes with instance masks, building meshes, and placement annotations. Experiments on CityLift-5K and scene blocks from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved building geometry and scene composition. The project page is available at https://ranhaogong.github.io/CityLift/.
authors: Haoran Gong, Jie Feng, Chenxu Wang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and perspective ambiguity in reconstructing complete buildings with consistent scales and positions.
Uses coupled scene- and instance-level streams to produce coarse building shapes and placements in a shared coordinate system.
Introduces generative spatial inheritance to guide flow-based refinement of detailed textured building meshes.
Builds CityLift-5K, a dataset of 4,997 synthetic scenes with masks, meshes, and placement annotations.
Experiments on CityLift-5K and UrbanScene3D scene blocks show improved building geometry and scene composition.

(a) A shared scene–instance generator predicts coarse occupancy in a common scene frame, implicitly modeling building placement, scale, and geometry. (b) A scaffold-derived coordinate map Ti deterministically resamples occupancy and contextual features Fi into each building’s local volume, forming the aligned condition Ai. (c) Conditioned on Ai and building image features ei, a local flow model regenerates finer sparse structures from noise. papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology-guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen's $\kappa$ scores of 0.640--0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human--human agreement range of 0.616--0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology-grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96\% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available https://github.com/aayushacharya/climatekg.
authors: Aayush Acharya, Qi Zhang, Eduard Dragut, Longin Jan Latecki

Uses specialized agents for document understanding, extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking.

papers.abstract: Text-enhanced visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) exploits textual descriptions to compensate for appearance cues that are weak or unavailable under infrared imaging. Existing methods construct compensation from differences between modality-oriented textual representations, implicitly assuming that textual differences are visually complementary. We revisit this assumption through semantic superposition and show that dense textual residuals may entangle useful appearance variations with redundant, making direct residual fusion unreliable. We propose Superposition-Aware Residual Calibration, which transforms dense textual differences into selective and visually grounded complements. Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning represents modality-oriented text embeddings as sparse activation strengths over a shared dictionary, selects positive strength differences, and suppresses both dictionary-level overlap and activation-weighted interference to reconstruct a compact, selectively controlled residual. Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration further calibrates the residual against identity-specific RGB-IR visual discrepancies, encouraging retained semantics to provide meaningful compensation while preserving the residual structure. Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show that SARC consistently improves the VI-ReID backbone and remains competitive with text-assisted methods. Mechanism analyses show that SARC produces more concentrated textual variations, reduces dictionary-level feature interference, and improves residual-visual-complement alignment for most samples. These results demonstrate that effective cross-modal compensation requires textual residuals to be selectively represented and explicitly calibrated, rather than directly treated as visual complements. Code and implementation details will be released upon publication.
authors: Xiaoyang Li, Mingming Lu, Wei Zhou, Hao Li, Canhui Zhang
bullets: Dense differences between modality-specific text representations can mix useful appearance cues with redundant or interfering semantics.
Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning selects informative residual differences over a shared dictionary while suppressing overlap and activation-weighted interference.
Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration aligns retained textual semantics with identity-specific RGB–IR visual discrepancies.
Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show consistent backbone improvements and competitive performance among text-assisted methods.
Mechanism analyses report more concentrated textual variations, less feature interference, and better residual–visual-complement alignment for most samples.

Low-interference sparse residual learning selects strength variations between RGBand IR-oriented descriptions and reconstructs a textual residual. The calibrated residual supplements the infrared query representation for retrieval against the RGB gallery. The bottom panels illustrate semantic superposition, sparse feature-strength representation, and visual complement calibration.

Existing strategies inject a dense textual residual into the infrared representation, where overlapping semantic factors can produce mixed compensation. papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to learn from sequential tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting when historical data are no longer accessible. We study continual learning for high-dimensional sparse linear regression, where $\ell_1$ regularization creates a difficulty absent from continual ridge regression: that recursively reusing an $\ell_1$-penalized estimator can propagate earlier shrinkage and accumulate regularization bias across tasks. We propose score-preserving continual Lasso (SP-CL), which separates sparse estimation from state transmission by preserving the historical squared-loss score. Under squared loss, its cumulative estimator exactly recovers a full-history Lasso minimizer. When task coefficients coincide, it inherits the full-history sparse rate. For related task-specific coefficients, SP-CL uses a regularized current-task correction that leaves the transmitted state unchanged and attains the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition. We also derive Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions that distinguish historical information loss, task conflict, and current-task specialization, and validate the resulting regimes in simulation.
authors: Jingyi Guo, Runze Li, Lingzhou Xue
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting in high-dimensional sparse linear regression when historical data cannot be revisited.
Introduces score-preserving continual Lasso, separating sparse estimation from transmitted state.
Exactly recovers the full-history Lasso minimizer under squared loss.
Matches the full-history sparse rate for identical tasks and the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition.
Provides Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions and simulation-based validation of information loss, task conflict, and specialization regimes.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models can listen and speak at the same time, enabling natural, low-latency interaction. In counseling, however, these models often focus on the latest utterance and lose track of the seeker's underlying problem. We call this failure Stressor Blindness. We propose CounselPlex, a stressor-aware full-duplex framework that uses two operations. CounselPlex updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects this state into positions while listening. We also introduce RoPE Position Shift Augmentation (RPSA), which broadens positional coverage during training and improves performance at longer turn depths in our evaluation. LLM-judge evaluations show improved counseling quality and stressor grounding over strong baselines.
authors: Yeonju Kim, Bella Godiva, Yong Man Ro
bullets: Addresses “Stressor Blindness,” where models overfocus on the latest utterance and lose the underlying problem.
Updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects it while listening.
Uses RoPE Position Shift Augmentation to broaden positional coverage for deeper conversation turns.
LLM-judge evaluations report better counseling quality and stressor grounding than strong baselines.
The evaluation focuses on counseling quality and stressor grounding, with no quantitative results specified.

papers.selection_reason: Stressor state as persistent dialogue memory and RoPE position augmentation for long turn depth are transferable to LLM memory and long-context methods.
papers.title: CounselPlex: A Stressor-Aware Full-Duplex Counseling Model
papers.tldr: CounselPlex improves full-duplex counseling by maintaining and injecting an evolving representation of the seeker’s underlying stressor.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (AVLN) requires a UAV to reach a language-described target from partial egocentric observations while reasoning over large outdoor scenes. Existing approaches typically fuse view-centered RGB observations and globally anchored history maps as generic visual embeddings, leaving cross-modal spatial alignment to be learned from sparse navigation supervision. We present SP-Guide, a transformer- based goal-prediction framework that addresses this weakness of alignment through a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, an Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and a Goal Convergence Filter for terminal target refinement. Experiments implemented on the CityNav benchmark show that SP-Guide improves success rate over the representative baselines, with the largest gains on unseen environments. These results indicate that physically grounded spatial priors provide an effective inductive bias for robust AVLN.
authors: Haoxiang Tang, Dong Zhou, Shen Tan, Minxuan Jiang, Xitong Li
bullets: AVLN must guide UAVs to language-described targets from partial egocentric views in large outdoor scenes.
Existing methods often use generic visual embeddings, leaving spatial cross-modal alignment to sparse navigation supervision.
SP-Guide combines a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and Goal Convergence Filter.
On the CityNav benchmark, it improves success rate over representative baselines, with the largest gains in unseen environments.
The approach suggests spatial priors can provide a robust inductive bias for AVLN.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial priors for aerial vision-language navigation directly match the vision-language navigation subtopic.
papers.title: SP-Guide: Enhancing Aerial Vision-Language Navigation with Spatial Priors
papers.tldr: SP-Guide improves aerial vision-language navigation by using physically grounded spatial priors to better align visual observations with language instructions and refine terminal goals.

papers.abstract: Inspired by infants' ability to learn novel tasks by imitating others, in this work we evaluate to what extent Conditional Neural Processes can autonomously learn representations of actions that are informative about their underlying goal. We show that the addition of an attention mechanism in the hidden space fosters the emergence of robust goal representations early on in the observation of an action sequence, making it a promising model for a robotic self-supervised general learner.
authors: Marco Gabriele Fedozzi, Yukie Nagai, Francesco Rea, Alessandra Sciutti
bullets: Evaluates Conditional Neural Processes for discovering task goals from observed actions.
Targets representations that capture an action’s underlying goal rather than only its motion.
Adding hidden-space attention promotes robust goal representations early in action sequences.
Suggests potential for self-supervised, general-purpose learning in robots.

papers.title: Conditional Neural Processes for Self-Supervised Goal Discovery in Action Imitation
papers.tldr: Conditional Neural Processes with hidden-space attention can learn robust representations of an action’s goal early during observation, supporting self-supervised robotic learning.

papers.abstract: Quality-Aware Decoding (QAD) improves machine translation through test-time scaling, generating multiple candidate translations and selecting the final output with a quality-aware decoder. Usually the same candidate budget N is spent on every source sentence, assuming that all inputs require the same amount of search. We show that this assumption does not hold and that the quality gain obtained from additional candidates varies across sentences. We study search utility through three quantities: total scaling gain, how much quality a sentence can gain from a much larger candidate pool; marginal scaling gain, the expected gain from generating one additional batch of candidates; and the sampling saturation point, the candidate budget required to realize most of the total scaling gain. We investigate two sources of information for predicting these quantities: signals available before candidate-set expansion, and statistics computed from the candidate pool accumulated during search. We find that sentence-level signals correlate with total scaling gain but are less informative about the sampling saturation point. In contrast, properties of the current candidate pool provide useful signals of marginal scaling gain. Finally, we show that these signals can identify sentences that obtain larger gains when additional search is selectively applied.
authors: Javier Garcia Gilabert, Rico Sennrich, Andr\'e F. T. Martins
bullets: Quality-aware decoding does not benefit equally from the same candidate budget on every input.
The study defines total scaling gain, marginal scaling gain, and the sampling saturation point to characterize search utility.
Pre-expansion sentence-level signals predict potential total gain but are weaker for predicting when search will saturate.
Statistics from candidates accumulated during search provide useful estimates of marginal gain.
These signals support selectively applying additional search to sentences likely to benefit most.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive allocation of test-time search budget for MT offers transferable efficiency insights for inference-time compute reduction.
papers.title: When is more search useful? An Empirical Study of Search Utility in Quality-Aware Decoding for Machine Translation
papers.tldr: Search benefits vary by sentence, and candidate-pool signals can help allocate extra translation search where it is most useful.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text classification tasks, where they not only output class predictions but also generate explanations that highlight the tokens deemed most relevant for reaching the predicted label. Yet it remains unclear whether these highlighted elements are behaviorally consistent with the model's own predictions under targeted interventions, which we refer to as functional auto-consistency. While much of the literature evaluates the textual plausibility of such explanations, few studies assess their functional consistency with the model's actual behavior. In this work, we propose an experimental framework based on the principle of auto-consistency: if a model identifies certain tokens as decisive, then isolating, removing, or semantically inverting them should produce systematic and interpretable changes in its predictions. We operationalize this evaluation through sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics, and conduct experiments on IMDB and Steam reviews across both closed-source (GPT-4o-mini) and open-source LLMs (Gemma3, Granite8B, DeepSeek). Results show that GPT-4o-mini follows the expected progression across all metrics, Gemma3 and Granite8B maintain coherence under sufficiency but lose consistency under more demanding interventions, while DeepSeek variants display structural deviations, either failing to preserve sufficiency or overreacting under comprehensiveness and counterfactuality. These findings show that explanation reliability varies across LLM families and scales, with smaller models displaying contradictions and larger ones exhibiting over-sensitivity. By combining sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality, our approach provides a systematic methodology for assessing the functional consistency of LLM self-explanations.
authors: Alisson Rosa Pereira, Bruno Iochins Grisci
bullets: Tests explanations through targeted interventions: retaining, removing, or semantically reversing highlighted tokens.
Introduces a combined evaluation using sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics.
Evaluates GPT-4o-mini, Gemma3, Granite8B, and DeepSeek variants on IMDB and Steam reviews.
GPT-4o-mini shows the expected behavior across all metrics; other models exhibit inconsistencies or over-sensitivity.
Findings suggest explanation reliability differs across LLM families and model scales.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an evaluation framework for functional consistency of LLM self-explanations, relevant to LLM reasoning and interpretability.
papers.title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency
papers.tldr: The study evaluates whether LLM-highlighted evidence actually drives their predictions, finding substantial variation in functional consistency across models and interventions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read images through visual tokens, and under the small per-image budgets that efficient deployment requires, the fine text of documents, charts and infographics becomes illegible. Zooming in recovers the evidence, but the region must be chosen before the model answers. We find that MLLMs know where the evidence is, but not in a form that can be read before they answer: the answer tokens localize it from the middle layers on, whereas the attention available before answering does so only in the top layers, at a depth that varies across models, and diffusely. Supervising the pre-answer attention to point degrades reading, and the benefit of zooming is governed by each image's information gap. Building on these findings, we introduce ours, which lets an MLLM look where its answer would. A dedicated look token, processed in a single prefill and kept out of the answering pass, learns in hindsight to attend as the model's own correct answers do, extracting this knowledge into a concentrated pointer before any answer exists. Its hidden state then selects how to look, from no zoom to crops, square windows, windows that adapt to the pointer and foveated warps, supervised by the counterfactual outcome of every view. ours needs no box annotations, per-model layer search, external localizers or generation before the answer. On Qwen3-VL at three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it surpasses the strongest baseline by 4.8-9.1 points at 98 visual tokens per view and attention-guided zooming by 11.1-17.0 points, while running faster than attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
authors: Zhensheng Hu, Guanglong Xu, Guanqiang Hu
bullets: Small visual-token budgets make fine text in documents, charts, and infographics difficult to read.
Answer tokens localize relevant evidence earlier and more clearly than pre-answer attention, whose useful depth varies by model.
OURS uses a dedicated look token trained from correct-answer attention to produce a concentrated pointer before answering.
The pointer selects among no zoom, crops, adaptive windows, square windows, and foveated warps using counterfactual view outcomes.

On Qwen3-VL across three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it improves over the strongest baseline by 4.8–9.1 points and attention-guided zooming by 11.1–17.0 points at 98 visual tokens per view, while running faster than both attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of LookZoom. (1) A dedicated <look> token is appended to the prompt and processed in a single prefill on the low-resolution view v. Its attention to the image tokens tells where to look, and its hidden state tells how to look. (2) The selected view transform is applied to the full-resolution image and re-encoded within the same per-view budget. (3) The reader answers from the low-resolution view and the selected view; the <look> token never enters this pass. Training: the <look> attention is distilled from the answer-time attention of the model’s own correct rollouts (hindsight distillation), the action head is supervised by the counterfactual outcomes of every view, and the reader is adapted with GRPO.

Figure 5. Qualitative results (Qwen3-VL-4B, 196 tokens). Top: input with the window selected by LookZoom (red). Middle: the zoomed view as the model reads it, re-encoded within the budget. Bottom: answers (green: correct, red: wrong). The selected views make units, numbers and brand names legible that the single view misreads.

Figure 1. The answer knows where to look (Qwen3-VL-4B, 196 visual tokens, V-CoT-Doc). (b) Before answering, the attention of the model’s middle layers barely touches the evidence (green box). (c) With the correct answer teacher-forced, the same layers attend to the evidence, but only once the answer is known. (d) Our <look> token concentrates on the evidence in a single prefill, and (e) the view it selects makes the value legible. Numbers give the fraction of attention inside the evidence box.

Figure 3. The information gap governs the value of looking again. Accuracy gain of a zoomed view (a 0.7 crop placed by the pre-answer attention of the base model) over the single view, against the information gap ρ (native over budget pixels). (a) Quintiles of ρ over 9,200 image–budget pairs per model (2,300 questions, 4 budgets). (b) Per benchmark (4B): the same images at budgets from 784 to 98 tokens.

Figure 2. Where the model looks before and while answering (V-CoT-Doc, 196 tokens). In the middle layers, the attention before answering places little mass on the evidence, while the attention of the answer tokens already localizes it. Before answering, comparable localization appears only in the top layers (best band of four layers per model). Our <look> token, read from the middle layers, concentrates the most mass on the evidence before any answer is produced.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a mechanism for MLLMs to intelligently zoom into images before answering, optimizing visual token usage. This addresses spatial intelligence (understanding where to look) and efficient AI (token budget management).
papers.title: The Answer Knows Where to Look: Zooming before MLLMs Answer under Visual-Token Budgets
papers.tldr: OURS lets MLLMs identify where answer-critical visual evidence lies before answering, enabling effective zooming under tight visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: We introduce SemGeo-Gen, an unsupervised method for generating approximate cross-instance semantic-geometric supervision from weakly aligned 3D object collections. Our goal is not to recover exact point-level correspondences, which are often ambiguous across different instances and would require expensive, impractical manual supervision at scale. Instead, we automatically produce approximate correspondences that are semantically meaningful, geometrically consistent, and diverse enough to train modern correspondence models. Given only coarse category-level rotation alignment, SemGeo-Gen lifts multi-view DINOv2 features to 3D, aligns object instances using continuous piecewise-affine registration, and prunes candidate matches using semantic consistency. The resulting 3D correspondences can be projected into rendered views, yielding scalable 3D-3D, 3D-2D, and 2D-2D supervision without manual annotation. We validate the generated correspondences against sparse human annotations from KeypointNet, obtaining 93% PCK@0.10 and 97% PCK@0.15. More importantly, we show that using the generated correspondences for synthetic pretraining improves recent state-of-the-art semantic correspondence models on SPair-71k after fine-tuning on real data, with gains of up to 5 PCK@0.10 points. Together, these results indicate that approximate semantic-geometric supervision generated from 3D assets can improve real-image correspondence learning and serve as a scalable alternative to costly manual annotation. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/SemGeo-Gen/.
authors: Roy Amoyal, Shira Ifergane, Oren Freifeld
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity and cost of exact point-level correspondence annotation across object instances.

papers.abstract: Continual Wi-Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi-Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per-class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed-form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new- and earlier-domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six-order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank-32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge-node storage budgets.
authors: Chunchun Yang, Yang Cao, Zhitang Chen
bullets: Stores each earlier domain’s per-class feature means and covariances rather than raw CSI samples.
Restricts representation updates to affine transformations on a frozen basis, applying the same transport to stored statistics.
Combines supervised contrastive learning for new domains with a closed-form statistical loss and a Gaussian discriminant classifier.
Achieves low forgetting (at most 0.58 percentage points) across 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, matching or outperforming replay baselines in reported settings.
Rank-32 covariance factors reduce moment memory to 6.4% with at most 0.49 percentage points of accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: LLM inference is increasingly deployed as a core service for enterprise and interactive applications, but sovereignty, compliance, latency and resource-locality requirements can limit the suitability of centralised cloud deployments. Telco operators offer geographically distributed compute and network infrastructure for addressing these constraints. However, existing LLM serving frameworks are designed for tightly coupled data centres and provide limited support for coordinating geographically distributed and heterogeneous resources. We present InferSlice, a reference architecture for Service-Level Objective (SLO)-driven LLM inference over a telco infrastructure, integrating network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving and observability. Led by BT in collaboration with the University of Bristol and NVIDIA, and realised on the JOINER UK national-scale wide-area network (WAN), InferSlice is evaluated on service differentiation across tiers, elastic scale-out, client-edge bandwidth as a bottleneck, and the reach of tensor, pipeline, data parallelism, and prefill/decode disaggregation over the WAN. Our results show that, on a general-purpose telco network, tiers yield distinct latency-throughput regimes, and weight streaming shortens scale-out time. Replication is placement-insensitive but memory-bound; pipeline parallelism tolerates near- and mid-cross-site hops, while tensor parallelism and disaggregation fail beyond a single subnet hop. We share practical insights from operating SLO-driven inference on a telco network, lessons learned and open questions, and hope to encourage further research on distributed and heterogeneous LLM inference systems.
authors: Juan Parra-Ullauri, Anthony Chiu, Hari Madhukumar, Zhaozhou Wu, Anderson Bravalheri, Alex Healing, Andy Corston-Petrie, Dimitra Simeonidou, Nektaria Efthymiou
bullets: Addresses sovereignty, compliance, latency, and resource-locality constraints that limit centralized cloud inference.
Combines network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving, and observability for SLO-driven operation.
Evaluated on the JOINER UK wide-area network across service tiers, elastic scale-out, bandwidth bottlenecks, and distributed parallelism strategies.

Findings: service tiers create distinct latency-throughput regimes; weight streaming speeds scale-out; replication is memory-bound; pipeline parallelism tolerates near- and mid-site hops, while tensor parallelism and prefill/decode disaggregation require a single subnet hop.
Provides operational insights, lessons learned, and open questions for distributed LLM inference over telco networks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. InferSlice reference architecture. Geographically distributed edge Points of Presence (PoPs) provide GPU-accelerated compute interconnected over a WAN, and are virtualised and containerised to give isolated, portable execution environments. Network slicing maps each service tier (Free, Standard, Premium) to its own logical network with differentiated QoS, while compute orchestration assigns each tier a guaranteed share of GPU and CPU capacity. A distributed serving layer expresses workloads as models and replicas and scales them within each tier’s resource envelope, and an inference optimisation layer manages model execution on the accelerator, including batching and KV-cache management. A control plane for planning, traffic forecasting, semantic routing, and prompt and KV-cache reuse configures these layers against per-tier SLOs, using cross-layer telemetry from the observability layer.

papers.title: InferSlice: A Reference Architecture for SLO-driven LLM Inference over a Telco Wide-Area Network

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the non-blank predictor of a factorized transducer on target-domain text improves recognition on that domain but degrades performance on the source domain. A single interpolation weight between base and adapted predictors cannot resolve this: the adapted predictor helps at some prefixes and hurts at others, often within one utterance. We propose conservative residual routing: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, and a 16k-parameter gate decides at each prefix how much of it to admit. Closing the gate reproduces the base exactly. On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retains essentially all of the text-only gain on two held-out domains (19.89 to 16.74, 20.91 to 16.21 WER) while leaving source-domain WER unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone costs 1.08 WER. Routing needs no per-domain tuning on target-domain audio. Analysis reveals the gate does not behave as a simple domain-level switch: it modulates intervention through the disagreement between the two predictors, suppressing it in-domain and amplifying it out-of-domain.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: Text-only fine-tuning improves target-domain recognition but can harm the source domain, and a single interpolation weight cannot resolve prefix-level conflicts.
The method treats the adapted predictor as a residual correction to the base predictor.
A 16k-parameter gate dynamically controls how much correction to apply at each prefix; closing it exactly recovers the base model.

On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retained target-domain gains while leaving source-domain WER essentially unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone degraded performance by 1.08 WER.
The gate responds to predictor disagreement rather than acting as a simple domain switch, suppressing corrections in-domain and amplifying them out-of-domain.

The gate reads the same signal as specialization on target-like data and as risk on source-like data.
