papers.selection_reason: Proposes residual expert routing for domain adaptation in ASR, allowing the model to dynamically switch between base and adapted predictors based on context.
papers.title: Residual Expert Routing for Text-Only Domain Adaptation of Factorized Transducer ASR
papers.tldr: A small prefix-level gate safely routes text-only domain-adaptation corrections, preserving source-domain ASR while retaining target-domain gains.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editing models exhibit pronounced sample-specific performance variation: different models can produce substantially different results for the same source image and editing instruction, and the best-performing model often varies across requests. These models also differ substantially in inference latency, making fixed-model deployment inefficient. We therefore study image editing model routing, which dynamically selects an editor from a candidate pool given an input image and editing instruction. We introduce EditJev, a System One routing model that directly predicts sample-level preference scores over candidate image editing models in a single forward pass. A lightweight preference head on a vision-language backbone produces a fixed-dimensional score vector without autoregressive model-name generation or response parsing. To train EditJev, we construct pairwise preferences from offline candidate outputs and optimize a pairwise ranking objective to learn relative model suitability. At inference time, EditJev combines the predicted preference scores with model-level speed scores to balance editing quality and generation latency. Experiments on ImgEdit and GEdit-En show that EditJev improves aggregate quality over the strongest fixed editor, from 4.540 to 4.592 and from 8.194 to 8.255, respectively, while reducing estimated end-to-end latency by 60.8% and 31.7%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of direct, structured model routing for efficient image editing.
authors: Zhile Guan, Xu Jiang, Yule Duan, Gongbo Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Xiao Chen, Jian Zhang
bullets: Image editing models vary significantly in performance across individual images and instructions, and also differ in inference speed.
EditJev predicts preference scores for all candidate editors in one forward pass using a vision-language backbone with a lightweight preference head.
It learns relative model suitability from pairwise preferences derived from offline candidate outputs.
Routing combines predicted quality preferences with model speed scores to balance editing quality and latency.
On ImgEdit and GEdit-En, EditJev improves aggregate quality while reducing estimated end-to-end latency by 60.8% and 31.7%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities, where navigation must adapt to changing operating conditions. Sensor observations reveal physical obstacles, but do not by themselves specify temporary access rules, route preferences, or exceptions known to operators. This paper presents a natural-language policy interface that brings this knowledge into ROS 2 Nav2. A local large language model converts instructions into JSON policies specifying destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions. Deterministic checks govern mission acceptance, and three costmap adapters project accepted policies into the existing navigation stack without changing its planner or controller. On 150 researcher-authored English commands, four local models produce 107-142 correct accepted policies, compared with 44 for a rule-based parser, with 3-20 incorrect acceptances per model. Fault injection records rejection of eight endpoint/JSON faults and 29 validator-stage faults. Navigation experiments use correct task policies to evaluate keepouts, zone costs, person-dependent regions, and event-conditioned passage in simulation and on a TurtleBot3. For Tasks 1-3, mean travel times are 18.4-24.5% lower in simulation and 23.1-35.0% lower on the physical testbed than with the baseline lacking those policies. A native KeepoutFilter comparison and two-robot demonstrations examine basic keepout behavior and shared policy projection. The interface connects operator instructions to explicit navigation policies while retaining Nav2's planning and control components.
authors: Jiyeong Chae, Hyunkyo Seo, Heonjae Lee, Kyung-Joon Park
bullets: Addresses the gap between sensor-detected obstacles and operator-defined access rules, route preferences, and exceptions.
A local language model generates JSON policies for destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions; deterministic validators accept or reject them.
Three costmap adapters project accepted policies into ROS 2 Nav2 while preserving its existing navigation stack.
Across 150 researcher-authored commands, models produced 107–142 correct accepted policies versus 44 for a rule-based parser, with some incorrect acceptances.
Simulation and TurtleBot3 tests showed lower mean travel times for policy-enabled tasks, while fault injection demonstrated rejection of multiple malformed or invalid inputs.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as reasoning components in modern software systems, yet a model that answers a logical query correctly can contradict itself when the same problem is restated in an equivalent form. Static benchmarks evaluate queries in isolation and therefore fail to expose such inconsistencies. To address this limitation, we present LGMT, an open-source tool that detects reasoning inconsistencies through metamorphic relations grounded in first-order logic. Given a source test case in premise-conclusion form, LGMT generates logically equivalent follow-up cases and checks whether the model's entailment predictions agree across the pair, without ground-truth labels. The tool provides 20 built-in metamorphic relations, supports custom ones verified by the Z3 theorem prover, and runs from a CLI or a web studio, including an offline mock mode requiring no API key. Across six widely used LLMs on a bundled benchmark of 3,091 metamorphic groups, LGMT reveals inconsistency rates ranging from 20.84% to 29.44%. LGMT is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MaxwelsDonc/lgmt-tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/gou4opptu1U.
authors: Zenghui Zhou, Xiaoke Fang, Zheng Zheng
bullets: Addresses a gap in static benchmarks, which may miss contradictions across logically equivalent queries.
Uses first-order-logic metamorphic relations to generate equivalent follow-up premise–conclusion cases and compare entailment predictions without ground-truth labels.
Includes 20 built-in relations, supports Z3-verified custom relations, and offers CLI, web, and offline mock modes.
Evaluated six LLMs on 3,091 metamorphic groups, finding inconsistency rates of 20.84%–29.44%.
Open-source implementation is available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D semantic segmentation have significantly improved scene understanding in autonomous driving. However, existing methods are typically developed under a closed-set assumption and evaluated under standard driving conditions, where all categories are known in advance. In real-world driving, autonomous vehicles inevitably encounter previously unseen objects, making closed-set perception insufficient for safe deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce DriveOSS, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first real-world multimodal dataset and benchmark specifically designed for 3D anomaly segmentation and open-set semantic segmentation. It contains 12,661 synchronized and annotated frames captured using six surround-view RGB cameras, a 128-beam LiDAR, and a GPS/IMU unit. The dataset comprises 52 real-world driving scenes collected under clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions and is organized into ID (in-distribution) and OOD (out-of-distribution) subsets. The ID scenes contain only known classes and are used for training, whereas the OOD scenes additionally contain unknown objects annotated as the outlier class and are used for validation and testing. Extensive experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems. The dataset, benchmark protocols, and code are available at https://github.com/chrisyan/DriveOSS.
authors: Zhiran Yan, Savankumar Bhanderi, Sourabh Lolge, Rui Song, Girdharbhai Paneliya, Shiva Agrawal, Gordon Elger
bullets: Addresses the safety gap caused by closed-set 3D perception systems that cannot recognize previously unseen objects.
Provides 12,661 synchronized, annotated frames from six RGB cameras, 128-beam LiDAR, and GPS/IMU sensors.
Covers 52 driving scenes across clear, nighttime, cloudy, rainy, and snowy conditions.
Separates known-class ID training scenes from OOD validation and test scenes containing annotated unknown objects.
Experiments show that unseen objects remain a major challenge for current 3D perception systems; data, protocols, and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion models have emerged as a promising non-autoregressive paradigm for text generation over continuous embedding spaces. Along the continuous trajectory, the residual token identity directly shapes the denoising objective. However, the geometric trajectory misaligns with temporal progression, triggering severe temporal compression. In this paper, we show that embedding norm decay causes Euclidean distance to yield spurious overtaking, indicating that token competition must be evaluated directionally. In this space, a candidate overtakes the source token only when the effective noise magnitude surpasses their semantic separation. We formalize these pairwise dynamics as the Competition Threshold Theory (CTT). Crucially, high-dimensional overtaking requires extreme noise levels, causing standard trajectories to concentrate identity decay into a narrow window near the noisy endpoint. To resolve this, we propose Semantic Retention Scheduling (SRS) to align time allocation with the progression of identity decay, and demonstrate that existing token identity metrics are fundamentally statistical aggregations of these pairwise crossings. Building on these theoretical insights, we introduce LLaCO, a generative framework powered by competition-aware semantic scheduling. LLaCO adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous representations via an embedding directional adapter and timestep-conditioned modulation. To operate within the directional space, LLaCO employs a spherical noising process formulated as a geodesic interpolation toward a mask-biased endpoint, eliminating norm decay while preserving accurate token competition. Guided by SRS, LLaCO reallocates the denoising trajectory proportionally to the logarithmic rank decay. Instantiated as an 8B model, LLaCO outperforms previous continuous diffusion baselines and rivals discrete diffusion models of comparable scale.
authors: Zijian Jia, Peixuan Zhang, Genying Li, Di Wu, Yujie Fu, Si Li, Boxin Shi, Shuchen Weng
bullets: Identifies embedding norm decay as the cause of misleading Euclidean token overtaking and severe temporal compression.
Introduces Competition Threshold Theory to characterize when candidate tokens overtake source tokens based on directional semantic separation and noise.
Proposes Semantic Retention Scheduling to allocate denoising time according to logarithmic token-identity rank decay.
Implements a spherical noising process with an embedding directional adapter and timestep-conditioned modulation.
An 8B LLaCO model outperforms prior continuous diffusion baselines and rivals similarly sized discrete diffusion models.

papers.abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery.
authors: Chahyon Ku, Erica Tevere, Georgios Georgakis, Rudra Mukherjee, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Addresses navigation in unfamiliar terrain by using semantic appearance as a proxy for physical traversability.
Scores each image pixel with a language-conditioned VLM prompt describing traversable terrain.
Projects scores onto the ground, adapts them with morphological operations, and plans a minimum-time trajectory incorporating obstacle clearance.
Requires only a camera, with no terrain annotations, task-specific training, or persistent map.
Evaluated on physical indoor and off-road rovers, simulated Mars and Moon rovers across 200 procedural terrains, and real planetary imagery.

papers.abstract: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.
authors: Alban Farchi, Marcin Chrust, Massimo Bonavita, Marc Bocquet, Wei Pan, Patrick Laloyaux
bullets: Targets state-dependent model-error corrections in ECMWF’s Integrated Forecasting System using a neural network trained through 4D-Var.
Estimates only neural-network parameters while using a precomputed atmospheric analysis, then extends this with random-order mini-batch assimilation windows.
Sequential online learning improves training-period forecasts but fails to generalize to unseen data.
The batched formulation consistently improves out-of-sample forecast skill; larger batches accelerate convergence and reduce update noise.
Corrections preserve realistic forecast variability rather than gaining skill through artificial smoothing.

papers.abstract: Large language models and agents have shown significant power in advanced physical research. In this paper, We introduce PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical-physics reasoning with 63 Reproduce and 43 Discover problems. Reproduce tests derivation of published results; Discover tests consequences of modified theoretical conditions. FormulaForest constructs the tasks with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics. Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21% to 68.25% on Reproduce and from 18.60% to 74.42% on closed-book Discover. With tools, four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments persist. Besides, our experimental results demonstrate the value of FormulaForest as synthetic data. On FrontierScience, a benchmark developed by OpenAI, it raises the accuracy of a Qwen-35B-A3B model from 61% to 72%.

papers.abstract: Camera-trap species classification is dominated by large models from well-resourced organisations, which often lack the species-level distinctions regional conservation needs, such as native red versus invasive grey squirrels in the UK. We ask whether open weights let a small team with a modest dataset and a single GPU take a real part in AI development. We fine-tuned the open DeepFaune classifier on 28 UK classes, paired it with the unmodified MegaDetector v6, and compared the resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.2 with DeepFaune v1.5.0 and SpeciesNet on 20,212 hand-verified MammalWeb citizen-science images, after removing sequences sharing any of 1,039 images with our training archive. DeepFaune-UK achieved a strict image-level accuracy of 88.8%, including empty frames, against 56.5% and 59.0% for the baselines, but at DeepFaune's coarser label resolution DeepFaune v1.5.0 was more accurate, though not significantly under contributor resampling (91.4% vs. 88.8%). As DeepFaune v1.5.0 uses a newer DINOv3-based classifier, we applied the identical recipe, without new data, to that classifier. The resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.3 reached 90.6% strict accuracy, narrowed the like-for-like gap to 0.8 points and reduced roe deer misclassified as fallow deer by 69%. On 1,850 images from the 26 contributors with no overlapping images, the three DeepFaune-based models did not differ significantly (90.5%, 90.6%, 89.9% like-for-like). Fine-tuning on 10% of the training crops (about 150 per class) gave out-of-distribution accuracy similar to using all of them, and a DINOv2 run on this subset took about 22 minutes with under 4 GB of GPU memory. Open weights thus make regional model development feasible for small teams, but the largest like-for-like gain came from a newer base model trained by others, so this democratisation depends on large actors continuing to release open weights, under licences that may change.
authors: Paul Fergus
bullets: A UK-specific model was fine-tuned for 28 classes, including native red and invasive grey squirrels, using an open DeepFaune classifier and unmodified MegaDetector.
DeepFaune-UK v1.2 reached 88.8% strict image-level accuracy, outperforming the reported baselines, but was less accurate at DeepFaune’s coarser label resolution.
Applying the same regional fine-tuning recipe to the newer DINOv3-based classifier produced 90.6% accuracy and reduced roe-deer/fallow-deer confusion by 69%.
Using only 10% of training crops produced similar out-of-distribution accuracy; one subset training run took about 22 minutes and under 4 GB of GPU memory.
The approach supports small-team regional model development, but its largest gain came from a newer model released by a larger organisation, with licensing remaining a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates efficient fine-tuning of open-weight camera-trap models for regional wildlife classification with modest data. This is a relevant case study in test-time adaptation and continual learning for embodied perception.
papers.title: Standing on Open Shoulders: Regional Fine-Tuning of Open-Weight Camera-Trap Models for UK Wildlife with Modest Data and Compute
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning open-weight camera-trap models with modest UK data and compute can deliver strong regional species classification, though progress still depends on access to newer open base models.

papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Yanis Labrak, Sergio Burdisso, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: SFT makes students inherit nearly all teacher transcription errors, while GRPO passes through far fewer.
GRPO improves relative WER over SFT by 29.3%–56.2% in banking-domain adaptation using Whisper-generated labels.
The benefit holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains, and four languages.
On-policy rollouts rarely contain erroneous pseudo-label words, preserving useful group-relative reward signals.
Scope: results concern semi-supervised ASR adaptation with untranscribed audio and pseudo-label supervision.

Figure 1. Fraction of erroneous pseudo-label (PL) words that the student reproduces verbatim in its final output, as a function of the number of word errors in the utterance’s pseudo-label.

papers.selection_reason: Applies Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to semi-supervised ASR, using pseudo-labels as rewards to improve robustness against label noise.
papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.tldr: Using pseudo-labels as reward references rather than hard targets makes GRPO substantially more robust to noisy ASR supervision than SFT.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.
authors: Mario Hamon, Pierre Adorni, Minh-Tan Pham
bullets: Distills frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers using patch-level feature matching.
Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind and CROMA models improve over scale-matched released models and often reach the performance of larger ones.
TerraMind-Base distillation used approximately 0.5% of the reported cost of training an independent model.
TEDI combines TerraMind’s multispectral expertise with DINOv3’s high-resolution RGB features through separate patch embeddings and a shared Transformer trunk, without co-registered data.
TEDI-Large achieves the highest reported PANGAEA-9 single-model mean, while TEDI-Base offers a lower-parameter alternative with competitive performance.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates efficient feature distillation for geospatial foundation models, significantly reducing compute costs while maintaining or improving accuracy. This addresses both spatial intelligence (geospatial understanding) and efficient AI (distillation).
papers.title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
papers.tldr: Feature distillation efficiently repurposes geospatial foundation models into smaller, multimodal models that match or outperform larger pretrained counterparts at much lower cost.

papers.abstract: Real-time decoding of omnidirectional images is essential for immersive virtual reality (VR) experiences. Compared with conventional transform-based learned image compression (LIC), overfitted codecs offer lower decoding complexity by representing each image with a lightweight implicit neural representation (INR). However, existing approaches typically operate on the equirectangular projection (ERP), which introduces nonuniform spherical sampling and spatial distortion, leading to redundant sampling near the poles and latitude-dependent receptive fields. To address these limitations, we propose a spherical overfitted codec based on a multi-scale Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (HEALPix) representation, which enables equal-area sampling and efficient hierarchical modeling of spherical signals. Building on this representation, we develop a Spherical Inter-Scale Conditional entropy model that exploits spatial dependencies and cross-scale correlations among HEALPix latents to improve coding efficiency. We further introduce a Multi-Ring Spherical Convolution that aggregates neighboring pixels over a nearly uniform spherical receptive field across latitudes. Experiments on a public omnidirectional image dataset demonstrate BD-rate reductions of 16.3%, 26.5%, and 19.5% over VVC in terms of V-PSNR, V-MS-SSIM, and V-LPIPS, respectively. Our method also achieves a 13.1% BD-rate reduction over ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in terms of V-PSNR, while providing 2.6-3.6x faster decoding than the evaluated learned autoencoder codecs.
authors: Yulong Cheng, Youneng Bao, Junfeng Zhou, Mu Li, Jie Wen
bullets: Addresses ERP distortion and redundant polar sampling in omnidirectional image compression.
Uses multi-scale HEALPix representation with a spherical inter-scale conditional entropy model.
Introduces multi-ring spherical convolution for nearly uniform receptive fields across latitudes.
Reduces BD-rate versus VVC by 16.3% (V-PSNR), 26.5% (V-MS-SSIM), and 19.5% (V-LPIPS).
Achieves 13.1% lower BD-rate than ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in V-PSNR and 2.6–3.6× faster decoding than evaluated learned autoencoders.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture. Each panorama is represented by hierarchical latent grids {Yi}Ni=0 on the HEALPix sphere (Nside ∈ {2, 4, . . . , 256}), which are quantized and fitted to the image. Top: the SISC entropy model fφ predicts the Laplace parameters of each latent from same-level and ancestor contexts (Fig. 3) for the arithmetic coder. Bottom: the spherical upsampler fγ merges the levels from coarse to fine, and the multi-ring synthesis network fθ (Fig. 4) reconstructs the sphere. The latents and the decoder weights are trained with SOAP on D+ λRlatent/(HW ); the weight rate R(φ, γ, θ) of Eq. (12) is not differentiated and is handled by a rate–distortion search over the weight quantization at the end of fitting (Sec. III-E).

Fig. 3. Spherical Inter-Scale Conditional (SISC) Entropy Model. Left: for a latent Ŷi,j (red dot), the intra-scale context collects its K nearest decoded neighbors (pink), and the inter-scale context is obtained by Lineari from its decoded ancestors on the coarser levels (colored dots). Right: the shared predictor fφ maps the concatenated contexts to the Laplace parameters (Eq. (5)).

In both rows, the rate follows the image structure rather than the latitude. Without the inter-scale context, the finest level costs 46% more (0.026 → 0.038 bpp), and the total rate rises by 29% (0.127 → 0.164 bpp) at a similar V-PSNR.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an implicit neural compression scheme for omnidirectional images using HEALPix representation. This contributes to 3D perception and representation techniques, specifically for spherical geometry.
papers.title: HEALPix-Based Implicit Neural Compression of Omnidirectional Images
papers.tldr: A HEALPix-based implicit neural codec improves omnidirectional image compression efficiency and decoding speed by modeling spherical signals with uniform sampling and cross-scale dependencies.

papers.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.
authors: Oleg Sautenkov, Yasheerah Yaqoot, Muhammad Ahsan Mustafa, Grigorii Kalinin, Chih-Yung Wen, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: A ground-station agent converts a one-sentence mission description into per-UAV routes and executable code.
The system grounds targets on aerial maps, balances route lengths across UAVs, and assigns onboard agents to verify incidents.
In simulation, it detected incidents in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%) across four incident types and three foundation models.
Scaling from one to five UAVs followed an Amdahl-type pattern, with speedup capped at 1.52× and the second UAV providing half of the attainable saving.
False alarms remain a concern, and a user study is still needed to evaluate operator supervision.

Figure 4: One example mission per scenario (𝑁 = 3). Insets show the reported frame with the highest score; dashed lines are the return legs to the base station. The collision and oil-spill examples use the refined verifier questions.

papers.selection_reason: Language-driven mission specification, VLM grounding, and per-UAV route generation fit embodied vision-language navigation and planning.
papers.title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: UAV-SwarmAgent uses natural-language mission commands, vision-language reasoning, and code-generated routes to coordinate scalable multi-UAV reconnaissance.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
authors: I-tak Ieong, Hao Tang
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.

papers.selection_reason: The paper presents HGWM, a hierarchical system for zero-shot object navigation that integrates LLM-generated priors with persistent spatial-semantic memory. It uses a graph-matching approach to combine visual observations with language instructions, directly fitting the Vision-Language Navigation and Robot Navigation subtopics, and utilizes persistent memory for the Embodied Memory subtopic.
papers.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
papers.tldr: HGWM improves zero-shot object navigation by combining an LLM-derived room prior with persistent graph-based spatial-semantic memory and hierarchical graph matching.

papers.abstract: These lecture notes provide an introduction to optimization, optimal control, and reinforcement learning for robotics, emphasizing their mathematical connections and practical relevance. They present established material compiled and edited by Yonghyeon Lee, rather than new research results. The notes were developed through a human and AI collaborative writing process, with AI assistance in drafting, organizing, and refining the exposition. This first version is a preliminary collection of notes, not yet a fully developed textbook, and currently contains no figures or graphs. The notes may be revised, corrected, and expanded in future versions.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.
authors: Yuan Bi, Fangxu Han, Ye Su, Yiping Zhou, Zhongliang Jiang, Nassir Navab

papers.abstract: Single-stage fine-tuning is pervasive, yet catastrophic forgetting persists when the source pre-training data is inaccessible. Data weighting affords a natural lever to modulate sample influence. Yet existing weighting methods lack a principled mechanism to explicitly arbitrate knowledge retention against new-task adaptation, and provide no unified differentiable objective to accommodate auxiliary signals such as sample diversity and sample characteristics. This is because current schemes privilege one goal over the other, and no explicit gradient-compatible encoding exists for such signals. To address this, we propose DRIVE, a principled and efficient weight assignment framework. It derives per-sample weights via a unified differentiable objective where three coupled signals co-evolve: Shapley additivity splits contribution into anti-forgetting and adaptation components, which are reshaped by a covariance-based diversity term and stabilized by a sample-characteristic prior. Far from a mere combination, this yields an end-to-end gradient-based scheme balancing stability against plasticity. Theoretically, we prove that DRIVE enjoys superior stability-plasticity guarantees over existing weighting schemes and enhances parameter estimation robustness. Empirically, it attains superior overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness. Code at https://github.com/luciabcd/DRIVE.
authors: Qing Liu, Xinrui Chen, Yi Du, Ou Wu, Weiyao Zhu
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when source pre-training data is unavailable.

Theoretical analysis establishes stability–plasticity guarantees and improved parameter-estimation robustness.
Experiments report better overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness.

papers.abstract: People differ in how they perceive music, what associations they make with it, what they like about it, and how they respond to it. Computational models intended to simulate people in environments that include music should account for these differences. Although LLMs have been shown to reproduce aspects of human behavior, whether audio-language models (ALMs) can reproduce a specific person's responses to textual and musical stimuli remains underexplored. We introduce MusicTwins, a framework that combines persona summaries, personal memory, and post-training to generate person-specific responses. We construct persona representations from human writings, capturing background, views, personality, writing style, and a musical profile, and post-train Audio Flamingo Next through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Evaluation on ten held-out personas shows notable improvements for Audio Flamingo Next in persona fidelity, including personality, writing style, and responses to music, supporting MusicTwins as a foundation for training audio-language models to listen like their persona.

papers.abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang

Across 37 tasks, deeper inference improves macro-average performance by 3.01 points; the middle budget captures 89% of the gain with half the extra layer executions, while gains persist in math and code.

papers.abstract: Deploying Vision-Language Models for video anomaly detection confronts a fundamental constraint. Their semantic reasoning demands computational budgets incompatible with the scale of real-world video streams. We present Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF), a framework that achieves efficient zero-shot anomaly detection through three key innovations. First, we introduce a dual-signal adaptive sampler operating in semantic embedding space: a delta signal captures sudden events via frame-to-frame cosine distance, while a drift signal detects static and gradual anomalies through deviation from rolling temporal context. Their OR-gated combination with adaptive EMA-based thresholding provides comprehensive anomaly coverage without training data. Second, we propose a threshold-gated cascaded architecture where lightweight frame-level scoring precedes expensive video-level temporal analysis, invoking it only when confidence warrants additional context. Third, we design a signal-aware weighted fusion mechanism that dynamically adapts score combination based on which signal triggered frame selection. Across four benchmarks, SAAF delivers competitive accuracy at substantially lower cost. Among training-free zero-shot methods, SAAF sets a new state of the art on XD-Violence (92.07%), MSAD (86.70%), and ShanghaiTech (80.54%) AUC-ROC, with XD-Violence and MSAD also surpassing supervised baselines. SAAF sustains 44.95, 48.61, and 41.06 FPS on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, and MSAD, a 2.43$\times$, 2.63$\times$, and 2.22$\times$ throughput improvement over the prior best zero-shot method. Code: https://github.com/kdawoud91/SAAF
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Uses frame-to-frame semantic changes (delta) and temporal-context deviations (drift) to detect sudden, static, and gradual anomalies without training data.
Employs EMA-based adaptive thresholds and OR-gated sampling for broad anomaly coverage.
Cascades lightweight frame scoring before expensive video-level analysis, reducing unnecessary computation.
Dynamically fuses scores according to the signal that triggered frame selection.
Achieves competitive accuracy across four benchmarks and reports 2.22×–2.63× throughput gains over the prior best zero-shot method on three datasets.

Stage 3 conditionally invokes video-level temporal analysis for high-scoring frames, combining frame and video scores via signal-aware weighted fusion. Stage 4 propagates and refines sparse anchor scores to produce dense frame-level predictions.

papers.abstract: Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.
authors: Shengchao Chen, Ting Shu, Sufen Ren
bullets: Evaluates 26 tasks across six stages, from geometry perception and physics understanding to inverse-design decisions and code generation.
Built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples spanning 18 structurally diverse photonic crystal fiber families.
Tests both individual VLM capabilities and multi-agent systems across the full perception-to-design pipeline.
Models recognize fiber geometry with moderate success but often fail to convert visual understanding into physics-aware actions.
Sequential agent pipelines suffer from compounded upstream errors, indicating that physical grounding—not just scaling or agent chaining—is needed.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PCFBench overview. PCFBench formulates PCF inverse design as a multi-stage, multimodal reasoning problem, where complementary visual inputs, geometric cross-sections and mode fields, are processed through a sequential pipeline of perception, understanding, reasoning, and design. The benchmark comprises 26 tasks organized into a six-dimensional hierarchy spanning geometry perception, physics understanding, text generation, multi-modal reasoning, inverse-design decisions, and code generation, arranged along an increasing difficulty gradient that mirrors real-world workflows. Built on over 220K multimodal samples with human expert annotations across 18 fiber families, PCFBench supports both single-model and multi-agent evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) by enabling fine-grained emotion understanding through reasoning over multimodal evidence. However, they still exhibit systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with highly overlapping multimodal cues. Existing approaches typically address these errors through global parameter adaptation, making confusion correction costly and inflexible. We instead observe that emotion confusion is highly localized and therefore better addressed through reusable pair-specific expertise. Building on this insight, we propose Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution (CASE), the first agent-skill framework for MER. CASE maintains a sparse, self-evolving library of pair-specific EmotionSkills that externalize affective expertise from model parameters, enabling the learned expertise to be continuously refined and readily transferred across diverse frozen MLLM backbones. During inference, CASE dynamically retrieves the appropriate EmotionSkill to reinforce boundary-aware reasoning while keeping the MLLM backbone frozen. Extensive experiments on CA-MER, DFEW, and EMER demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of CASE across both general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLMs. Notably, CASE improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B on the CA-MER benchmark from 46.80% to 59.13%, while achieving consistent gains across MLLMs.
authors: Siyu Wu, Zeyu Liang, Linghao Wang, Qiyun Zheng, Yi Yao, Ling Lo, Hongxia Xie
bullets: Targets systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with overlapping multimodal cues.
Represents affective expertise as sparse, self-evolving pair-specific EmotionSkills rather than global model adaptations.
Retrieves relevant skills at inference time to support boundary-aware emotion reasoning.
Transfers across frozen general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLM backbones.
Raises Qwen3-VL-8B’s CA-MER average accuracy from 46.80% to 59.13% and delivers consistent gains across evaluated MLLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the CASE localize–attribute–validate lifecycle. A frozen MLLM selectively reopens one ambiguous emotion-pair boundary. After ground-truth feedback becomes available, candidate-recall failures are excluded from pair-level learning, while attributable failures and successful anchors guide a local EmotionSkill revision. The revision affects future emotion predictions only after pair-specific behavioral validation.

Figure 1: Overview and cross-setting generalization of CASE. (a) CASE resolves Top-2 emotion ambiguity using a pair-specific skill. (b) Skills evolved only on closed-set in-the-wild DFEW are directly transferred to audio-visual conflict-aware CA-MER and open-vocabulary EMER, without target-dataset evolution or backbone updates.
Figure 4: Open-set generalization on EMER. CASE improves all three frozen backbones without EMER-specific adaptation, with the best result achieved by CASE-Retrieval with Emotion-Qwen.
Figure 6: PairAcc changes on the five most frequent first-round confusion pairs under CASE-Full and CASERetrieval.

Figure 5: Effectiveness across routing groups on CA-MER. Test samples are partitioned according to the routing decision and whether the confusion pair is covered by the skill library.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.
authors: Cristian Tommasino, Antonio M. Rinaldi
bullets: Addresses the lack of calibrated probabilities for user-defined diagnostic candidates in vision-language pathology models.
Uses MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head that outputs a normalized distribution in one forward pass.
Trained on 40,000 labeled patch states from three public collections, with organ-specific typed questions and a “none of these” option.
Achieved balanced accuracy of 0.541 versus 0.492 for a matched generative model, 0.345 for CONCH, and 0.213 for a general medical decision model.

Calibration depends on probability readout: PathJev-P is better than summed-log-likelihood generation, but comparable after length normalization and remains over-confident on unseen organs; a supervised linear probe calibrates better overall.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of PathJev. (1) Expert labels of six training sets from three public collections are turned deterministically into typed decisions: a patch carries a Choice (one of K candidates, including “none of these”), Noul (yes/no) and Score (ordered levels) question; the orange candidate is the label. (2) The image is encoded by MedSigLIP and enters the Gemma-3 decoder as tokens, followed by the question and all candidates, each closed by a marker token. One forward pass yields hidden states at the markers; a decision head shared by all questions sums a per-candidate score, a question–candidate interaction and a set-attention term, and a softmax returns the distribution. A generative read-out, as implemented here, needs one forward pass per candidate. Training: Stage A fits the head on the frozen 4-bit backbone; Stage B adds LoRA adapters. Whole-slide use is shown in Figure 3. Patches: SICAPv2 (CC BY 4.0). Bar heights in (2) are illustrative.

Figure 2: Reliability diagrams of the main Choice question before temperature scaling, one panel per clean test set: accuracy against top-candidate confidence in 15 equal-width bins (every non-empty bin; marker area ∝ share of the set’s states). Trained methods: one line per seed. Sparse bins (small markers) are noisy. The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration.

Figure 3: Whole-slide use of PathJev. Tiles of the slide are embedded with H-optimus-0 and clustered (PCA, Gaussian mixture with the number of components chosen by BIC, soft memberships rik). PathJev-P is run on the 16 most typical tiles of each cluster (4 shown for two clusters; one forward pass per tile answers all questions), and the cluster’s distribution P (c | k) is the mean of their raw probabilities. A cluster abstains when the top probability of its tissue-type distribution (11 candidates) is below 0.5. Cluster probabilities are propagated to every tile as Pi(c) = ∑ k rikP (c | k); their calibration was not evaluated. HiESD slide of Figure 4 (CC BY 4.0); bar heights are illustrative.

Figure 4: Whole-slide demonstration on two of the four HiESD slides (top: slide with adenocarcinoma; bottom: slide without; the other two are in Appendix G). Panels: thumbnail; region annotation (tiles whose mask is ≥90% one class); GMM clusters of H-optimus-0 tile features; cluster labels from PathJev-P (grey: cluster abstains, top probability < 0.5); PathJev-P applied to every tile (reference); probability of adenocarcinoma propagated from the clusters. The number of clusters chosen by BIC reached the upper bound of the search range (30) on three of the four slides.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.
authors: Kaiwen Wu, Chaochao Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of agents that mainly retrieve past records without forming causal understanding.
Combines stored causal knowledge with current evidence to build structured Causal Beliefs about factors and action effects.
Uses these beliefs for decisions and continuously updates both task beliefs and longer-term Causal Cognition.
Evaluations show causal knowledge accumulation and transfer across financial, scientific, and everyday tasks.
In financial research, it improves mean rank correlation by 25.4% over a baseline and raises prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic settings.

papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.
authors: Tianyu Yang, Yijun Tian, Lars Benedikt Kaesberg, Jan Philip Wahle, Bela Gipp, Terry Ruas, Daniel Kurzawe
bullets: Existing embedding training specifies relevance relations but does not guide the latent reasoning used to augment inputs.
PILOT models reasoning with input-only prior and relation-informed posterior modes of a shared MLLM.
An importance-weighted variational objective enables prior–posterior co-evolution and selective transfer of useful, reachable posterior traces.
On MMEB-V2, PILOT improves over the primary baseline across all 12 task groups for both 2B and 7B models.
Overall gains are 3.2 and 3.3 points, with the largest improvements in visual-document retrieval: 6.1 and 6.4 points.

papers.abstract: Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.
authors: Geetika, Shivani Singh Chauhan, Gauranshi Gupta, Anant Jain, Kaushik Kalyanaraman, Bapi Chatterjee
bullets: Addresses the unexplored interaction between sharpness penalties, Muon optimization, and heavy-tailed gradient noise.
Uses stale stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations, avoiding SAM’s additional gradient computation.
Provides a theoretical result showing sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction.
Explores robustness under heavy-tailed noise and evaluates mitigation of post-training quantization degradation and catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.
authors: Sugam Karki, Ra\'ul V\'azquez, Yova Kementchedjhieva
bullets: Studies how vision encoders process rendered text across orthographic, grammatical, and semantic levels.
Combines cross-modal alignment, probing, and retrieval analyses to examine representational hierarchy.
Finds object and text recognition emerge before strong text–concept mapping.
The hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, but larger self-supervised models and text-rich data show partial similar behavior.
Results suggest scale and text-rich training can partly offset the lack of explicit language supervision.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and motion imitation have enabled increasingly capable whole-body control for individual humanoids. Cooperative carrying is more challenging because successful coordination requires not only plausible individual motions, but also consistent cross-agent and agent-object relations, including shared grasp, relative configuration, and whole-body support. We introduce CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset containing 220 synchronized two-person sequences across 21 task schemes, five shared-object geometries, four terrain types, and approximately 61 minutes of motion. We further propose Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting, which starts from nominal individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids around the same prescribed object trajectory. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors preserve compatible four-hand grasp relations, while complementary upper object-interaction and lower support structures retain object-relative geometry and coordinated support. Across all 220 CoCarry sequences retargeted to two A3 humanoids, our method achieves 0.9995 contact preservation, reduces penetration duration by 67.0% and 71.0% relative to GMR and OmniRetarget, respectively, and maintains a 100% retargeting success rate. On CORE4D with Unitree G1 humanoids, it achieves 0.9906 contact preservation with zero measured sliding. We further validate the generated references through physics simulation and multiple real-world cooperative carrying experiments on two physical A3 humanoids, demonstrating their usability for downstream dual-humanoid control.

Achieves high contact preservation, reduced penetration, and 100% retargeting success on CoCarry; also shows zero measured sliding on CORE4D.
Physics simulations and real-world trials on two A3 humanoids demonstrate usability for downstream cooperative-carrying control.

papers.abstract: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.

papers.abstract: Developing multiple instance learning pipelines for the classification of whole-slide images involves many interdependent design decisions and expertise in both pathology and machine learning. We present AutoMIL, an open-source framework that applies principles from the field of automated machine learning to tackle this task by automating integral pipeline steps, such as preprocessing, training and evaluation. In a benchmark evaluation with default settings, AutoMIL reached ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam and 0.93-0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset, comparable to specialised pipelines in related work. Ensembling mainly improved performance on imbalanced data, showing that an automated pipeline must adapt to dataset characteristics. AutoMIL thus provides an accessible baseline for whole-slide image classification without manual pipeline configuration.

papers.abstract: Multimodal healthcare data contain relational information that extends beyond individual patient observations. Effective clinical outcome prediction therefore requires not only integrating information from multiple modalities, but also modeling the relationships between them. Standard fusion approaches do not explicitly capture these interactions, while existing graph-based approaches typically model only a subset of them. We propose DIGOM (Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare), a graph-based framework that jointly models three complementary interaction types: Intra-patient cross-modal, Cross-patient same-modal, and Cross-patient cross-modal interactions. DIGOM learns a sparse multiplex graph with disentangled views, each encoding interactions between pairs of modalities across patients. Discrete adjacency matrices with patient-adaptive connectivity are sampled via a differentiable mechanism, enabling end-to-end learning and allowing the model to select informative relationships without imposing a fixed number of neighbors. A regularization objective maintains overall graph sparsity, while message passing integrates this relational context into patient representations for outcome prediction. We evaluate DIGOM on two multimodal healthcare datasets, MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB, across five clinical prediction tasks. DIGOM achieves the highest AUROC on all five tasks while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction approaches. Ablation studies reveal that each interaction type's contribution varies across tasks, highlighting the need to adapt relational structures per task. DIGOM also demonstrates greater robustness to missing modalities, suggesting learned relationships provide complementary information when modalities are unavailable. Post-hoc analyses further reveal task- and outcome-specific connectivity patterns in the learned graphs.

papers.abstract: Pre-consultation medical dialogues are essential for collecting comprehensive patient information, but are costly to obtain at scale due to privacy and ethical constraints. Existing LLM-based synthesis methods often rely on prompt engineering or rigid rules, limiting their ability to balance clinical relevance with realistic patient diversity. We propose CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent framework for pre-consultation medical dialogue synthesis that integrates patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. CoRPS-Dial generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by post-hoc quality control for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency. Experiments on coronary heart disease demonstrate that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment between synthetic and real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and dialogue naturalness. Downstream fine-tuning experiments further confirm the utility of the generated synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT). Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert-validated LLM-based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Experiments with 10 frontier LLM agents reveal substantial performance gaps: GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall score of 80.9, yet only 26.0% of its runs exceed the 0.95 success threshold. Further analyses uncover distinct capability profiles across scientific task types and substantial variation in execution efficiency and stability. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/Sci-Agent-Exam.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding with vision-language models such as CLIP typically produces a single deterministic relevance map for an image-query pair, without indicating whether the localisation is reliable or whether the referent is present at all. We introduce \textbf{PROVE} (\textbf{Pro}babilistic \textbf{V}isual Grounding via Patch-Level \textbf{E}vidence), a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions without modifying the backbone. PROVE casts grounding as per-patch membership: each patch accumulates positive and negative evidence for whether it belongs to the referent, so a query may match zero, one, or many patches. We train PROVE with an evidential objective on soft patch-coverage targets, and define a prior-pull objective that keeps absent-referent examples near an uninformative prior, so that vacuity serves as an absence signal without a dedicated presence classifier. During inference, a single forward pass yields, in closed form, a posterior-mean grounding map, a spatial vacuity map, and an image-level absence score. We evaluate PROVE on referring-expression benchmarks: it is competitive in localisation with state-of-the-art CLIP grounding methods, its uncertainty tracks localisation error and supports selective prediction under abstention, and its image-level score detects when the referent is absent altogether. Our evidential patch-membership modelling offers a simple, drop-in mechanism for probabilistic verification in frozen vision-language grounding systems.
authors: Mayank Nautiyal, Tianru Zhang, Li Ju, Ekta Vats, Prashant Singh
bullets: Addresses the limitations of deterministic relevance maps, which do not show localisation reliability or referent absence.

A single forward pass produces a grounding map, spatial uncertainty map, and image-level absence score.
On referring-expression benchmarks, PROVE is competitive in localisation; its uncertainty tracks error, supports abstention, and detects absent referents.

papers.abstract: Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Shouhao Chang, Xuan Liu, Hongye Zhu, Xinning Chen, Shigeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the costly manual trial-and-error required to design effective RL reward functions.
Uses an Explorer for novelty, a Guardian for stable refinement, and an Evolver for crossover and mutation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of R2E. The framework operates in three main stages: (Stage 1 Initial Iteration): Reward candidates are generated through a broad exploration phase based on the environment code and task descriptions, and then trained on IsaacGym or Bi-DexHands tasks to initialize the Global Elite Pool with the Top 5 functions. (Stage 2 Dynamic Role-driven Iterations): In each iteration, a total of N = 16 candidates are generated through dynamic scheduling by the Explorer, Guardian, and Evolver roles. After RL training and evaluation, the pool is dynamically updated by replacing the worst-performing reward. (Stage 3 End of Iterations): After the search concludes, the Top 1 reward is selected and re-evaluated across five random seeds to produce the final output. (Global Elite Pool): A fixed-capacity memory (K = 5) that stores and ranks the best-performing reward functions across iterations.

Figure 1: Comparison of reward design paradigms. (Eureka) generates homogeneous rewards and lacks memory. If iteration T + 1 regresses, the LLM references only T + 1 for T + 2, discarding high-performing rewards from T . (Our Method) populates a Global Elite Pool via initial exploration. Specialized roles query historical elites from the pool to iteratively evolve diverse reward candidates.
