papers.abstract: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.

With an SOP- and RAG-based agent, achieves the strongest reported colloquial naturalness and profile adherence, while handling long-tail intents and shorter utterances at comparable compliance.
Supports intent-recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.

papers.abstract: Video reasoning requires understanding how events unfold over time, yet videos with accurate temporal annotations are expensive to collect. Self-play offers an alternative by letting a model generate and solve its own tasks without manual annotation. However, existing video self-play methods train on fixed sets of recorded videos, so they cannot alter the underlying event dynamics and rely on noisy pseudo-labels derived from the model's own outputs, such as majority voting, that risk reinforcing shared model errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Tempo-Zero, a self-improvement framework that closes a loop of executable environments, execution-verified self-play, and environment evolution, where executing a program renders a video with the ground-truth option and interval of every question. A single policy plays both Questioner and Solver, proposing questions and answering them with timestamped evidence lines, and is trained on execution-grounded rewards instead of model consensus. The Solver's performance steers a curriculum over tasks and difficulty levels, and the policy selects rule changes that enrich the event dynamics of later rounds. Despite being trained solely on simple programs, without supervised fine-tuning or external video data which prior methods typically require, Tempo-Zero outperforms the base models and recent self-play baselines on average across twelve real-world video benchmarks at different model scales, with particularly strong gains on temporal grounding tasks. authors: Jingmin Zhu, Yanyan Zou, Xiuyu Li, James Bailey, Dinh Phung, Tao Yu, Yunyun Hou, Jun Liu, Jun Zhou, Sirui Wang, Nan Duan, Jiachen Liu, Qiuhong Ke

A single policy alternates between Questioner and Solver, producing timestamped evidence and receiving execution-grounded rewards.

Trained only on simple programs, it outperforms base models and recent self-play baselines across twelve real-world video benchmarks, especially for temporal grounding.

papers.abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.
authors: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu
bullets: GRPO assigns one trajectory-level advantage to every action, so recovery attempts in failed rollouts may be penalized with preceding errors.
The method uses success-probability and policy-score martingales to characterize stopping points where removing later gradients has zero conditional expected effect.
A LoRA-fine-tuned VLM identifies the last visible error without observed recovery in complete rollout videos and retains feedback only through that interval.
For retrospective boundaries, the work analyzes changes in gradient expectation and variance relative to ideal stopping conditions.
Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 report higher success rates than full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved Visual Question Answering (VQA) performance, yet their reasoning over structured content such as tables remains inconsistent, often plagued by spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations. Existing approaches for improving table VQA typically rely on architectural modifications or expensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which impose high barriers to entry due to the need for large-scale, expert-annotated datasets and significant computational resources. In this work, we propose Self-RefineVQA, a training-free, inference-time self-correction framework that improves table VQA performance without additional labeled data or model updates. Inspired by human revision behavior, our method enables a single VLM to iteratively act as a generator, critic, and refiner, forming a closed self-feedback loop that corrects common reasoning errors through prompt-guided re-evaluation. Experiments on tabular VQA benchmarks demonstrate that Self-RefineVQA yields consistent accuracy gains in monolingual and cross-lingual understanding, with a particularly significant boost for small models, enabling lightweight models (e.g., 2B-7B parameters) to rival the performance of significantly larger counterparts. Furthermore, we provide a comparative complexity analysis demonstrating that while inference cost increases linearly, our framework offers superior data efficiency and a lower cumulative cost by eliminating the prohibitive annotation bottleneck of human labeling required for fine-tuning. Our results highlight the potential of prompt-based self-improvement as a scalable, accessible paradigm for reliable table reasoning in VLMs.
authors: Somraj Gautam, Gaurav Harit
bullets: Targets spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations in VLM reasoning over document tables.
Uses one VLM as generator, critic, and refiner in a prompt-guided self-feedback loop.
Requires no labeled data, architectural changes, or model updates.
Improves accuracy across monolingual and cross-lingual tabular VQA, especially for small models.
Inference cost grows linearly with iterations, but avoids the annotation burden of supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Introduces a seven-dataset benchmark spanning domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and five independent human labels per instance.

Improves agreement@≥2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves near-best distributional alignment, within 2 Fleiss-kappa points of the best result.
Targets complex, evolving guidelines and reasonable annotator disagreement, especially on boundary cases.

papers.abstract: Environments with randomized dynamics are widely used to ask whether world models need explicit context inference. However, randomization can leave little predictive information for a context encoder to add, because distinct latent parameters may produce similar transitions at visited states, or those states may already reveal the active context. We formalize the remaining one-step information as predictive headroom and compare kernels under fixed and visited state--action distributions to distinguish changes in query coverage from changes in context weights. We analyze discrete and continuous environments and find low headroom both when kernels differ little and when visitation reduces an otherwise large discrepancy. At the same time, resetting state components increases headroom, showing that context evidence accumulates in state. We propose reporting this headroom alongside the randomized parameters, so that gains from explicit context inference can be interpreted relative to the information missing from the current state and action.
authors: Oleg Smirnov, Sofiane Ennadir, John Pertoft, Bjartur Hjaltason, Sara Karimi
bullets: Introduces predictive headroom: the remaining one-step information a context encoder could provide beyond the current state and action.
Separates changes in kernel differences from changes caused by which states and actions are visited.
Finds low headroom when randomized kernels are similar or when visitation already reveals the active context.
Shows that resetting state components increases headroom, indicating that context evidence accumulates in state.
Recommends reporting predictive headroom alongside randomized parameters to interpret context-inference gains.

papers.abstract: Recursive large language model (LLM) agents solve long-horizon tasks through decomposition, execution, and environmental feedback. Yet after producing an atomic subtask, they often invoke the same large model again to translate a familiar instruction into an executable action. We observe that high-level planning is task-specific, whereas leaf-level action grounding recurs across tasks and can be checked against environment-admitted actions. We introduce LeafSkill, an external reuse layer that retrieves semantically related grounding experience, binds action templates to current objects and admissible actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector to choose a bound action or defer the unchanged subtask to the original agent. Skills remain outside the model parameters, allowing a frozen selector to use post-training additions. Under lexical and syntactic paraphrases, exact matching retrieves none of the reference actions, while semantic retrieval preserves 96.0% and 97.0% candidate coverage; the frozen selector adopts 97.34% of unseen skill types. On an independent confirmation set of 200 Robotouille tasks, LeafSkill completes 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%, exact McNemar p=.0259). On the 106 tasks completed by both, it reduces Qwen3.5-27B tokens by 14.42% and calls by 14.08%. A separate held-out repeat yields a consistent 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction. Reusable leaf grounding can thus improve task completion while reducing host-model inference without replacing high-level planning.
authors: Shen Liu, Ze Zhou, Zhenguo Xu, Shaopu Wang, Yike Gao, Chunlei Wang

Retrieves semantically related experiences, binds templates to current objects/actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector or defers to the original agent.
Skills are stored externally, so a frozen selector can incorporate post-training additions.
On 200 Robotouille tasks, it completed 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%); shared-task usage fell 14.42% in tokens and 14.08% in calls.
A held-out repeat showed a 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction.

papers.abstract: Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2\% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.

papers.abstract: The 3rd WEAR Dataset Challenge asks for an activity label for every one-second window of four unseen participants. Each window has 15 VideoMAEv2 frame embeddings, the accelerometer signal of one random limb, and the windows are shuffled. This report is an empirical analysis of one system built after the challenge deadline. Window classifiers are stacked with features averaged over per-participant graphs of video neighbours and scored successor candidates, and a mean-field style decoder with a soft count constraint per activity labels all windows of a participant together. The setting is offline and transductive, and the count constraint relies on each activity being performed once. In a participant-wise simulation with participant-level bootstrap intervals, stacking added 0.051 macro F1 over stage-1 fusion and the count constraint 0.011 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.017). A quadratic seam distance ranks the true same-limb successor first among about 720 candidates in 83.9% of cases, but adding it to the link model changed macro F1 by -0.0001 (-0.0006 to 0.0005). With the decoder settings and the mixing weight chosen inside the folds and the mislabelled spans left out of training, the system scores 0.936 in simulation (0.940 for participants who performed each activity once); the submitted configuration scores 0.938 (0.943). Per-participant scores range from 0.80 to 0.97. These results come from a non-nested stacking protocol that uses unlabelled features transductively, so they are not a fully inductive estimate. An oracle that averages the final unary scores over the true segments reaches 0.973, and 79% of the remaining errors involve the null class. On the private leaderboard, which no choice used, the selected Kaggle submission scored 0.9231 (public 0.9254, with bounds partly tuned there), and a later one with bounds chosen in simulation scored 0.9247 (public 0.9253).

bullets: Stacking graph-based video-neighbour and successor features improved macro F1 by 0.051 over initial multimodal fusion; the count constraint added 0.011.

Quadratic seam matching identified the true same-limb successor first in 83.9% of cases but changed macro F1 by only -0.0001.
The simulated system scored 0.936 macro F1, while private leaderboard scores were 0.9231 and 0.9247 for two submissions.
Remaining errors were concentrated in the null class; results are limited by a non-nested, transductive stacking protocol and the once-per-activity assumption.

papers.abstract: Multi-task deep learning has been developed to ensure explainability in computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems. These systems simultaneously predict interpretable characteristics of findings in auxiliary tasks to help radiologists assess the reliability of the diagnostic prediction. However, the CAD's opinion would not be referred to when the auxiliary task prediction deviates from the radiologist's expectation. To further leverage CAD's knowledge in the above situation, we proposed a multi-task gradient assist (MGA) method that brings interactivity to multi-task models without additional training. MGA allows radiologists to give feedback to the CAD and ask for additional diagnostic suggestions. Using two datasets of mammography and CT, we show that MGA successfully improves diagnostic accuracy upon feedback on various auxiliary tasks. Compared to an existing method using forward propagation only, MGA performs more robustly and can be combined to further improve accuracy. Our method paves a promising way for integrating artificial intelligence into image diagnosis.
authors: Takuro Shimaya
bullets: Addresses cases where CAD auxiliary predictions conflict with a radiologist’s expectations.
Introduces multi-task gradient assist (MGA), enabling interactive feedback without additional training.
Uses radiologist feedback to request updated diagnostic suggestions.
Improves diagnostic accuracy across auxiliary tasks on mammography and CT datasets.
MGA is more robust than a forward-propagation-only method and can be combined with it.

papers.abstract: Trajectory transfer from rollout to training affects both learning quality and system efficiency in large language model reinforcement learning (RL). Enforcing batch-wide training requirements can delay the admission of completed trajectories, resulting in higher architectural staleness: the additional parameter-version gap from disaggregated pipelining relative to colocated execution. Beyond admission, misalignment between data access and training consumption causes redundant movement and unnecessary waiting when transferring large trajectory payloads. We present KnitTrans, a system that coordinates the rollout-to-training path through three designs. First, constraint-preserving mini-batch admission allows flexibility in early mini-batch composition, while checking that enough capacity remains to satisfy the remaining quotas. Second, on-demand trajectory data access matches storage units to consumer assignments and overlaps micro-batch data preparation with computation. Third, multimodal encoding deduplication supports reuse across a mini-batch while preserving gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches. Experiments show up to 93% lower architectural staleness than with train-batch admission, narrowing the learning-quality gap between disaggregated execution and colocated execution. On multimodal workloads, KnitTrans reduces transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and achieves a speedup of up to 5.8 times in transfer plus training over the baseline.
authors: Bangjun Xiao, Chiheng Lou, Xiaodong Ji, Xiangwei Deng, Yikai Zhao, Gang Huang, Hailin Zhang

papers.abstract: Continuous visual world simulation requires coupling evolving scene geometry with temporally persistent appearance. We present UniWorld, a unified framework that integrates depth trajectories and reference appearance within a shared video generation model. The central design maintains visual and geometric histories on a common timeline. Noise-aligned overlapping continuation places generated history at the prescribed sampling noise level and commits only newly generated latents. Rolling depth latent state preserves the corresponding geometric controls, incrementally reads newly available geometry, and keeps the conditioning fixed within each sampling window. Together, these mechanisms ensure exact preservation of latent history while bounding the active depth state by the window size. We evaluate continuous generation, paired history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scene categories. The same generator supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, while cached and incremental execution paths produce bitwise-identical outputs. Appearance changes and geometric control branches operate through the same interface without modifying committed history. The measured steady-state DiT execution path achieves real-time generation throughput, demonstrating the efficiency of UniWorld for continuous visual world simulation.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling temporally persistent visual appearance with changing scene geometry.

Evaluations cover continuous generation, history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scenes; the steady-state DiT path achieves real-time throughput.

papers.abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Hongwen Li, Yiding Yu, Zhuang Fu, Siqi Ding, Zhengyuan Chen, JianGuo Chen, Hanyue Zhao, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses shot-to-shot NBI ion-source tuning when hidden operating conditions evolve and responses are nonstationary.
Combines deterministic extraction of physical and visual features, two-layer trajectory/knowledge memory, MLLM action generation, and independent feasibility checks.
In chronological replay of 455 shots across four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols outperformed waveform images alone for quality classification.
Retrieved context improved agreement with historical action directions, while visual evidence had model-dependent effects.
Demonstrates engineering feasibility for supervised sequential tuning on five ion sources; scope is limited to supervised operation and the evaluated platforms.

papers.abstract: Cognitive workload estimation from physiological signals is increasingly relevant in high-risk environments, where continuous and unobtrusive monitoring can inform adaptive systems and safety interventions. This paper presents FOCUS (Frequency-band Optimized Cognitive-load Ultralight SSM), a compact Mamba-2-based model for EEG-based binary workload classification under constrained data conditions. Rather than learning frequency sensitivity from data, FOCUS encodes preprocessed multi-channel EEG using a fixed FFT decomposition that covers the five canonical EEG bands. The proposed model combines depthwise-separable convolution and a weight-shared encoder-bottleneck Mamba-2 pair, with 0.04 million parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs. Evaluated in a pilot study with 11 participants under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across three cognitively distinct tasks, FOCUS achieves 74.75% accuracy on the full dataset at 0.08 ms GPU model-forward latency. In the weight-sharing ablation, the shared configuration achieves 4.55 percentage points higher accuracy on the full dataset than the non-shared variant while reducing the SSM parameter budget; however, this difference does not reach statistical significance under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p=0.083$). Overall, the selected FOCUS configuration provides a favorable trade-off between classification performance and computational cost within this controlled pilot setting.
authors: Ioannis Kyprakis, Stefanos Gkikas, Chariklia Chatzaki, Zongyi Jiang, Randy Gomez, Raul Fernandez Rojas

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process images and text jointly, yet robustness evaluations often perturb these inputs separately or assess only predefined corruption levels. Such evaluations provide limited evidence of which modality is more susceptible to perturbations and whether smaller changes across both modalities can jointly expose failures. We present MoST, a black-box testing framework that characterizes modality sensitivity by comparing image-only, text-only, and joint perturbations. MoST uses multi-objective search to select and combine perturbations and adjust their severity, seeking prediction degradation while limiting changes to images and prompts. We evaluate MoST on four VLMs performing object localization on ImageNet and driving images. The models exhibit distinct sensitivities: textual perturbations dominate for some, whereas others are susceptible across both modalities. In several configurations, joint perturbations match or exceed the effectiveness of single-modality perturbations with smaller modifications to each input. In a human study, 60-76% of assessments across models judge the perturbed inputs sufficiently understandable to perform the task, and human localization is more accurate than that of the corresponding VLMs. These results show that evaluating modalities separately can overlook failure-inducing combinations and that modality sensitivity provides a more detailed account of VLM robustness than aggregate failure rates alone.
authors: Oliver Wei{\ss}l, Eduardo Breitembach, Andrea Stocco
bullets: Evaluates modality sensitivity through image-only, text-only, and combined perturbations with adjustable severity.
Tests four VLMs on object localization using ImageNet and driving images.
Finds model-specific vulnerabilities: text dominates for some models, while others are sensitive to both modalities.
Joint perturbations can match or exceed single-modality effectiveness while making smaller changes to each input.
Human evaluators generally found the perturbed inputs understandable, suggesting failures can occur without obvious loss of task clarity.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.

papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners

papers.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
authors: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Pengkun Jiao, Sihan Yang, Ming Ma, Steven Hoi, Erik Cambria

4DMemoryBench evaluates reasoning across diverse context lengths, targeting persistent memory over long video streams.
The 4DMemory Harness combines four skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval-augmented generation.
Across 13 leading models, the harness improves performance by over 50%, while models perform over 10% worse than on a previous benchmark.
The benchmark targets development of agents for complex, long-horizon spatiotemporal tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation for 4DMemory Agent. (a) Traditional models with limited active context may lose access to earlier observations, leaving relevant evidence unavailable for temporal reasoning. (b) 4DMemory Agent coordinates persistent memory and task-specific skills through a harness to retrieve evidence and reason over events and their relations. 2024b; Bai et al., 2025). At the method level, adaptive spatiotemporal compression removes redundant frames and visual tokens, sparse memory consolidates dense observations into long-term representations, and query-adaptive hierarchical selection allocates computation across temporal granularities (Shen et al., 2025; Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). Together, these advances improve access to long-range evidence, but their gains are typically evaluated under different datasets, interfaces, and access conditions, making it difficult to isolate improvements in the base model, evidence acquisition, memory, and final reasoning. Moreover, these components are not readily composable across systems, since methods such as LongVU require access to the internal visiontoken pipeline, whereas LongVT learns its tooluse protocol through model-specific post-training of Qwen2.5-VL-7B rather than through a modelagnostic plug-in interface (Shen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026).

Figure 3: Overview of the LongVideo construction pipeline. Hours-level videos undergo audio-text screening, clip construction, and evidence refinement to obtain coherent clips with grounded captions. Visual evidence, audio captions, and transcripts are aligned to original source timestamps and organized into chronological multimodal evidence chains. QA pairs are then constructed from multiple evidence chains and checked for answer correctness, clip necessity, and potential shortcuts.

Figure 4: Illustration of 4DMemory Agent framework. (a) The harness builds persistent, question-independent memory of events, entities, and spatial relations, preserving source timestamps for reuse across questions. (b) A foundation model retrieves timestamped evidence and iteratively refines its queries and reasoning, with optional tools provided by a skill library.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation. Code is available at \href{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}.
authors: Meng Li, Lijiang Chen, Qi Zhao, Jun Jiang, Longhao Zou, Shuchang Lyu, Guangliang Cheng
bullets: Addresses scene-level dynamics modeling, which conflates multiple moving parts and incorporates task-irrelevant content.
Decomposes point-cloud frames into a small set of temporally consistent slots without actions or labels.
Learns per-slot latent actions through inverse dynamics and predicts future slot states with diffusion-based forward dynamics.
Uses a self-supervised interaction head to capture pairwise proximity-and-motion relationships.
Outperforms scene-level baselines in Meta-World and Adroit, with robust performance amid clutter and unseen objects on a RealMan RM65-B robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. DynaSlots framework. (a) Three point-cloud frames are encoded by a shared Point Transformer and propagated by a temporal slot binder into K=6 aligned soft slots. An EMA target branch supplies noised future slot features, while an auxiliary interaction head predicts pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. The displayed losses are noise prediction, slot VICReg, relation BCE, and assignment entropy. (b) Previous slots query current point tokens through competitive assignment, weighted aggregation, and residual refinement, repeated three times per frame. (c) Two observed point clouds and the robot state produce slot condition tokens for the diffusion policy, which predicts the action sequence using cross-attention and FiLM.

papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting plays an important role in real-world applications, where probabilistic approaches provide uncertainty estimates for decision-making. Real-world systems are inherently non-stationary, leading to distribution shifts between training and test data. However, existing probabilistic methods mainly focus on modeling data distributions under standard settings, while distribution shift methods often handle such shifts in a coarse manner, failing to characterize shift degree and adapt prediction strategy accordingly. As a result, they often produce miscalibrated and unreliable forecasts. To address this issue, we propose REMIND, a retrieval-guided probabilistic framework for spatiotemporal forecasting under distribution shift. REMIND leverages retrieval to estimate how well current observation are supported by historical patterns, enabling adaptive prediction under different shift regimes. It employs spatiotemporal retrieval to construct a memory bank and introduces a dual branch architecture, combining a memory-calibrated probabilistic branch for mild shifts with a deviation-aware probabilistic branch for severe shifts. A shift-adaptive gate, guided by retrieval similarity and memory dispersion, balances the two branches according to shift degree. We further design a hierarchical Gaussian mixture to capture heterogeneous uncertainty over the dual branch predictions, and introduce a memory perturbation training scheme to improve generalization. Experiments on real-world datasets with distribution shifts demonstrate that REMIND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and probabilistic prediction quality.
authors: Haochen Lv, Jianhao Zhang, Zhichen Lei, Yang Jiang, Xiaowei Mao, Shengnan Guo, Youfang Lin, Huaiyu Wan

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but uniformly assigning a single response-level advantage to all tokens overlooks the distinct roles of visual observations and subsequent reasoning. Visual affinity alone is insufficient: predictive states may align with both image and prompt-context representations, and upweighting valid visual observations can amplify their negative-advantage updates when later reasoning fails. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{Outcome-Conditioned Visual Credit (OVC)}, a plug-in framework that separates visual-association measurement from token-level credit assignment and is adaptable to policy-optimization methods with uniform response-level advantage allocation. Relative Visual Encoding constructs a context-relative visual coordinate by contrasting each predictive state's affinity to image and prompt-context representations. Outcome-conditioned Evidence Calibration combines this coordinate with uncertainty-scaled predictive features and calibrates their contributions to outcome-discriminative evidence through mean contrasts between positive- and negative-advantage responses, scaled by regularized within-side variation. Visual association thus informs credit through observed outcome differences rather than directly determining update priority. Normalized Credit Allocation conditions the calibrated evidence on the response's advantage sign to produce positive token weights with unit global mean. These detached weights preserve advantage signs while modulating individual token-gradient contributions. OVC reuses existing rollouts without auxiliary reward models, process annotations, or inference-time modules. Instantiated through GSPO-token, OVC retains sequence-level clipping and consistently improves six-benchmark mean accuracy over GSPO across three models, with gains of 1.86-2.39 percentage points.
authors: Yuhang Han, Dingning Liu, Yujie Chen, Yaojie Zhang, Jingwei Song, Zequn Yang, Xuanming Shang, Li Ding, Zhijiang Guo, Linfeng Zhang

OVC separates visual-affinity measurement from token-level credit assignment using relative visual encoding and outcome-conditioned evidence calibration.

The framework reuses existing rollouts and needs no auxiliary reward model, process annotations, or inference-time module.
With GSPO-token, OVC improves mean accuracy across six benchmarks and three models by 1.86–2.39 percentage points over GSPO.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised Temporal Action Localization (PTAL) aims to localize action instances using only a single annotated timestamp for each instance. Such sparse supervision offers limited guidance for modeling the structural organization of an action instance. Existing PTAL methods primarily infer action regions from classification responses, leaving the structural organization of multiple action-related parts within each instance insufficiently modeled. To address this problem, we propose DeformStruct, an instance-level deformable structure modeling framework for PTAL. DeformStruct progressively constructs the structure of each action instance through three stages. First, Structural Anchor Mining discovers multiple anchors from annotated points and action-responsive regions, providing structural nodes grounded in the current instance. Second, Deformable Part Alignment associates latent structural parts with these anchors through deformation-aware matching, allowing their temporal supports to adapt to instance-dependent variations. Third, Relational Structural Organization explicitly models the relative temporal relations among the aligned parts, forming a relational representation that characterizes how different action-related parts are organized together. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID demonstrate consistent improvements in point-supervised temporal localization and validate the effectiveness of deformable structural modeling.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Yonghao Dong, Jie Wang, Gang Hua
bullets: PTAL uses only one timestamp per action instance, providing limited structural supervision.
DeformStruct progressively builds instance structure through anchor mining, deformable part alignment, and relational organization.
The method adapts part temporal supports to instance-specific variations and models relations among aligned parts.
Experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID show consistent localization improvements.
The approach is scoped to point-supervised temporal action localization and depends on sparse point annotations.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed DeformStruct framework. Given pre-extracted video features and point annotations, a Transformer Encoder first produces the encoded feature sequence XE . DeformStruct progressively models each action instance through three stages: Structural Anchor Mining discovers multiple action-related anchors, Deformable Part Alignment adaptively aligns latent parts with these anchors to accommodate temporal variations, and Relational Structural Organization models the relative temporal relations among the aligned parts to characterize their structural configuration. Finally, the Transformer Decoder predicts candidate action segments, and the framework is jointly optimized with localization and structural objectives.

Fig. 7. Qualitative comparison of our proposed method with QROT [14] and HR-Pro [7] on THUMOS14 [10]. We provide two test videos with action classes of GolfSwing and HighJump, respectively. It can be seen that our detection results show higher IoUs with the ground truth.

Fig. 1. Motivation of deformable structural modeling for PTAL. A complete action instance may contain multiple temporally distributed action-related stages, whose locations, durations, and relative configurations vary across instances. Existing holistic modeling tends to overlook such regional evidence, temporal variation, and structural relations. Our DeformStruct instead models the action as a deformable structure composed of multiple action-related parts, adaptively aligning them to instance-specific temporal evidence and capturing their structural relations.

papers.abstract: Video moment retrieval aims to localize a query-relevant temporal segment in an untrimmed video. Existing methods typically perform video-text alignment in Euclidean space, where representations are embedded in a flat geometry. However, accurate moment localization requires organizing query-relevant evidence across multiple grounding states, where target regions, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors exhibit distinct temporal structures and relevance patterns. Such Euclidean representations lack an explicit geometry to jointly capture these relationships, motivating us to explore structured temporal evidence organization from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we propose Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO), a geometric framework that organizes query-aware temporal memory in hyperbolic space. HTEO maps temporal representations into a Poincar\'{e} ball and organizes temporal evidence through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR). REO adjusts temporal tokens' radial positions to encode the structural differences among temporal evidence, while OAR enhances query-conditioned semantic alignment through orthogonal rotation. The organized representation is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space and injected into the decoder through a lightweight residual memory update, enabling hyperbolic geometric cues to be incorporated into standard Transformer decoders while preserving the original cross-modal memory. Furthermore, we introduce radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to explicitly guide temporal evidence organization and query-conditioned semantic alignment, respectively. Extensive experiments and analyses across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HTEO improves temporal localization while providing an interpretable geometric organization of temporal evidence.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Gang Hua, Le Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of modeling target moments, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors with flat Euclidean representations.
Uses a Poincaré-ball memory with Radial Evidence Organization for temporal structure and Orthogonal Angular Refinement for query-conditioned alignment.
Projects the organized features back to Euclidean space and adds them through a lightweight residual memory update.
Introduces radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to guide the learned organization.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved temporal localization and interpretable evidence structure.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO) framework. Given a video-query pair, HTEO first constructs query-aware temporal memory through multimodal feature fusion and maps it into a Poincaré ball via the exponential map. In hyperbolic space, temporal evidence is organized through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR), where REO regulates the radial structure to capture different temporal grounding characteristics, and OAR refines angular directions to enhance query-conditioned semantic relevance. The organized memory is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space via the logarithmic map and incorporated into the decoder through a lightweight residual update for moment localization. The bottom panel illustrates the detailed geometric operations.

Fig. 4. Visualization of hyperbolic radius-angle organization for temporal evidence modeling. (a) The radius-angle feature space shows the geometric separation among target, boundary, and background tokens. (b) The angular similarity curves demonstrate that angular direction provides query-conditioned relevance cues. (c) The temporal evolution of radius reveals structural variations around different temporal evidence regions and boundary transitions.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison of HTEO with TR-DETR and LD-DETR on the QVHighlights dataset. HTEO achieves more accurate temporal localization with better alignment to GT. The queries are displayed as provided in the original dataset.

Fig. 1. Motivation of hyperbolic temporal evidence organization for video moment retrieval. (a) In flat Euclidean memory, query-relevant tokens and contextual distractors may exhibit similar feature distances, making them difficult to distinguish based on flat similarity alone. (b) Such ambiguity can lead to false response peaks on distracting background regions, resulting in inaccurate temporal localization. (c) HTEO organizes query-aware temporal evidence in hyperbolic space through radius-angle geometry, where angular direction captures query-conditioned relevance and radial distance provides structural cues for temporal evidence organization. By introducing geometry-aware organization, HTEO enhances the discrimination between relevant evidence and semantically similar distractors, leading to more structured temporal representations for moment retrieval.

Fig. 6. Qualitative analysis of false peak correction using hyperbolic angular refinement. Four representative validation samples are shown where Euclidean similarity produces distractor-induced response peaks. Hyperbolic angular organization shifts dominant responses toward the ground-truth moments and suppresses irrelevant activations.

Fig. 7. Visualization of temporal evidence organization in Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. Compared with flat Euclidean representations, hyperbolic geometry yields more structured distributions of target, boundary, and background tokens, indicating improved evidence separability. The query texts are displayed as provided in the original dataset.
Fig. 3. Visualization of hyperbolic radius-angle behavior.

Fig. 5. Illustrative analysis of inside-outside response gaps. The left panel compares the maximum query-conditioned responses inside and outside the ground-truth interval, while the right panel shows the corresponding per-query inside-outside response gaps.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the engineering implementation methods of the SKG inference framework and provides complete case studies across four domains. Case 1, 2D Dissipative Mechanical System: OOD MSE is 1.69 to 4.12 times lower than the best neural baseline; the state-dependent metric yields a 10^8-order improvement under controlled conditions. Case 2, Target Detection Sim-to-Real: Real-machine mAP increases from 0.2564 to 0.4964 (+24.00 points, single-run experiment, 32 images, point estimate), and AP75 increases from 0.1736 to 0.5765 (+40.29 points), with no real-machine retraining required. Case 3, Sequence Modeling sine to square: OOD MSE is 0.0296 versus Transformer 0.0641 (mean of 5 seeds, p=0.024). Case 4, Molecular Dynamics MD17: ID@100 ADE is 0.0285 versus ESTAG 0.1467; OOD@100 is 0.0316 versus 0.1411 (single seed). For each case, we present the objective, applied SKG theory, parameter settings, baseline comparison protocol, data results, and sources of advantage. Following the cases, we provide the complete methodology: pre-validation, task invariant construction, three-stage training, residual training, and the four theorems and one proposition supporting these methods. This paper not only demonstrates effective configurations of SKG across four domains but also honestly reports the variance of single-run experiments, limitations of single-seed results, negative updates caused by parameterization mismatch, and practical experience of using engineering thresholds as diagnostic signals rather than hard constraints.
authors: Jian An, Chaoshi Wu, Xinpan Luo
bullets: Covers dissipative mechanics, sim-to-real target detection, sine-to-square sequence modeling, and MD17 molecular dynamics.
Methodology includes pre-validation, task-invariant construction, three-stage and residual training, plus supporting theoretical results.
Reported gains include lower OOD error in mechanics and sequence modeling, improved real-machine detection without retraining, and lower MD17 ADE than the cited baseline.
Results include single-run, single-seed, and small-sample experiments, so several findings have limited statistical reliability.
The paper discusses parameterization mismatch, experiment variance, and using engineering thresholds as diagnostics rather than hard constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Presents engineering implementations of the SKG inference framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across various domains, focusing on robustness.
papers.title: SKG in Practice: OOD Generalization Cases Across FourDomains
papers.tldr: SKG is implemented and evaluated across four domains, showing promising in- and out-of-distribution performance while documenting practical limitations and diagnostic lessons.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
authors: Jiachi Yang, Zhiyi Xu, Hongquan Zhang, Xin Tan, Zhizhong Zhang, Jingyu Gong, Yuan Xie
bullets: Addresses insufficient modeling of primitive skill choice and object contact/movement in vision-language-action policies.
Uses skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts adapters with skill-query tokens and routing biases in the language-model backbone.
Converts affordance heatmaps into patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial priors for the action head.
Achieves an Avg. Len of 4.65 on CALVIN ABC→D long-horizon cross-scene evaluation and is validated in real-robot sequence experiments.
Scope includes robustness to real perception and control noise; broader limitations are not specified in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.
authors: Radoslaw Malek, Szymon Soltysiak, Aleksandra Kawala-Sterniuk, Piotr Szymanski
bullets: Addresses the underuse of structured map data in geospatial multimodal representation learning.
Aligns H3-indexed regions across OSM-derived graph embeddings, satellite image crops, and textual descriptions.
Uses frozen pretrained encoders with trainable residual projection heads and a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective.
Introduces chained cross-modal recall, routing image–text retrieval through the graph modality under a matched candidate budget.
Graph-mediated retrieval improves R@1@1 over direct image–text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points; downstream gains are task-dependent and largest on Airbnb and Beijing housing.

papers.abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
authors: Tianyi Xu, Huazheng Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of using expanding interaction histories when context capacity is limited.
Uses a frozen language model with bidirectional memory–skill learning: recurring episodes create or revise skills, while skill-guided interactions generate future memories.
Combines retrieved facts and learned procedures in the agent’s context, adapting retrieval influence based on task outcomes without rewriting stored records.
Evaluated across ten settings covering embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code.
On ALFWorld, joint memory-and-skill serving reached 63.17% success, versus 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving.

papers.abstract: Learned humanoid controllers are usually trained in one simulator and then checked in a second one before they go near hardware. We ask what that check says about command delay. We train motion-tracking policies for a 24-joint humanoid on five motions taken from monocular video and test them in an independent CPU MuJoCo harness, which we first verify against the training model. Every policy completes its motion in at least 26 of 30 episodes under the training randomization. With 40 ms of constant command delay, however, survival drops to 15% on average (0% - 45%), and the delay margin is only 20 - 30 ms. Randomizing the delay during training (0 - 50 ms) lifts survival at 40 ms to 95% on average (75% - 100%) and moves the margin to 50 - 70 ms. A control arm trained for the same number of extra iterations without delay does not improve, so the gain comes from the randomization itself. This holds for all five motions with three training seeds each, and a policy trained in PhysX behaves the same way. The price is slightly looser tracking (0.02 - 0.06 rad on four motions) and, for the most dynamic motion, less robustness to other perturbations. We also show that the first sim-to-sim gap we saw came from the harness, a missing floor and a wrong timestep, and not from the physics engines. The 0 - 20 ms delay ranges common in locomotion training lie inside the margin an unrandomized tracker already has. The benefit comes from randomizing beyond it, so the range should be set from the robot's measured latency, and delay margin belongs next to other sim-to-sim metrics.
authors: Shaoqin Li, Yi Sun
bullets: Without delay randomization, 40 ms of constant command delay reduced average survival to 15%, with a 20–30 ms delay margin.
Randomizing delays from 0–50 ms raised 40 ms-delay survival to 95% on average and extended the margin to 50–70 ms.
The improvement was consistent across five video-derived motions, three seeds, and a policy trained in a different simulator.
Extra training alone did not produce the gain, indicating that delay randomization was responsible.
The approach slightly worsened tracking and reduced robustness to some other perturbations in the most dynamic motion; simulator discrepancies were traced to harness errors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are typically pretrained on broad, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuned on a comparatively small dataset tailored to a specific target robot. Such adaptation recipe is now widely established, achieving its most mature results on fixed-base arms due to their static base dynamics and consistent reference frame. Mounting the same arm on a quadruped extends the workspace to the entire floor, but fundamentally changes the embodiment: rather than controlling the arm in isolation, the policy must jointly coordinate base navigation, body posture, and end-effector motion. In this work, we study the practical demands of this embodiment change across data collection, model adaptation, and inference design to achieve closed-loop loco-manipulation on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm. We report the choices that made this real-robot deployment feasible, namely model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions, together with a study tailored to a pick-and-place task, separating data coverage from model capacity. We show that expanding demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%, and incorporating secondary skills (such as pushing rather than grasping) introduces new behavioral modes without degrading baseline performance. Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation.
authors: Giovanni Minelli, Antonio Langella, Giovanni B. Dessy, Lorenzo Amatucci, Giulio Turrisi, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
bullets: Studies the embodiment shift from fixed-base manipulation to coordinated navigation, posture, and end-effector control on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm.
Examines practical deployment choices across data collection, model adaptation, and inference, including model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions.
Finds that broader demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%.
Shows that adding secondary behaviors such as pushing introduces new modes without degrading baseline grasping performance.
Validates the pipeline in closed-loop real-world pick-and-place experiments and analyzes how dataset composition affects success and failure.

papers.abstract: Class imbalance and errors near anatomical boundaries remain challenges in medical image segmentation, motivating loss functions that account for these difficulties. Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss adjusts the similarity function during training but requires hyperparameter tuning. We propose Self-Tuned Boundary-Aware t-vMF Dice Loss (STB-tvMF Dice), which adapts the function separately for boundary and interior regions without tuning shape-adaptation parameters. Each region's shape parameter of t-vMF function is determined from its mean prediction-target cosine similarity in the preceding epoch and remains fixed throughout the current epoch. This rule maximizes the slope of the similarity function at the observed mean similarity, providing a principled basis for adaptation without validation-based parameter selection. Experiments on three datasets and architectures demonstrated its effectiveness. On Synapse with U-Net, STB-tvMF Dice achieved a mean DSC of 70.75%, compared with 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss. Our code will be available soon.
authors: Hinako Mitsuoka, Kazuhiro Hotta
bullets: Targets class imbalance and boundary errors in medical image segmentation.
Computes separate t-vMF shape parameters for boundary and interior regions from the preceding epoch’s mean prediction-target cosine similarity.
Keeps parameters fixed within each epoch and selects them to maximize the similarity-function slope at the observed mean similarity.
Evaluated across three datasets and architectures; on Synapse with U-Net, it achieved 70.75% mean DSC versus 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss.
The abstract does not specify the method’s limitations; code is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of intraoperative laparoscopic videos has the potential to improve surgical decision-making and precision. However, effective surgical assistance requires models that can generalize across diverse intraoperative tasks. Here we present LapaFM, a foundation model for laparoscopic surgery trained on more than 20,000 minutes of surgical videos using a multi-stage continual learning strategy that mitigates catastrophic forgetting and inter-task interference. LapaFM learns multimodal visual representations and supports multiple tasks, including smoke removal, surgical phase recognition, instrument and polyp segmentation, and lesion identification. The model was evaluated on 13 retrospective and two prospective cohorts collected from different imaging devices. LapaFM consistently outperformed task-specific models and existing foundation models across datasets, and also generalized to gastrointestinal endoscopy tasks, including polyp detection and classification. Notably, it recovered over 90% of smoke-obscured frames and achieved clinician-level or superior performance in lymph node metastasis prediction and prospective polyp classification.
authors: Xiaobo Zhu, Shiwei Wu, Yu An, Yuechen Tao, He Sun, Song Zhang, Jianbo Wang, Xiaojing Wang, Junwei Liu, Wei Guo, Yanfei Shao, Xuan Zhao, Jiangwei Xiao, Wenbo Niu, Bo Wei, Yuhan Wang, Gang Hu, Fei Liu, Kunshan He, Chongwei Chi, Jianqiang Tang, Kang Zhang, Jie Tian, Zhenyu Liu
bullets: Addresses the need for laparoscopic AI that generalizes across varied intraoperative tasks and imaging devices.
Uses multi-stage continual learning to reduce catastrophic forgetting and interference between tasks.
Supports smoke removal, surgical phase recognition, instrument and polyp segmentation, and lesion identification.
Evaluated on 13 retrospective and two prospective cohorts, with reported performance exceeding task-specific and existing foundation models.
Recovered over 90% of smoke-obscured frames and reached clinician-level or better performance for lymph node metastasis prediction and prospective polyp classification.

Fig. 1. A multi-stage continual learning strategy is employed during pretraining. In Stage I, the model learns white-light imaging (WLI) representations. In Stage II, pseudo-color imaging (PCI) features are introduced while reviewing white-light features via a frozen teacher network to mitigate modality conflict and catastrophic forgetting.

Fig. 3. Laparoscopic smoke removal visualization. Qualitative results demonstrate that LapaFM effectively removes surgical smoke while preserving anatomical details, outperforming other methods on both synthetic and real data.

Fig. 8. Robustness of LapaFM under limited supervision. Performance on instrument segmentation and polyp detection with 10%, 30%, and 50% training data demonstrates superior robustness compared to competing models.

papers.abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.
authors: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Pattern-matching 3D MLLMs struggle to distinguish geometrically similar objects, with accuracy dropping sharply on highly ambiguous samples.
The method reverses the usual information flow: geometry → function → identity, using part-level segmentation and functional chain-of-thought supervision.
PFIR trains on 507K functional QA pairs with a progressive curriculum and combines functional reasoning with descriptive grounding through dual-objective GRPO.
Under Objaverse→ModelNet40 and XYZRGB→XYZ-only zero-shot evaluation, accuracy improves from 60.5% to 66.7%.
Improvements are concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples, supporting part-level functional reasoning for recognition.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PFIR framework. The part-level functional pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functionas-evidence reasoning chains. The three-stage curriculum progressively builds function-guided recognition: Stage 1 aligns part-aware representations, Stage 2 teaches the reasoning format via SFT, and Stage 3 trains two complementary RL experts (functional reasoning + descriptive grounding) composed via Task Arithmetic.

Figure 1: Motivation. Pattern matching collapses on geometrically ambiguous objects (a). A per-sample GCS reveals that the hardest 20% reach only 33.7% baseline accuracy. PFIR addresses this via part-level functional reasoning, with gains concentrated 2.6× more on the most confused quintile (b), by shifting from function-as-annotation to functionas-evidence (c).

Table 2: Qualitative comparisons. The classification and caption results of models on ModelNet40 and Objaverse are presented. Correct answers and fine-grained functional descriptions are highlighted in green bold.

Table 1: Generative zero-shot 3D classification and captioning. (I)/(C): instruction-/completion-typed prompt. Captioning: GPT-4o image-based scoring on 200 Objaverse objects following [39]. ModelNet40 [36] is OOD and XYZ-only for all methods. Best in bold, second best underlined.2

Table 3: GCS-aware ablation of RL strategies (%). PLLM-V2 denotes PointLLM-V2 [39]; † marks our reproduction. S1/S2 are checkpoints; S1→ RL skips Stage 2 CoT SFT. ⊕ denotes Task Arithmetic, OB-I is Objaverse instruction accuracy, and Δ is PFIR minus PLLM-V2. Best/second-best scores are bold/underlined; bold Δ marks the largest quintile gain.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D scene construction is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Recent methods such as SAM-3Dfy enable end-to-end reconstruction of 3D assets and their scene layouts, but still struggle with fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality. Meanwhile, specialized 3D object generators provide detailed object geometry, while 3D foundation models offer strong and generalizable spatial understanding. We propose Easy-3Dfy, a compositional workflow that decouples object generation from scene layout estimation, allowing specialized models to fully exploit their respective strengths. An RPF-based aligner then bridges these capabilities by establishing geometric correspondence between object-local meshes and partial scene pointmaps, recovering object layout for scene composition. Without requiring complete scene-level supervision, the proposed workflow consistently outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Our results demonstrate that explicit geometric composition can effectively combine high-quality object generation with strong spatial understanding, while enabling the workflow to benefit independently from advances in both 3D object generation and foundation models.
authors: Ziang Zhang, Wenyou Yi, Zehan Wang, Jiachen Xu, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Targets limitations in fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality in existing end-to-end methods such as SAM-3Dfy.
Uses specialized 3D object generators for object geometry and 3D foundation models for spatial understanding.
An RPF-based aligner matches object-local meshes with partial scene pointmaps to recover object layouts.
Requires no complete scene-level supervision and outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200.
Its modular design can independently benefit from advances in object generation and foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Easy-3Dfy. Given object masks, a spatial model predicts a scene pointmap. For each object, an image editor produces a completed object image and a replaceable image-to-3D provider generates a local mesh. The RPF-based aligner matches its anchor point cloud to the object-specific partial query extracted from the pointmap, predicts correspondence positions, and recovers a uniform-scale similarity transform via Umeyama fitting. Transforming all complete meshes assembles the final scene.

Figure 5: What direct alignment improves. Matched comparisons of MIDI, SceneGen, SAM-3Dfy, and Easy-3Dfy under a common rendering protocol. The multi-view results show that Easy-3Dfy reduces floating and interpenetrating objects while improving object ordering and placement.

Figure 4: How mesh quality affects visual and layout quality. Matched input–panorama–close-up comparisons. Each case consists of two columns, with the first showing the reconstructed full 3D scene and the second showing close-up views of the same asset regions.

Figure 3: Object-level data construction and RPF training. Aligned RGB–depth renders yield a monocular partial query and pixel-matched ground-truth correspondence positions. Independent anchor- and query-side geometric augmentations define the registration task, on which RPF learns the conditional velocity field.
Table 1: Main results on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Easy-3Dfy and SAM-3Dfy share identical meshes, isolating layout prediction. Bold marks the best result per dataset.
Table 7: Complete Mesh-provider comparison with all other Easy-3Dfy components fixed. GT provides an upper-bound reference under the current layout workflow.
Table 4: Mesh-provider comparison on the Scene-Maker dataset with all other Easy-3Dfy components fixed. GT provides an upper-bound reference under the current layout workflow.
