papers.abstract: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.
authors: Tsung-Han Wu, Minsuk Heo, Kenny Tan
bullets: Mixed-iteration training can predict early stopping but fail under the standard stopping rule because the actual stopping iteration is not scored.
Scoring every iteration improves halting, but the reported runs required a strong penalty favoring early stops.
Batch generation runs until the slowest token finishes, so average iterations per token can overstate practical savings.
The authors recommend reporting actual iterations run, stopping threshold, and batch size.
They also propose a pretraining test to bound the potential benefit of a halting head.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A batched pass costs more than the average token. (a) Four tokens processed together: the pass keeps running until its deepest token stops. (b) Two 370M-parameter models: the predicted average (what the head’s probabilities predict), spent (what its exit rule runs) and paid (what a batched pass over 32 sequences runs). Mixture: trained on a mixture of all iterations; per-step: every iteration scored. Thresholds as in Section 2.2.

Figure 3: The cost in quality of exiting early. BPB against realized steps, the average number of iterations the exit rule actually runs. Each dot is one exit threshold of a 370M model. The dotted line is the sampled-depth baseline run for that many iterations; a curve below it is a lead at that cost. The mixture-loss model is above the baseline until 7.3 steps; the per-step model is on or below it at every threshold shown.

Figure 1: A head can predict 3.7 iterations and still run all eight. (a) A transformer stacks eight different blocks of layers; a looped model runs one block up to eight times. (b) After each iteration, a halting head gives the probability that the token stops there. Its average, the expected halting steps, is 1×0.33 + 2×0.15 + · · ·+ 8×0.18 = 3.7 iterations. An exit rule stops the token once the running total reaches 90%, which for this illustrative token happens only at iteration 8.

Figure 4: A batched pass costs the maximum, not the mean. Measured speedup over T=8 at 370M: the exit rule (filled) beside the same weights at a fixed depth equal to their realized steps (open, interpolated). Thresholds differ between points (Table 9): compare filled with open at one x only. Per-step prefill at b=32 was not timed at 370M. The x-axis is tokens per batched pass (sequences × positions). This count, not the number of sequences, decides how deep the deepest token goes.

Figure 5: The per-step loss with a strong prior, and what pricing the pass does to it. 370M, CC; model three seeds, baseline seed 42. Against the sampleddepth baseline read at N̄ the model wins everywhere. Read at the depth a batched pass runs, R N̄ , the baseline improves as the pass widens until it straddles the model, and further left, the baseline at the widest pass is ahead outright. Legend: the baseline read at R N̄ for a pass of 32 tokens (decoding 32 sequences; R counted in a real decode) and of 2048 tokens (one prompt; R from the timing table). Here “static” in the legend is the sampleddepth baseline. Dashed line: ε = 0.7, the threshold used. The point at 1.1689 lies above the axis. Model BPB is teacher-forced. The band is the evaluation noise floor, either side.

Figure 6: The speedup is largest when one token is generated at a time and is gone in large batches. Horizontal axis: how many tokens share one batched pass; 1 and 32 are decoding one or 32 sequences at once, and 2048 and 65,536 are processing one or 32 prompts of 2048 tokens. Vertical axis: how many times faster the 370M per-step model at ε=0.95 is than the sampleddepth baseline at T=3, whose teacher-forced quality it matches; above 1 is faster. Iterations: the speedup if only the core cost compute (3 divided by the iterations each pass runs). Throughput: the speedup of the whole pass, as predicted by the cost model of Section 8; it is smaller because the prelude and coda run once however many iterations the core runs (at one token per pass, 1.33× against 1.75×). In a real decode with reused keys and values, the per-step model is slightly worse than that baseline (Appendix E.6).

Table 19: Threshold early exit on the per-step model under a strong prior, CC; larger ε exits earlier. “Baseline” is the sampled-depth baseline interpolated to the same realized steps. The depth equivalent is the depth that baseline needs to match the model’s BPB, so 1.86× means the baseline needs 1.86 times as many iterations as the model runs. The bracketed interval recomputes it after moving the model’s BPB by the evaluation noise floor and is the figure to read; it includes only the evaluation noise floor, so the true uncertainty is at least this large. “Open” intervals have no upper end (see below the table). papers.selection_reason: Reevaluates compute savings of halting heads in looped LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.

papers.tldr: Halting heads may provide far less real compute savings than average iteration counts suggest, especially in batched generation.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.
authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap caused by direct FP4 post-training quantization.
Stores low-rank factors as binary ±1 sign vectors, reducing storage per rank-one component by 16× versus high-precision corrections.
Runs the correction through additions/subtractions on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM.
On 4B–72B LLMs, matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ.
A fused B300 kernel is at most 11% slower than FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for ranks up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 through batch size 8.

papers.tldr: BiLoCo uses binary low-rank corrections to recover FP4-quantized LLM accuracy with far less storage and limited inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Small language models deployed under cost, latency, or privacy constraints cannot simply switch to larger models when reasoning fails. Multi-candidate generate-then-rerank offers a natural test-time scaling route. However, more candidates do not always yield higher accuracy. We identify a previously overlooked bottleneck between generation and selection: a correct answer may appear in the candidate pool yet fail to be selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or misaligned with the answer mode the fixed selector expects. We term this loss the hidden interface tax and formalize a coverage-conversion decomposition that distinguishes raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage, the subset of problems where a correct candidate can actually be consumed by the selector. We propose Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction (CACC), an interface layer between the candidate source and the fixed selector that repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining either component. On numeric reasoning (GSM8K, competition_math), CACC raises both oracle coverage and final accuracy. On GPQA Diamond, CACC alone improves final accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2% (+13.6 pp); combined with proposer-side strengthening it reaches 25.8% (+20.2 pp). On MMLU-Pro, CACC exposes a coverage-conversion gap: answer-mode-compatible construction raises oracle coverage, but final accuracy decreases by 0.85 pp under the original selector; adding proposer-side strengthening improves final accuracy.
authors: Qianli Ma, Zhiqing Tang, Fanshuai Meng, Zhi Yao, Hanshuai Cui, Weijia Jia
bullets: Multi-candidate generation can contain a correct answer that is not selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or in the wrong answer mode.
The paper formalizes a coverage–conversion decomposition separating raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage.
Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining the generator or selector.
CACC improves GPQA Diamond accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2%; combined with proposer strengthening, accuracy reaches 25.8%.
On MMLU-Pro, improved answer-mode compatibility raises oracle coverage but slightly lowers final accuracy under the original selector, showing the method is selector-dependent.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies and mitigates the 'hidden interface tax' in multi-candidate reasoning for LLMs, proposing Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction to improve answer selection.
papers.title: Correct but Unselectable: The Hidden Interface Tax in Multi-Candidate Reasoning
papers.tldr: CACC improves multi-candidate reasoning by making correct generated answers compatible with a fixed selector, substantially boosting accuracy in some settings while revealing selector-dependent limits.

papers.abstract: Scientific, engineering, and mathematical reasoning tasks can admit multiple valid solutions, while exhaustive annotation of the full solution set is often prohibitively costly. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) applies reinforcement learning to unlabeled test instances, offering a label-free approach to multiple-solution reasoning. In this setting, generation frequency serves two opposing objectives: correctness estimation favors frequent outcomes, whereas outcome-level diversity preservation favors less frequent outcomes. We term this tension the \textbf{Frequency Conflict}. To resolve this conflict, we propose MS-TTRL, which obtains frequency-independent correctness estimates through Outcome-Level Self-Verification while reserving generation frequency solely for diversity preservation. Three-State Outcome Cache and the Candidate State support verification reuse across repeated observations and confidence-aware handling of ambiguous outcomes, while Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling selectively strengthens the learning signals of rare, reliably verified outcomes. Experiments across two benchmarks, four multiple-solution tasks, and three backbone models, each evaluated with five random seeds, show that MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the best-performing label-free baseline and approaches the performance of the supervised IPS-GRPO.
authors: Zhixia Zhang, Binqian Xu, Huaiyang Wang, Yikun Ban, Dianbo Liu
bullets: Multiple-solution reasoning lacks exhaustive labels, motivating reinforcement learning directly on unlabeled test instances.
The method uses outcome-level self-verification to estimate correctness independently of generation frequency.
A Three-State Outcome Cache and Candidate State reuse verification and handle ambiguous outcomes with confidence awareness.
Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling amplifies learning signals for rare outcomes that are reliably verified.
Across two benchmarks, four tasks, and three backbones, MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the strongest label-free baseline and nears supervised IPS-GRPO.

papers.abstract: Fixed-window Vision Transformer (ViT) decoders run at deployment resolution as overlapping tiles: every token in an overlap band is processed by several full decoder instances. In the 2.4B-parameter MiniMax-H3 video decoder, about half of all per-token computation is duplicated. Removing the tiles fails because attention, global tokens and coordinates are bound to them. TileShare keeps each released tile's attention and computes every other operation once per token. The released computation changes at one kind of step only: an overlap token's per-tile results are blended into one shared state with the released weights. Interventions show that this blend costs quality where attention reads the shared states, mainly in the first few layers, which TileShare therefore keeps per tile. Without training, keeping six layers per tile decodes 1.38-1.51x faster than batched and compiled tiling on two GPU types (up to 1.96x with FP8) and is equivalent to the released decoder in PSNR, LPIPS and DISTS on DAVIS videos. On unseen UVG videos with the setting frozen beforehand, it matches PSNR and DISTS and improves LPIPS. TileShare carries over to two further decoders and is again confirmed on unseen data. It is equivalent in PSNR and DISTS on MAGI-1. On the ViTok-v2 image autoencoder at 2K-4K, it matches overlapping tiling in PSNR, improves LPIPS and DISTS and decodes 1.5-1.8x faster. How many layers stay per tile is measured once per model (for decoders, without labels); we report it for 14 decoders and encoders. Optionally, two GPU-hours of self-distillation let MiniMax-H3 share every layer without a loss in PSNR, and a coordinate field trained while the network stays frozen brings fully shared CLIP-based open-vocabulary segmentation to parity with sliding windows on seven benchmarks.
authors: Xiangzhong Ye, Zhongshen Li, Shen You, Ziyang Meng, Liang Xu, Junkai Ji, Qiuzhen Lin, Xiangtao Li, Ka-Chun Wong
bullets: Overlapping tiles duplicate roughly half of per-token computation, but naively removing tiling disrupts attention, global tokens, and coordinates.
TileShare preserves tile-specific attention and blends overlap-token states, while keeping early layers per tile to protect quality.
Training-free decoding is 1.38–1.51× faster, up to 1.96× with FP8, while matching or improving reported perceptual metrics across tested video and image decoders.
The approach transfers to additional decoders and encoders, with validation on unseen video data and high-resolution image autoencoding.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
authors: Han Wang, Zhitao Wang, Natalia Frumkin, Xuanwu Yin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
bullets: MXFP4 training is challenging because FP4 quantization error can destabilize optimization.
ALTO combines hybrid block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, stochastic rounding, and simplified weight de-oscillation.
On C4 validation, the recipe reaches loss 3.3350 versus 3.3283 for BF16, recovering about half the gap from MXFP4 without de-oscillation.
De-oscillation reduces convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0% at the MLPerf quality target.
Differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling did not improve end-to-end results despite operator-level SNR gains.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce \textsc{RoboCode}, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single discrete code, \textsc{RoboCode} represents it as a soft composition of multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks address three questions. First, the learned primitive interface reconstructs action chunks with an average reconstruction MSE of 0.0187. Second, analysis of code activations reveals structured code reuse across tasks. Third, \textsc{RoboCode} achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success rate on all evaluated tasks, with an average success rate of 75.6%, compared with 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for the larger Diffusion Policy baseline. These results suggest that soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective and interpretable intermediate action representation for robot manipulation.
authors: Xianyue Peng, Devi Amarsaikhan, Iman Soltani
bullets: Addresses the lack of reusable action structure in policies that directly predict continuous action chunks.
Learns a shared soft-gated primitive interface, representing each action chunk as a composition of multiple primitives rather than one discrete code.
The primitive interface is learned from action chunks across tasks and frozen while task-specific encoders map states into the shared latent space.
On five ManiSkill tasks, it reconstructs action chunks with 0.0187 average MSE and reveals structured cross-task code reuse.
Achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success on every task, averaging 75.6% success versus 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for Diffusion Policy.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.
authors: Shibo Hong, Siyu Ren, FengJiao Chen, Zhongyuan Peng, Wei Shi, Yixin Cao
bullets: Existing rewards assess either visual quality with ground-truth videos or action fidelity without reliably handling visual artifacts.
AVM-Eval benchmarks inverse dynamics model reliability on real and generated videos using 67.2k pairs.
AVM-Pref provides complementary action-mismatch and video-mismatch preferences across 506.3k pairs.
The model transfers forward dynamics learned from real videos to generated-video assessment via joint training with a patch-weighted score head.
Experiments show IDMs are unreliable on generated videos, while ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines on both criteria in downstream reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.
authors: Jiaxing Sun, Junyuan Gao, Ruikang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Lingli Ge, Xiao An, Jiang Wu, Huazheng Zeng, Jiahe Song, Chen Zhu, Haote Yang, Jingchao Wang, Lu Chen, Yuanyuan Cao, Ruijie Zhang, Shengxin Lu, Weijia Li, Lijun Wu, Conghui He
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures from high-impact chemistry journals.
Uses a unified schema covering 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation.
Adds a reasoning-based difficulty taxonomy, modular annotation pipeline, and Oracle-MolRec protocol to separate molecular recognition from reasoning.
Evaluation across 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows performance drops with greater schema complexity and reasoning demands.
Data and code are released to support chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry research.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to ground generated text in the correct image regions, and existing explainability methods, such as attention maps and Logit Lens, often produce poor spatial explanations due to weak text-to-vision attention and sink tokens. We propose \textbf{Angular Relevance} ($R_L$), a simple visualization measure based on cosine similarity between visual token embeddings and unembedding-matrix rows. Because $R_L$ is invariant to token norm, it produces substantially sharper and more faithful heatmaps than attention maps or Logit Lens on out-of-the-box models. Without any training, $R_L$ yields competitive referring-expression segmentation (RES), outperforming prior diagnostic maps and CLIP-based training-free methods. To preserve localized object information during cross-modal mixing, we introduce \textbf{Angular Object-Aware Loss (AOL)}, an auxiliary loss that directly supervises visual token embeddings to align angularly with the vocabulary directions of their corresponding object concepts. Finetuning with AOL alongside the standard next-token prediction objective significantly sharpens object localization in heatmaps, showing that the VLM's own visual tokens can be used directly for grounding and improving RES, without training any segmentation heads and without degrading general VQA performance. We further demonstrate that the learned grounding also transfers to category-level segmentation of object categories not seen during training.

papers.abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Junxin Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Xiangchen Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runsong Zhao, Xinyu Liu, Shunjie Xing, Yifu Huo, Dingyang Lin, Qiuyu Gu, Yongyu Mu, Chenglong Wang, Changliang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the underweighting of high-entropy, low-visual-dependency tokens in prior advantage-reshaping methods.
Uses visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain selectively at high-entropy positions.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.
authors: Seiya Tokui, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Sosuke Kobayashi
bullets: The study examines whether fewer, wider heads better support retrieval under a fixed parameter budget.

Improvements persist with frozen attention projection weights, indicating benefits beyond attention-module updates.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.

papers.abstract: Continual survival analysis on whole-slide images (WSIs) requires models to integrate knowledge from sequentially arriving cancer cohorts while preserving previously learned information. Model merging offers a data-free alternative by combining independently fine-tuned task experts without retaining previous training data. However, the relative behavior of different merging strategies for WSI-based survival prediction remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we establish an end-to-end benchmark for data-free continual model merging, covering task-specific fine-tuning, sequential merging, and inference under both TASK-IL and CLASS-IL settings. We systematically evaluate six representative merging strategies across four TCGA cancer cohorts and three task orders using C-index, IPCW C-index, Forgetting, and Backward Transfer under a controlled protocol. Results show that no merging strategy consistently dominates across all evaluation criteria, while censoring-aware evaluation can substantially alter the relative ranking of the compared methods. This benchmark provides a unified foundation for developing and evaluating more effective continual model merging methods for WSI-based survival analysis.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.
authors: Dongki Kim, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Sung Ju Hwang

Retrieved hypotheses and principles guide subsequent prediction or candidate generation. New observations are then used to revise the hypotheses involved, and the updated hypotheses support principle reconstruction, forming a continuous cycle of scientific knowledge construction and application.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains a popular on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm owing to its stability and ease of implementation. Its clipping threshold, however, is fixed, so every training sample receives the same trust-region width regardless of how reliable the corresponding policy update is. This work examines adaptive-clipping variants of PPO in which the constant clipping parameter is replaced by sample-dependent thresholds computed from policy and return statistics. The central method, Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO (PPO-DAZ3), sets the clipping interval for each sample from two signals: action confidence, given by the probability of the selected action under the current policy, and update confidence, given by the normalized advantage magnitude. The rest of the standard PPO training pipeline is left unchanged. Evaluation on three classic control benchmarks (LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1) indicates that adaptive clipping improves learning in some settings but not all. PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, the smooth advantage-based variant PPO-AZ3S leads on Acrobot-v1, and standard PPO stays competitive on CartPole-v1, suggesting that adaptive clipping is most beneficial on harder control tasks.
authors: Taha M. Mahmoud, Naima Kaabouch
bullets: Standard PPO uses the same trust-region width for every sample, regardless of update reliability.
PPO-DAZ3 adapts each clipping interval using selected-action probability and normalized advantage magnitude.
The standard PPO training pipeline remains otherwise unchanged.
Across LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1, adaptive clipping helps in some environments but not all.
PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, PPO-AZ3S on Acrobot-v1, while standard PPO remains competitive on CartPole-v1.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly prediction (AP) aims to estimate future anomaly risks from current observations, providing early-warning signals for proactive intervention and maintenance in complex systems. Existing unsupervised AP methods follow a perturbation-based paradigm, where predefined or random perturbations are injected into historical windows to simulate abnormal future evolution. However, these methods share perturbations across different variables and contexts, and learn deterministic history-to-future evolution. In reality, anomaly evolution is variable- and context-dependent: the same perturbation may be amplified into abnormal future dynamics in one variable or context, while being absorbed as normal fluctuation in another. In addition, future evolution is not uniquely determined by a historical window, since similar histories may lead to multiple plausible trajectories, such as gradual degradation or abrupt changes. To address these problems, we propose EVOLVE, a unified framework that models unsupervised AP via variable- and context-conditioned perturbations and uncertainty-aware future reasoning. EVOLVE constructs context-specific anomaly perturbations through an adaptive anomaly prototype memory, which can dynamically update and retrieve relevant perturbations at the variable level. EVOLVE models uncertainty by sampling multiple latent historical states and decoding through complementary smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses, and the disagreement among decoded future trajectories is used to estimate future anomaly risk. Extensive experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that EVOLVE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly prediction baselines.
authors: Jianxin Jin, Kai Zhao, Shiyan Hu, Yang Shu, Peng Chen, Meng Wang, Zhongwen Rao, Yijie Li, Jing Wang, Bin Yang, Chenjuan Guo
bullets: Addresses the limitations of shared perturbations and deterministic history-to-future assumptions in unsupervised anomaly prediction.
Uses an adaptive anomaly prototype memory to retrieve and update variable- and context-specific perturbations.
Samples multiple latent historical states and decodes them with smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses.
Estimates future anomaly risk from disagreement among the resulting possible future trajectories.
Experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets show consistent improvements over existing anomaly-prediction baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of EVOLVE. Given a historical window, EVOLVE first encodes the input into a normal historical representation Hn T . During training, Adaptive Anomaly Injection (AAI) retrieves variable-conditioned perturbations from the Anomaly Prototype Memory (APM) and constructs an anomaly-aware historical representation Ha T , while Anomaly Pattern Analysis (APA) progressively updates the dynamic prototype bank using residual-based anomaly-aware future representations. Both the normal and anomaly-aware historical views are then processed by Uncertainty-Aware Latent Modeling (UALM), which samples multiple latent semantic hypotheses and estimates their evolution-mode probabilities. The Dual-Structured Decoder (DSD) decodes these hypotheses through smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses to generate multiple plausible future trajectories. During inference, anomaly-aware injection, APA, and dynamic prototype updating are disabled, and future anomaly scores are computed from the predictive disagreement among decoded trajectories.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.

Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are well suited to modeling the hierarchical structure of multimodal data, because hyperbolic volume grows exponentially with radius, enabling low-distortion representations of tree-like taxonomies from general to specific concepts. However, existing pretraining objectives for hyperbolic vision-language models entangle semantic alignment with entailment modeling, forcing radial coordinates to simultaneously encode semantic matching and hierarchical structure, leading to conflicting geometric constraints. In this paper, we introduce AURORA, a hyperbolic vision-language framework that decouples the objectives through angular alignment and a novel Radial-Angular Order Cone (RAOC) for entailment modeling. Angular alignment captures semantic similarity while preserving the radial structure for representing hierarchies. Unlike conventional entailment cones, RAOC determines angular allowance from relative parent-child radial gaps. It is incorporated into hierarchical entailment contrastive training to capture partial-order relations. We further introduce a norm regularization term that prevents undesirable radial degeneration for stable training. We train models on millions of image-text pairs and evaluate them across zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, and compositional understanding. Our model consistently outperforms strong Euclidean and hyperbolic vision-language baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of decoupling semantic alignment from hierarchical entailment modeling.
authors: Mingyang Gao, Yuwei Wu, Shiyu Luo, Wei Wu, Xiaomeng Fan, Qihao Lv, Haoyu Zhang, Rui Gao, Bingzhen Liu, Zhi Gao, Che Sun
bullets: Hyperbolic models can represent tree-like multimodal taxonomies efficiently, but existing objectives entangle alignment and hierarchy in radial coordinates.
AURORA uses angular alignment for semantic similarity while preserving radial structure for hierarchical organization.
Its Radial-Angular Order Cone (RAOC) models entailment using angular allowances based on parent–child radial gaps.
Hierarchical entailment contrastive training and norm regularization support partial-order learning and stable radial representations.
Evaluations on zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, and compositional understanding show consistent gains over Euclidean and hyperbolic baselines.

papers.abstract: Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion. We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7 +- 1.2% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/20 real-robot trials.
authors: Takuma Tsukakoshi, Elle Miller, Tamon Miyake, Namiko Saito, Yushi Wang, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Sethu Vijayakumar

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $\eta_B / \eta_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $\eta_B$, the initialization scale $\beta$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $\sigma_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $\eta_B \approx n \eta_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.
authors: Disen Liao, Yaoliang Yu
bullets: LoRA+ can improve adaptation with a larger learning rate for the up-projection matrix B, but its LR ratio is brittle under standard initialization.
A signal–noise analysis attributes instability to an initialization-induced noise term affected by the B learning rate, initialization scale, and adapter rank.
The proposed initialization scales A’s variance as proportional to n⁻² while retaining zero-initialized B, preserving zero initial adapter output.
It reduces initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1/n and substantially broadens the stable LR region across tested scales, ranks, and update multipliers.
Across tasks and models, it prevents high-ratio collapse and makes ηB ≈ nηA a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

papers.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.
authors: Jiazheng Li, Huaqing Zhang, Jing Xu, Tianle Cai, Jingzhao Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Sequential pretraining can improve specialized abilities but may cause forgetting of previously learned knowledge.
Core method: LARE automatically adjusts domain loss weights using running loss statistics, following a normalized inverse-square-root rule motivated by gradient-noise analysis.
Key finding: Loss reweighting provides an independent control beyond data-mixture ratios and can outperform both stages of sequential pretraining in controlled knowledge–mathematics experiments.

Results: On a 1.5B-parameter model trained on 240B tokens, LARE improved all five evaluated benchmarks across knowledge, mathematics, and code, averaging 7.84 percentage points over a matched direct mixture.
Scope: The approach improves capabilities without changing sampled data exposure or requiring additional weight-search runs.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.
authors: Xueyun Tian, Bingbing Xu, Jiaming Liu, Jinpeng Yu, Yang Shi, Yu Zhao, Ruihua Huang, Yuanzhuo Wang, Huawei Shen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding when to update internal reasoning and when to respond as streaming video events unfold.
Uses dual Inner and Response branches that share causal history but activate independently.
Allows relevant evidence changes to trigger reasoning updates while responses proceed concurrently when enough evidence is available.
Trained on 189K dual-stream examples using supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level reinforcement learning.
Improves response timing and answer accuracy across three proactive video understanding benchmarks.

(b) Specialized roles: reasoning supports event monitoring, while responses deliver the requested output. (c) Decoupled activation: responses supported by prior monitoring and current evidence need not await further reasoning.

papers.abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. An overview of our network architecture. The TravSUITE network first starts with a ResNet-style encoder (either 2d or 3d depending on the input modality), followed by BEV-space inpainting and parallel BEV decoder FCN heads. Since the individual prediction heads are relatively lightweight, the backbone and encoder must handle the majority of the feature extraction.

Fig. 5. Two scenarios from the test set. Cost and speed maps are cropped and enlarged to highlight regions of interest. (Top row): The robot must navigate through a path obscured by dense vegetation (cyan arrow). The Voxel+Inpaint network does the best at assigning low cost to the trail and high cost to the surrounding unobserved space, which is likely vegetation. (Bottom row): The robot is traveling at high speed on an open trail. Due to the speed, LiDAR measurements are relatively sparse. The inpainting method is able to fill in the missing trail features and keep a consistent speed map.

(Right) IRL with CVaR assigns enough cost to the cones for the vehicle to plan around into the grass.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.
authors: Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
bullets: Reframes row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks.
Identifies GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent as hard, zero-temperature decisions that discard alternative codewords.
Uses vector approximate message passing for soft blockwise posteriors, followed by exact block coordinate descent for refinement.
Evaluated on 2-bit lattice and 3-/4-bit scalar quantization across Llama, Qwen, and Mistral models.
Reports improved perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over hard-decision baselines, with compatibility with activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing.

papers.abstract: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits H\"older regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any H\"older index $\beta$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
authors: Hao Cheng, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong
bullets: Addresses offline soft Q-learning when reward distributions and dynamics are unknown.
Uses conditional diffusion models based on probability-flow ODEs to estimate reward and transition distributions.
Learns Q* with deep neural networks through a data-driven soft Bellman operator.
Provides nonasymptotic total-variation and excess Bellman-residual guarantees, without requiring Bellman completeness.
Experiments support the theory and show the method is effective; the stated rate depends on Hölder regularity and state-action dimension.

papers.abstract: Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably. Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. We present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline updating of the judge. Candidate experiences enter the library only after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image-judgment records and evaluated before reuse. We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. ImageRSI achieves a Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare system outcomes across judge-training configurations.
authors: Shuo Han, Zhilin Wang, Peng Ling, Wenjia Gong, Yang Liu, Guanjun Jiang, Yukun Cao, Xike Xie
bullets: Targets unreliable satisfaction of complex text-to-image requests and limited transfer of successful repairs across tasks.
Uses a frozen image generator with five-dimensional verification and repair, a shared experience library, and an offline-updated judge.
Adds experiences only after paired A/B validation; trains and evaluates the judge on accumulated image-judgment records before reuse.
Introduces ImageReq-Bench, containing 961 difficult real-world image requests with evaluation checklists.
Reports 52.6% CSA on MindBench and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and compares different judge-training configurations.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce EDWARD-NMT (Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for NMT), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a train once, deploy anywhere paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En-Vi), WMT-14 (En-De), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De-En benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.
authors: Edward Nguyen, Thai Tran, Kiet Anh Hoang, Duy Hoang, Duy Vo, Khanh Le, Vu Le
bullets: Addresses MoE deployment constraints: large expert memory requirements and fixed per-token top-k computation.
Uses elastic Matryoshka-style dimensions to reduce memory footprint at inference.
Employs an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned task-conditioned threshold for token-dependent expert selection.
Adds dual-consistency training to preserve the quality of extracted sub-networks.
Experiments across multiple translation and multilingual benchmarks show strong full models and sub-networks outperforming comparably sized dense Transformers without retraining.

papers.abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Tampered ML, a benchmark of 1,858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 86% of items are valid (95% CI: 81-91%). Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.
authors: Soroush Ebadian, Parand A. Alamdari, Joe Benton, Hailey Joren
bullets: Introduces 1,858 paired proposals: a reconstruction of a published ML experiment and a minimally edited flawed counterfactual.
Models must select the more methodologically sound proposal under both presentation orders.
Human validation estimates that 86% of benchmark items are valid (95% CI: 81–91%).
Frontier models perform above chance but remain unreliable; Opus 5 reaches 77.9% accuracy.
Models often favor flawed proposals that seem more specific, transparent, or conventional, and are sensitive to ordering.

Light bars show per-order accuracy, which scores each ordered presentation separately. The gap between light and dark bars reflects position sensitivity. papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk. This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.
authors: Hanwen Zhang, Enyi Jiang, Ruike Zhu, Qinan Yu, Sanmi Koyejo
bullets: Studies whether the best time to detect risk is also the best time to intervene.
Learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories, then applies one edit to an early hidden state while freezing model weights.
Evaluates interventions at each of the first five CoT positions with full post-edit regeneration across three distilled reasoning models.
Finds the strongest control effects at roughly two to three tokens; later states may predict risk better but can be ineffective for control.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, fully safe CoT-answer outputs increase from 29.06% to 82.05% on StrongREJECT-273, with benign refusal and usefulness near baseline.

papers.abstract: Language models can answer a question from a supplied document or from their parametric knowledge. When later asked where the answer came from, what determines their source report? We study this by intervening on the model's key-value (KV) cache after the answer is generated and before the source question is asked. On a controlled factual task with four models (7B-32B), changing or removing the document's cache never changes the report. In contrast, transplanting the question-and-answer (Q+A) cache between runs with identical question and answer tokens transfers it: every eligible report follows the donor, while the recipient's document is unchanged. On the two smaller models, steering Q+A values along directions fitted before any source question reverses 98.9-100% of reports across four document conditions at a fixed strength, while norm-matched random directions flip at most 1.1%. The components of keys and values along fitted directions carry the transplant effect: copying them alone nearly reproduces the report change; holding them fixed nearly prevents it. Applied during answer generation, the same value directions also change which source supplies the answer, though more weakly and depending on the prompt. Source reporting in this setting thus depends causally on cached state produced while answering. We do not establish general reporting accuracy or a complete interpretation of this state.
authors: Kirill Afendulev, Alexey Dontsov, Alla Chepurova, Elena Tutubalina, Anton Korznikov
bullets: Across four 7B–32B models, changing or removing the document’s KV cache did not alter source reports.
Transplanting the Q+A cache transferred the donor run’s source report while leaving the recipient document unchanged.
On two smaller models, fitted Q+A value directions reversed 98.9–100% of reports; random directions flipped at most 1.1%.
Key/value components along fitted directions largely reproduced or prevented the transplant effect.
The same directions influenced source selection during answer generation, but more weakly and prompt-dependently.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The document changes; the source report does not. The LLM answers “Tokyo” with a counterfactual document. Each edited branch keeps the original question-and-answer cache, and either removes the document entries or replaces them with an irrelevant fact, which remains readable. All three branches then report context to the source question, and the answer shown was generated before either edit. Schematic example; Table 2 gives results for all four models.

Figure 3: Source report follows the transplanted cache. Both runs answer “Paris”, but report different sources. We copy the donor’s Q+A cache into the recipient after answering, retaining the recipient’s document. Asked anew, the source question now elicits context. Colours identify the origin of cached state; the original question and its answer are not regenerated.

Figure 7: The report moves with question state, not with the edited document. Question swaps exchange counterfactual and irrelevant-fact runs; coloured dots show the fraction whose report follows the donor. Document swaps replace a counterfactual with an irrelevant fact (left), or an irrelevant fact with a true fact stating the answer (right): zero flips on every model. Document deletion also produces zero flips. Question swaps are asymmetric at 32B, motivating the answer-cache tests. Controls: Table 7.

Figure 4: Steering Q+A values changes the source report. Left: addition makes irrelevantdocument runs report context; both reach 100% at α = 2. Right: subtraction makes counterfactual runs report knowledge; both reach 100% by α = 3. The answer tokens remain fixed. Dotted curves show mean random-control rates over three draws, at most 1.1% on the left and zero on the right. Rates are over eligible item–split pairs. papers.abstract: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Due to the differences in their underlying assumptions and conceptual frameworks, these theories can disagree in their predictions about what tasks transformers find easy or hard. We map out seven theories of transformer capability (Star-free, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, $\mathsf{TC}^0$, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity) and translate their results into a common matrix of predictions across a suite of tasks covering different computational structures. We provide new theoretical results to complete this matrix. We then evaluate theoretical predictions through controlled experiments measuring in-distribution sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained language model performance. We find that no single theory explains the observed pattern of successes and failures. When a theory does not capture the transformer behaviors relevant to a task, its predictions break down; for instance, we show that the $k$-hop induction task is predicted hard by C-RASP because it does not model content-dependent attention, but we train small transformers on this task that length-generalize. Similarly, theories assuming hard attention like $\mathsf{AC}^0$ and BAPO predict binary majority to be hard, for which we also find success in practice. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.
authors: Awni Altabaa, Tobias Schnabel, Kiran Tomlinson
bullets: Maps seven theoretical frameworks to common predictions across tasks with varied computational structures.
Adds theoretical results to complete the comparison matrix and tests predictions using sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained-model behavior.
Finds theory–practice mismatches, including transformers length-generalizing on k-hop induction despite C-RASP predicting difficulty.
Finds practical success on binary majority despite hard-attention theories predicting it is hard.
Identifies soft attention, content-dependent retrieval, bounded per-position computation, inductive biases, and both upper and lower bounds as important ingredients.

papers.abstract: In drug development, lead optimization must improve competing properties, such as increasing permeability and reducing toxicity, while limiting scaffold changes that could compromise the lead's potency. RL-based post-training, such as C-MORAL, addresses this problem by fine-tuning molecular language models to directly optimize molecular leads for objectives of interest, which relies on expensive task-specific datasets and faces challenges in achieving multi-objective optimization (MOO). We argue a pre-trained model may already contain useful molecular edits that zero-shot generation cannot efficiently reach. Motivated by the limited search capabilities of zero-shot generation, we develop an efficient Metropolis-Hastings search strategy to better explore the proposal distribution. We propose ReMedI, which uses the molecular language model as a base proposer for inference-time alignment. Given a lead and a set of multi-objective tasks, the model proposes edits conditioned on the current molecule, while Metropolis--Hastings refinement guides sequential edits under an objective for property improvement, preservation, and lead similarity. On both C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD benchmarks, refinement improves frozen base models across three backbones, reaching significantly higher multi-objective optimization success rates compared to baselines. These search traces can then distilled into the base model which improves zero-shot generation and subsequent search using approximately 7.8 times less training molecular leads than that of C-MORAL. ReMedI achieves approximately 2.8 times the strict-success coverage of RL baseline C-MORAL, including on out-of-distribution tasks, with matched lead-relative similarity.
authors: Jia Yi Zhang, Shivanshu Shekhar, Allison McLevige, Tong Zhang
bullets: Targets simultaneous property improvement, preservation of lead quality, and minimal scaffold changes without task-specific RL fine-tuning.

Distills refinement traces into the base model to improve later zero-shot generation and search.
Improves frozen models across three backbones on C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD, with higher multi-objective success than baselines.
Reports approximately 2.8× the strict-success coverage of C-MORAL and uses approximately 7.8× fewer training molecular leads, while matching lead-relative similarity.
