papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/
authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Problem: Solver depth and open-loop execution horizon are usually tuned independently, creating a responsiveness–stability trade-off.
Method: Jointly adjust numerical sampling depth and execution horizon, using coarse integration as an implicit regularizer during extended open-loop execution.
Key insight: Numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, reducing compounding drift.
Results: The approach consistently improves task success and substantially lowers inference latency across simulated and real-world manipulation settings and multiple VLA backbones.
Scope: Coarse integration can hurt precision during rapid replanning, so its benefit depends on the execution horizon.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of computational-execution co-design in flow-matching Vision-Language-Action policies. Top: The policy conditions on multimodal observation ot and integrates linear probability flow with N forward Euler steps from prior noise x(0) ∼ N (0, I) to generate action chunk ât, committing to an open-loop prefix of length s on the robot before replanning at t+ s. Bottom: The coupling mechanism. Early solver truncation (N=2) contracts sample dispersion around the conditional centroid (R(2) < R(10)). Under rapid replanning (s=5), high-frequency closed-loop feedback exploits sample diversity; under extended commitment (s=20), coarse integration suppresses compounding lateral drift, reversing solver degradation and delivering up to 5.6× inference speedups.

Over 40 matched rollouts per cell across four configurations ((s=10, N0), (s=10, 2), (s=H,N0), and (s=H, 2)), all four quasi-static tasks consistently replicate the sign reversal; shallow sampling degrades success under rapid replanning (s=10) but systematically outperforms deep sampling under full-horizon commitment (s=H). papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.
authors: Qixin Xu, Zihan Zhu, Xiaojiang Liu, Bohan Lyu
bullets: Addresses mode collapse, where repeated sampling produces semantically repetitive outputs and misses rare strong solutions.
Uses submodular curation to pair prompts with diverse but correct multi-teacher answers.
Applies stochastic perturbations to special-token embeddings to implicitly condition the model toward distinct outputs.
Improves the quality–diversity frontier on WritingPrompts and BookMIA across two open-weight model families, while also improving sampling efficiency for math and code.
Supports reinforcement learning by sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating diversity collapse during training.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support bidirectional denoising and iterative refinement, but generation remains largely controlled by token-level masking schedules. This leaves draft-level refinement implicit and limits explicit control over when to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, revisit uncertain regions, or stop editing. We introduce Diffusion Editing Language Adapter (DELA), a plug-in framework that enables controllable draft refinement with a frozen DLM. DELA operates on clean, variable-length drafts using four explicit editing actions: Insert, Delete, Remask, and Stop. The controller determines when and where to edit the draft, while the frozen DLM fills masked regions through denoising, separating high-level edit control from token-level generation. A naive single-phase editor would be computationally expensive because arbitrary interior edits can disrupt prefix stability and limit reliable KV-cache reuse. To address this, DELA uses a two-phase decoding procedure: a fast, append-only drafting phase that supports KV-cache reuse, followed by a global refinement phase that enables targeted non-monotonic edits to the full draft. We train the controller using a staged curriculum that begins with learning local edit priors from synthetic recovery tasks and mined actions that improve draft quality. Subsequent stages refine edit selection through rollout-based outcome preferences and alignment with downstream task feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that DELA achieves gains of up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding while keeping the backbone frozen. DELA thus provides a modular approach to explicit draft-level control in diffusion language models.
authors: Xinsong Feng, Chenan Wang, Leshu Tang, Johnny Liu, Dong Li, Da Li, Haipeng Chen
bullets: Addresses the limited draft-level control of token-masking schedules in diffusion language models.
Uses a controller to choose when and where to edit, while the frozen backbone denoises masked regions.
Combines fast append-only drafting with global refinement to support efficient KV-cache reuse and non-monotonic edits.
Trains the controller with staged synthetic recovery, mined actions, rollout preferences, and downstream feedback.
Improves mathematical reasoning and code generation by up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding, with the backbone frozen.

The global refinement phase then unlocks the full action space to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, remask uncertain regions, or stop.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.
authors: Qiangong Zhou, Jiafeng Liang, Yimin Dong, Yang He, Hongxiang Li
bullets: Targets long-horizon robot tasks that require retaining information from human demonstrations.
Adds TTT with fast-weight context memory to InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5, using paired demonstrations and robot trajectories.
Studies memory transfer, truncated backpropagation, training objectives, gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization across video and image cues.
At the tested scale, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations.
In real-robot tests with single-frame cues, behavior still favored cups at fixed positions, suggesting limited cue use.

The left path queries the updated model with Q, then applies an output projection and a gated residual connection. The two MLPs depict two calls to the same inner model, before and after the update. The batch dimension, head splitting, and inner normalization and residual details are omitted for clarity.

Inner fast-weight updates and state transfer across segments are not drawn separately.

Figure 3: Memory operations in human demonstrations and robot trajectories. Blue denotes the human phase, and green denotes the robot phase. Figure 5: Incremental and absolute action targets during state autoregression. papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Behavior cloning is limited by costly, narrow demonstration data and insufficient coverage of successful states.

Generated behaviors are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for imitation learning.
Across four manipulation tasks, downstream success rises from 40% to 62% in simulation and from 39% to 78% on a real robot.
The approach is evaluated with a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection.

papers.abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
authors: Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses provenance verification when prompts can obscure semantic behavior and watermarking conflicts with constrained tool generation.
Injects structurally ambiguous probes that expose tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at tool interfaces.
Models the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations with lightweight Markov chains.
Sequential repair patterns distinguish intra-family variants with identical tokenizers, including evaluated Llama-3 8B and 70B variants.
Remains robust to prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling in the reported evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Attribution accuracy under defensive interventions. (a) Semantic baselines degrade substantially under prompt-based obfuscation, whereas AgentTrace remains stable across different system prompts. (b) Although higher generation temperatures introduce stochasticity, the Markovian trajectory modeling in AgentTrace maintains robust attribution performance.

Figure 1: Conceptual workflow of AgentTrace. A genuine target model may reproduce a structurally ambiguous identifier successfully. A spoofed model with a different tokenization pattern may produce malformed escaping or other serialization anomalies rejected by the parser. AgentTrace combines the tokenization-sensitive failure category with the subsequent sequence of repair operations to identify the underlying model.

Figure 4: Multi-step execution traces induced by the same adversarial identifier. Despite identical initial JSON errors, the Llama-3 variants exhibit divergent repair dynamics: the 8B model falls into truncation retry loops, whereas the 70B model employs structured escaping. These distinct sequential trajectories provide robust execution-level fingerprints.

Figure 2: Empirical repair-transition graphs for Llama-3 variants (edge thickness corresponds to transition probability). While both models suffer identical initial tokenization crashes, their repair strategies strictly diverge: (a) Llama-3-8B is trapped in repetitive correction loops, while (b) Llama-3-70B navigates toward success via structured repair.

papers.abstract: Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy-protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy-preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero-shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full-body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM-assisted prompting and pool-scoring mechanisms for anomaly-type identification. We enhance Grad-ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt-guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state-of-the-art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade-offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. papers.abstract: Non-stationarity induces test-time distribution shifts in time series forecasting (TSF), resulting in forecast residuals between predictions and the corresponding ground truth. Recent works on test-time adaptation for TSF address this by introducing lightweight calibration modules around frozen forecasters, updated using observations that become incrementally available at test time. Existing approaches typically employ channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming that forecast residuals are inherently channel-specific. However, we observe that forecast residuals often exhibit substantial shared structure across channels, suggesting that fully independent channel-wise parameterization may be redundant. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM), which shares adaptation capacity across channels through a shared adapter while retaining limited channel-specific flexibility through a low-rank channel-wise adapter, further enhanced by channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation. Extensive experiments show that DBCM consistently outperforms prior methods across diverse datasets, horizons, and backbones.
authors: Jaebyeong Jeon, Kunwoo Kang, Sang Yup Lee, Kibok Lee
bullets: Forecast residuals under distribution shift often share structure across channels, making fully independent channel-wise adaptation potentially redundant.
DBCM uses a dual-branch module: a shared adapter plus a low-rank channel-wise adapter.
Channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation further refine the calibration process.
Experiments across diverse datasets, forecasting horizons, and backbones show consistent improvements over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM). papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
authors: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haichen Liao, Yinhai Wang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in MLLM-based driving, where committing to one interpretation can cause premature errors.
Uses particle-filter-inspired belief tracking: a VLM propagates, scores, and resamples diverse scene hypotheses as observations arrive.
On Bench2Drive, improves Driving Score from 68.50 to 81.37 and Success Rate from 41.36% to 54.09%.
Shows the largest gains in ambiguous situations, including unsignalized intersections and oncoming-traffic interactions.
Also improves interactive behaviors such as merging, emergency braking, and giving way.

figures.caption: Figure 2: DriveMind overview. (a) An asynchronous fast–slow architecture: a slow vision-language model (VLM) maintains a multi-hypothesis belief state, while a fast diffusion planner generates trajectories. (b) Belief tracking through hypothesis propagation and reweighting. (c) The belief state evolves as new observations arrive.

Figure 1: From single-chain reasoning to mind-evolving belief. (a) Instance-Based Framework: one rationale per timestep. (“CoT” stands for “Chain of Thought”) (b) Mind-Evolving Framework: multiple hypotheses {hk t } propagated over time; darker color indicates higher hypothesis weight.

Figure 4: Belief evolution and weighted action selection. The ego vehicle approaches an intersection with a left-turn command and a cyclist near the crosswalk. papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.
authors: Xiutian Zhao, Luqi Sun, Bj\"orn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
bullets: The study identifies cognitive-impairment contrast neurons (CICNs) in decoder MLPs across eight open LALMs using two speech corpora.
Ablating small CICN sets produces large, class-directed prediction shifts in 3 of 5 eligible models, including transcript-only decisions.
Interventions localize influence before the final answer position, especially after speech or transcript evidence, mainly by shifting decision direction.
Frozen CICN activations support strong within-Pitt linear readouts (0.92–0.97 AUC), but matched random and all-neuron readouts perform similarly.
Findings separate concentrated causal control of outputs from broadly distributed information useful for CI detection; CICN unit-budget advantages remain exploratory.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks. Yet the quantitative form of this influence--- and whether it is calibrated to source reliability--- remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form ``[Source] thinks the answer is (X)''. We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM. We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer's log-odds, with question--target susceptibility largely shared across sources. To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions. Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering.
authors: Anxin Guo, Chirag Pabbaraju, Sara Ahmadian, Kamesh Munagala, Aravindan Vijayaraghavan
bullets: Studies hint-induced answer changes on MMLU questions across Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM models.

A formal decomposition and synthetic experiments examine how KL-regularized reward training may produce these shifts.
The response is poorly calibrated to source reliability: shifts persist even when sources are labeled inaccurate or untrustworthy.

papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models (LVLMs), which aims to mitigate language bias during inference. Existing approaches typically adopt test-time scaling techniques such as contrastive decoding to improve inference performance. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches is far from satisfactory due to intentional evidence removal during perturbations and redundant inference cost. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration (MAGIC). The core of our MAGIC is to evaluate the decision margins of LVLMs to selectively activate textual and visual perturbation branches for efficient debiased inference. In particular, our MAGIC first measures the prediction margins of crucial tokens, and applies a gating function to identify low-confidence responses that are susceptible to language biases. For selected samples, we integrate the token logits from multiple textual and image perturbation branches with the original ones for debiased decision. More importantly, we selectively restore the most informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions for ambiguous samples after debiasing, enabling evidence recovery for discriminative decision-making. We further utilize a calibration dataset to actively identify and prune ineffective branches during contrastive debiasing for cost reduction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed MAGIC in comparison with extensive baselines.
authors: Shunshun Gu, Enze Zhang, Ming Pei, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse activation, but storing their expert parameters remains a major memory bottleneck. We introduce GS-MoE, a training-free compression framework that addresses redundancy across and within experts through two compression axes: shared-subspace rank and expert intermediate width. Groupwise low-rank representations capture shared structure across experts while retaining expert-specific projections, and Nystr\"om-based neuron compression reduces intermediate width within each expert. For fixed shared subspaces, we derive per-expert reconstruction-error reductions from the reconstruction objective and use them to guide expert grouping. Budgets are allocated hierarchically using a gradient-free layer-importance score to guide the allocation of rank and width budgets across layers, which eigenvalues and leverage then distribute as non-uniform ranks across groups and intermediate widths across experts. Experiments demonstrate the complementary benefits of compression along both axes, particularly at high compression rates on fine-grained MoE models. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, at a 60% reduction in total model parameters, GS-MoE retains approximately 90% of the uncompressed model's average reasoning performance, compared with 73% for D$^2$-MoE, while achieving 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity. We provide a code implementation at: https://github.com/cbacary/GS-MoE
authors: Carson Cary, Yukai Jin, Yihao Huang, Zhankai Ye, Fangyi Li, Ting Hua, Xin Liu, Shangqian Gao
bullets: Targets the memory bottleneck caused by storing parameters for many MoE experts.

Uses reconstruction error to group experts and gradient-free importance scores to allocate layer, rank, and width budgets.
On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, retaining about 90% of average reasoning performance at 60% parameter reduction, versus 73% for D²-MoE.
Also achieves 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity at that compression level; results emphasize fine-grained MoE models and high compression rates.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
authors: Siyang He, Qiqi Wang, Fan Liu, Yuncheng Huang, Pengfei Xu, Xi Chen, Ziwei He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Targets the trade-off between diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence in LLM-generated microdramas.
Uses trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation to explore varied causal story paths.
Builds a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to retrieve historical information relevant to future narrative goals.
Introduces MiDramaBench and causal-pattern metrics for evaluating script logic, creativity, repetition, and diversity.
Across three backbone LLMs, it reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and reaches a Logic score of 82.5 on 60-episode scripts up to 60k words.

Figure 3 Overview of our multi-agent pipeline for microdrama script generation. (1) Outline Planner creates a four-stage coarse outline. (2) Evolutionary tree search refines event sequences through mutation and trope-guided selection. (3) Develop into episode outlines.(4) Backward Narrative Dependency Tree is constructed from episode outlines to organize subsequent future-aware narrative memory, with episodes attached to goal nodes to guide retrieval. (5) Agents retrieve memories, plan scenes, generate scripts, and update memories after each episode.

Episode outlines guide the backward construction of goal dependencies and episode attachment. Generated events, clues, and foreshadowing are linked to goal nodes, enabling retrieval from the current episode’s goals and their prerequisite subtrees to support subsequent script generation.

Figure 6 Construction pipeline of MiDramaBench. Source texts are selected by length, deduplicated, and screened for dramatic adaptation potential. Core plot developments, character relationships, and world settings are extracted to guide the dramatic adaptation of each source into a microdrama idea. Qualityreviewed ideas are grouped by genre-label embeddings and sampled within each length–cluster group to form the evaluation subset.

Figure 7 A complete backward narrative dependency tree (BNDT) generated for a 40-episode wartime drama. Orthogonal connectors show parent–child dependencies and each child is a prerequisite for its parent. All 28 node goals are reproduced from the generated tree, in depth-first order.

papers.abstract: Regularisation-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods control the stability-plasticity trade-off through fixed coefficients tuned offline, independently of the continual learning objective and blind to phase-specific variations in data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity. We argue this is a fundamental mismatch and propose REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning, which treats regularisation strength selection as a sequential decision problem. At each incremental phase, a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) agent observes a compact state of current performance metrics and incoming data statistics, and outputs the distillation coefficients for that phase. To respect CIL's constraint on historical data access, the policy is trained entirely on pseudo-CIL tasks constructed from the initial phase, then deployed on the incremental sequence without further adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that REDAR reduces forgetting and improves forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and that policies trained on short pseudo-task horizons transfer effectively to longer incremental runs.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Fixed regularisation coefficients can mismatch changing data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity across phases.
A lightweight RL agent observes performance and incoming-data statistics, then selects phase-specific distillation coefficients.
The policy is trained on pseudo-CIL tasks from the initial phase, avoiding access to historical data during deployment.
Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet show improvements over fixed and heuristic baselines, with transfer from short to longer pseudo-task horizons.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of REDAR. (a) Reinforcement-driven regularisation is formulated as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP), M = (S,A, T ,R, γ), where the state si = (Ai−1, Fi−1, CRi, ISi) summarises the current learning dynamics, the action ai = (αi, βi) specifies the phase-specific regularisation coefficients, and the reward ri is the validation accuracy after CIL training. (b) The CIL model jointly optimises cross-entropy, feature distillation, logit distillation, and margin ranking losses while learning from replay memory and incoming samples. (c) The policy is trained offline on pseudo-CIL tasks using a distributed actor–learner architecture with prioritised experience replay before being deployed on the target incremental sequence.

Figure 2. Top: Phase-wise accuracy on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet under the N = 5 incremental setting. Accuracy is reported as the mean over all classes seen after each phase. Bottom: coefficients (α, β) used to train each phase.

Figure 3. Cross-setting transfer evaluation on CIFAR-100. Each cell reports ACC (%) for a policy trained on Ntrain phases and deployed on Ntest phases. Diagonal entries (pink outline) correspond to standard in-distribution evaluation.
Table 1. Performance comparison on average accuracy ACC, average forgetting FRG and forward transfer FWT on CIFAR-100.
Table 2. Performance comparison on average accuracy ACC, average forgetting FRG and forward transfer FWT on TinyImageNet.
Table 4. Ablation results of the state representation

papers.tldr: REDAR uses reinforcement learning to adapt regularisation strengths across class-incremental learning phases, reducing forgetting while improving forward transfer.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have been increasingly adopted in consumer smart-home camera systems to interpret recorded videos and provide insights. However, video clips captured from smart-home cameras are different from curated web videos dominating existing VLM benchmarks. Smart-home video clips often do not contain subtitles or narration and are captured from different viewing angles, under various lighting conditions, and in diverse scenarios. However, the capabilities of the model in this domain, under sparse visual signals and limited context, are not fully assessed by existing VLM benchmarks. To close this gap, we introduce OpenHome, a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating smart-home video understanding. It contains 2,254 questions on 1,118 real-world video clips and organizes 10 tasks into three capability levels. Perception evaluates visible content, Reasoning evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal relationships, and Insight evaluates subject intent, supporting evidence and appropriate homeowner responses. Based on the dataset, we describe the task design, data pipeline and evaluation protocol, and report results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 81.2% overall accuracy. Frontier closed-source models outperform open-weight models on every level. The best closed-source model leads the best open-weight model by 16.3% on Perception, 22.4% on Reasoning and 37.4% on Insight.
authors: Xianglong Wang, Neil Rodrigues, Pei Guo, Yiru Fang, Kevin Beussman, Shuyang Wang, Jingzhi Wang, Liangju Li, Shunyao Xu, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen
bullets: Introduces a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark with 2,254 questions across 1,118 real-world clips.
Organizes 10 tasks into Perception, Reasoning, and Insight capability levels.
Evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal understanding, plus subject intent, evidence, and homeowner response suggestions.
Reports results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs; the best model achieves 81.2% overall accuracy.
Closed-source models outperform open-weight models at every level, with the largest gap on Insight.

Each example includes three key frames with timestamps and a question with its correct answer. Answer options are omitted for readability; each benchmark question has four options.

Figure 1: The OPENHOME capability ladder. Three capability levels and 10 tasks, ordered from Perception to Insight. Perception and Reasoning check that a model saw and followed the clip correctly; Insight checks that it understood the subject and knows what the homeowner should do. Tasks are scored independently. The arrows indicate hypothesised relationships, not measured error propagation.

papers.abstract: Video encoder models are increasingly used as world models for physical AI, where a policy plans by rolling out the latent, so what physics the latent holds bounds what the agent can plan over. Moreover, existing interpretability work probes quantities belonging to a single object; the quantities that make physics relational, such as momentum transfer, restitution, and friction, are defined between bodies and have not been examined. We probe relational physics attributes in two frozen self-supervised video encoders (V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE) under two-body settings and test if they transfer across environments. Our early findings are mixed. Both encoders separate elastic from inelastic collisions reliably. V-JEPA2's own predictor is less likely to predict a collision that creates kinetic energy compared to one that loses it. Momentum-violation detection appears in only one of the two encoders, a kinetic-energy readout survives a change of environment for V-JEPA2 but not for VideoMAE, and neither model holds a friction coefficient that survives a change of geometry.
authors: Ayushi Mehrotra, Sai Vidyaranya Nuthalapati
bullets: Examines relational quantities between objects, including momentum transfer, restitution, kinetic energy, and friction.
Tests frozen V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE encoders in two-body interaction videos and evaluates cross-environment transfer.
Both encoders reliably distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions.
V-JEPA2 is less likely to predict collisions that create kinetic energy, while momentum-violation detection appears in only one encoder.
Kinetic-energy representations transfer across environments for V-JEPA2 but not VideoMAE; friction representations transfer across geometry for neither.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Whether attribute emergence is visible depends on the pooling, not on the model. Out-of-fold R2 across depth on the 150 momentum-conserving clips, mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. Solid: object-local pooling, object A’s own tokens. Dashed: frame-wide pooling, the protocol of the single-object literature. Under object-local pooling the quantities are already available at the patch embedding and nothing emerges; under frame-wide pooling every curve starts at zero and rises through the first third. Mask-only floors at A.pre, computed under the identical protocol, are negligible (−0.37 to +0.05 for VideoMAE-base, −0.15 to +0.22 for V-JEPA2-ViT-L).

Figure 6: A frame-wide pool carries the sum of the two objects and not their difference. Out-offold R2 across depth, pool all.pre, 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. The symmetric combination vA + vB reaches 0.955 and 0.938, well above either individual velocity, while the antisymmetric combination vA − vB peaks at 0.011 and 0.023—those are maxima over all 13 and 25 layers, so there is no depth at which the difference is recoverable.

Figure 7: The five two-body regimes. One clip per regime, cropped to the action; contact falls at frame 20 in every scene. Rows one and two are the same seed with and without the momentum edit, and share a crop, as do rows three and four: the members of a pair are identical up to the contact frame and diverge only afterwards, so nothing before contact distinguishes them. Green borders mark momentum-conserving clips, red momentum-violating ones, purple the physically impossible arm. The ratio at the right of each row is KEpost/KEpre. Reading that column shows why the energy experiment needs its own stimuli: the momentum edit moves kinetic energy as a side effect (the elastic violating twin lands at 2.15), so energy creation cannot be attributed to anything on the momentum axis. Only the last row creates energy while conserving momentum exactly.

Figure 3: Energy created against energy conserved, read two ways. Left: out-of-fold AUC of a linear probe separating the clips that create energy (e = k) from those that conserve it (e = 1) across depth, pooled all.pre; momentum is conserved in both sets. Both encoders peak far below an observer given the contact geometry, which reads the same label at 1.000. Right: the models’ own surprise, with nothing fitted. Each is shown only the pre-contact segment, which the three endings share exactly, and emits one forecast. Note the differing y scales.

Figure 4: The ingredients of friction decode; the coefficient does not follow. Out-of-fold R2 for incline angle θ, down-slope acceleration a and friction coefficient µ across depth on 150 incline scenes, mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. Each encoder is shown at its own best pool. The dotted line is the oracle ceiling: µ recovered from (a, θ) on ground-truth labels through the identical protocol, R2 = 0.997. θ is already at 0.957 and 1.000 at the patch embedding.

Figure 1: Momentum-violation detection across depth, by elasticity. Out-of-fold AUC of the norm route—regress the ∆p vector, take | · | outside the probem, pooled all.pre. The grey line is chance. Legend values give the best layer with its p corrected by a grid-max permutation null over all layers. VideoMAE clears the corrected null in both regimes; V-JEPA2 clears it marginally in the elastic regime and not at all in the inelastic one.

Figure 2: Elastic versus inelastic collisions across depth. AUC from the all.post pool on the 150 momentum-conserving clips (75 per class), mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. The distinction is built through the network, rising from 0.581 and 0.536 at the patch embedding. Both peaks lie below an observer given the contact geometry, which reads the same label at AUC 1.000 from restitution alone.

Table 2: A friction coefficient decoded within one floor geometry does not survive a change of geometry, while cube size does. Probes are trained on one dataset and applied unchanged to the other, restricted to the overlapping µ range [0.151, 0.399] (164 slide / 148 incline scenes), pool all.all, each domain standardised by its own moments so only the direction has to transfer. The two sets make µ a different function of the visible kinematics — flat: µ = a/g with corr(µ, a) = +0.9998; tilted: µ = (sin θ − a/g)/ cos θ with corr(µ, a) = −0.645 — so a readout that is really tracking acceleration cannot cross. SIZE is the control: it faces the identical domain gap (camera 14 vs 18, flat vs tilted, different band pattern). The third row of each block is the diagnostic: the same µ probe scored against the target set’s acceleration.

Table 3: The same four quantities, read from four pools. Out-of-fold R2 at the best layer. Objectlocal pools read their own object well and the other poorly; the frame-wide pools reverse this, reading each object worse than its own pool does while reading the sum better than any object-local pool reads anything.

Table 1: Reading µ directly and composing it from decoded (a, θ) give the same answer, because on this set they are the same function. Out-of-fold R2 on the incline set (n = 150), grouped folds with nested ridge penalty, mean ± sd over 12 fold seeds; each encoder at its own best pool. DIRECT regresses µ from activations. COMPOSED decodes a and θ separately and learns a second-stage linear map from the out-of-fold (â, θ̂) to µ. Every stage is out-of-fold, so no scene’s own â or θ̂ is used to fit the map that scores it. Over the sampled range µ is 0.997 linear in (a, θ), so the two routes are the same function and the tie is uninformative rather than positive.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video Encoders using Multi-Object Interaction Videos
papers.tldr: This study probes whether frozen video encoders represent relational physics, finding reliable collision-type distinctions but limited, encoder-dependent transfer across environments and geometries.

papers.abstract: In neural networks, continual learning (CL) is a prominent approach for enabling deployed systems to adapt to dynamic operational environments by effectively learning from new unseen data at runtime. Recently, the neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) concept has emerged as an energy-efficient alternative to CL by leveraging sparse event-based operations. However, NCL performance can be undermined by transient faults in the hardware platforms, which may come from high-energy particle strikes at any time. Currently, NCL reliability under transient faults has not been studied, and hence the corresponding fault-tolerance techniques remain unexplored. To address this, we propose a novel RobustNCL framework to improve NCL reliability in the presence of transient faults in the DRAM-based off-chip memory of hardware platforms through a lightweight detect-and-cure strategy. Specifically, it first monitors the presence of faults during weight data access from off-chip memory, and then cures the accessed weights if anomalous signatures are detected. It provides three curing variants: replacement with zero, min/max value, and most-probable value from the original/clean weight distribution. To support this, the weight curing values are stored in the radiation-hardened memory. Experimental results show that, in the presence of high fault rates (e.g., 5x10^{-4} for memory replay), RobustNCL maintains high accuracy close to the accuracy of fault-free models (i.e., within -0.5% accuracy for the best RobustNCL variant) and significantly improves accuracy from the baseline without fault mitigation across different NCL methods and datasets (i.e., Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100), while incurring negligible latency and energy overheads. These results highlight that our RobustNCL framework is a promising approach for enabling reliable and energy-efficient NCL systems.
authors: Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Shuochen Zhou, Muhammad Shafique
bullets: Targets transient faults in off-chip DRAM, a previously unexplored reliability threat for neuromorphic continual learning.
Monitors weight accesses for anomalous signatures and repairs affected weights at runtime.
Supports zero, min/max, or most-probable-value replacement using values stored in radiation-hardened memory.
Across Split MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, it stays within 0.5% of fault-free accuracy in the reported high-fault setting and outperforms mitigation-free NCL.
Scope: evaluates memory-fault mitigation for NCL; effectiveness depends on the tested fault conditions and curing variant.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The RobustNCL framework, showing the transient fault exposure stage, our detect-and-cure (D&C) strategy stage supported by weight replacement (curing) value selection, and the NCL training stage. RobustNCL variants depend on how the faulty weights are replaced by selected curing weights.

Figure 6: Experimental results from different NCL methods: (a) Subnet and (b) MR. These results show weight distributions of both the fault-free and faulty models from their layer 2 at certain model states (i.e., after training task 1 and task 2), inference tasks (i.e., task 1 and task 2), and fault rates (fR = 1×10−5 for Subnet and fR = 1×10−4 for MR).

Figure 3: (a) The NCL pipeline consists of three phases: the offline training at design time, the NCL training at runtime, and the inference at runtime. (b) DRAM organization overview, including channels, ranks, chips, and banks.

Figure 1: RobustNCL effectively improves NCL reliability againts transient faults in the DRAM off-chip/main memory under a task-incremental learning (TIL) scenario across different benchmarks: (a) Split MNIST, (b) Split Fashion-MNIST, and (c) Split CIFAR-10, across different NCL methods: task-specific subnetwork (Subnet) and memory replay (MR). The fault rate is denoted as fR considering a DDR3-1600 2Gb DRAM chip (Micron, 2010), RobustNCL variants are with v1-v3 codes.

Figure 5: Transient-fault modeling in the DRAM with several key steps: flattening multiple banks into a continuous memory space, injecting transient faults, and curing anomalous weights. Transient fault injection can happen at any time, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
Table 2: Final average accuracy (%) obtained by the MR method on the 5-task datasets evaluated across all trained tasks (task 1 – task 5) and across different fault-mitigation techniques.
Table 1: Final average accuracy (%) obtained by the Subnet method on the 5-task datasets evaluated across all trained tasks (task 1 – task 5) and across different fault-mitigation techniques.
Table 3: Final average accuracy (%) obtained by both the Subnet and MR methods on the 10-task dataset (Split CIFAR-100) evaluated across all trained tasks (task 1 – task 10).

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning methods, specifically neuromorphic continual learning under transient hardware faults.
papers.title: RobustNCL: Robustifying Neuromorphic Continual Learning under Transient Faults with Lightweight Detect-and-Cure Strategy
papers.tldr: RobustNCL improves neuromorphic continual learning reliability under transient DRAM faults using lightweight runtime detection and weight repair with negligible overhead.

papers.abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Architecture of one Kolibri block, which all 50 blocks share. The attention andMoE sublayers each read from the residual stream through an RMSNorm and write back through a second one. Orange marks what only the 40 SWA blocks have: RoPE on queries and keys, and amask over the 512 preceding tokens and the query token. The strip on the left shows which blocks use full attention. The router scores all 384 routed experts, sends the token to the 6 with the highest scores and weights their outputs by those sigmoid scores gi without renormalisation.

Figure 2. Post-training benchmark scores of Kolibri, Kolibri Origin and three openmodels in four domains, from Tables 28 and 29. Badges mark the English (EN) and German (DE) version of a benchmark; the scale runs from 0% at the centre to 100% at the outer ring.

Figure 1. Average English and German benchmark scores of base (top) and post-trained (bottom) models against decoded bytes of text per second and GPU, where higher and further right is better. Every model runs in its fastest configuration on eight B200 GPUs at a sequence length of 4k (base) or 16k (post-trained). Scores from Tables 17, 28 and 29; evals in Sections 2.4.1 and 3.3.1; plot details in Appendix A.

Figure 22. Steering the language of the teacher’s reasoning on German prompts, shown on amath problem. Both variants send the same system and user turns. Left, the system prompt instructs the model to reason in German, and the model opens the think block itself; its trace shows the case that switches to English partway. Right, the assistant turn is sent already opened with <think> and a German opener, which the model continues. We checked the language consistency of both approaches on more than 5000 completions each.

Figure 12. Documents entering each stage of the CC pipeline, split into the documents the stage kept and removed. Each stage receives what the previous one kept. Substring deduplication removes text within documents and drops a document only when fewer than 100 bytes of it remain, so its effect on bytes is larger than on documents.

Figure 3. Training loss of the three stages of Kolibri, each against the tokens of that stage and on its own token axis. Mid-training starts from the pre-training checkpoint at step 264750 and long-context extension from the mid-training checkpoint at step 34200. Thin lines are the per-step loss at a sample of the steps, thick lines its mean over bins of 20B, 5B and 1B tokens. Each stage trains on its ownmix, so the loss levels of different stages are not comparable.

Figure 37. Weight push from the trainer to the inference replicas. At startup, the receive buffers are mapped to the trainer parameters, and each parameter is assigned a trainer rank such that the bytes per rank are balanced. After every optimiser step, the trainer ranks push the new weights via RDMA into the single receiving replica of each node, from where they are broadcast to the node’s other replicas over NVLink. The conversion on the trainer side is batched and pipelined, and the intra-node NVLink distribution reduces load on the inference node’s NICs. The single-GPU replicas of our deployment skip the split of the weights into a per-replica layout.

Figure 6. Proxy at scale M trained with the Kolibri tokeniser and with plain BPE of the same vocabulary size. Left: BPB averaged over the English and German pre-training benchmarks after pre-training. papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one block of layers repeatedly, and the design pays off only if depth is reusable: loop steps beyond the trained budget must remain usable at inference. We ask whether that rests on normalising the state between loop steps, as the released Ouro models do, or on agreement between the loop a model is trained with and the loop it is run with. On released weights this loop-boundary normalisation can be removed without adding parameters and with the readout path bit-identical, and the operation is an identity at one loop step, which serves as an implementation check. Removing it takes Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B to zero accuracy by the trained budget on a balanced binary task (chance 0.500). State-norm growth, the failure that prior accounts predict, is not the cause: the norm stays within a factor of 2.021 while the head commits to a single wrong token. Yet in 19M-parameter models trained from scratch on two synthetic tasks, 16 seeds per configuration, training without the normalisation is never worse than training with it and extrapolates better: the two are closest at the trained depth and separate on both sides of it (Cliff's delta up to 0.867 beyond the budget). Both results follow if agreement, and not the normalisation itself, is what keeps depth reusable. The damage sits in the readout together with the last layer of the block: in the models trained from scratch, refitting the head over the frozen modified loop recovers a third of the lost accuracy and plateaus, while refitting the last block layer with it recovers all of it. Finally, comparing looped with stacked depth at an equal inference loop count is confounded by unequal overshoot of the trained budget; at matched overshoot the advantage of looping vanishes on one task and shrinks on the other.
authors: Ivan Viakhirev, Kirill Borodin, Maxim Abramov, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Removing boundary normalisation from released Ouro models causes performance to collapse by the trained depth, despite limited state-norm growth.
In models trained from scratch, removing normalisation is not worse and often extrapolates better beyond the trained depth.
The failure is localized to the readout and final block layer: refitting both restores the lost accuracy, while refitting only the head gives partial recovery.
Comparisons between looped and stacked models should match overshoot beyond the trained depth; under this control, looping’s advantage disappears on one task and shrinks on another.

papers.title: Agreement rather than normalisation keeps depth reusable in looped language models
papers.tldr: Depth reuse in looped language models appears to depend more on agreement between training and inference loops than on loop-boundary normalisation itself.

papers.abstract: PDE foundation models enable data-efficient adaptation but are deployed autoregressively, so short-horizon accuracy need not imply reliable simulation. We ask whether the short-horizon advantage of a foundation-model recipe persists when its predictions are repeatedly fed back as inputs for a long horizon. We define error amplification as G=E(H_f)/E(H_s), which measures full-horizon error relative to short-horizon error. We evaluate seven models on seven two-dimensional time-dependent PDE datasets: scratch-trained FNO and DeepONet; fine-tuned DPOT, GPhyT, Poseidon, and Walrus; and frozen in-context VICON. We report VRMSE, relative L_2, and relative MAE. Six datasets provide paired short- and full-horizon scores, while CE-RM contributes short-rollout sweeps only. At least one fine-tuned foundation model outperforms both scratch baselines in 26 of 30 short-rollout dataset--budget cells under every metric. Nevertheless, full-horizon VRMSE exceeds short-horizon VRMSE in 140 of 144 paired trained configurations, with a median error amplification of $2.04$. The count below VRMSE one falls from 104 to 53, and 12 full rollouts exceed ten although none does at the short horizon. Walrus achieves the lowest full-horizon VRMSE in 16 of 24 cells, yet its median error amplification is $2.70$. Relative L_2 and relative MAE show the same qualitative pattern. These results show that favorable short-horizon rankings can coexist with substantial error amplification. PDE foundation-model benchmarks should therefore report horizon-resolved absolute errors, amplification statistics, and failure incidence rather than a single local forecast score.
authors: Jaewan Park, Seid Koric, Giri Krishnan, Sudhakar Pamidighantam, Surresh Marru
bullets: Evaluates seven models across seven two-dimensional, time-dependent PDE datasets using VRMSE, relative L2, and relative MAE.
Fine-tuned foundation models beat both scratch baselines in 26 of 30 short-rollout dataset–budget cells.
Full-horizon VRMSE exceeds short-horizon VRMSE in 140 of 144 paired configurations, with median error amplification of 2.04.
Walrus has the lowest full-horizon VRMSE in 16 of 24 cells, but its median amplification is 2.70.
Results motivate reporting horizon-resolved errors, amplification, and failure incidence—not only local forecast accuracy.

papers.abstract: We introduce TWIG (Tree-structured Weights with Inherited Gates), a representation in which every weight of a neural network is the end of a path of small discrete decisions: a sign, a shift by a power of two, a zero gate, an index into a shared table. Weights that belong together share the upper part of their paths, and each decision is inherited by every weight below it, so it is stored once and applied once. This simple change has three consequences. Any trained network can be written as a TWIG, and when the decisions are powers of two its weight layers become circuits made almost entirely of wires and adders, suited to chips whose weights are fixed at fabrication. Pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks and weight sharing become edits of one object, so a single optimizer can choose among all of them for a whole network. And choosing the decisions is the ground-state problem of a higher-order Boltzmann machine whose interactions follow the paths of the tree, the problem class that annealers and quantum optimizers are built to solve. Today these questions are handled apart: each compression method brings its own format and solver, a circuit with fixed weights needs a dedicated constant multiplier for every weight, and discrete solvers reach only narrow subproblems such as rounding. Weight formats have long been moving toward shared decisions, through group scales, shared exponents, microexponents and sparse weights; TWIG takes this trend to its end, and every common format is a shallow TWIG at no extra cost. On five weight matrices of a large language model, a flat tree whose signed power-of-two terms are chosen per weight for circuit cost, with no group scales, needs 9--15\% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error at 3- and 4-bit accuracy on typical matrices, and 20--55\% fewer on matrices with strong outliers.
authors: Ammar Ali, Stamatis Lefkimmiatis
bullets: Each weight is formed by inherited choices such as sign, power-of-two shift, zero gates, or shared-table indices.
Shared path prefixes store and apply decisions once, making pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks, and weight sharing edits of one representation.
Power-of-two TWIG layers can be implemented largely with wires and adders, avoiding a dedicated constant multiplier per weight.
Selecting decisions corresponds to a higher-order Boltzmann-machine ground-state problem suitable for annealing and quantum optimization.
On five large-language-model weight matrices, TWIG used 9–15% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error for typical matrices, and 20–55% fewer for matrices with strong outliers.

(b) Each group keeps its largest exponent once; every weight keeps only its distance D below it, and its sign and mantissa. (c) The resulting tree has a fixed shape: one node per group, one state and one leaf per weight. Blue: shared decisions; orange: private decisions. The example uses groups of 4 weights; the format uses groups of 64.

Figure 2: A first example. (a) Two neighbouring weights stored in 16-bit floating point; their exponents are identical, yet the format stores them twice. (b) Because a weight is the product of its decisions, the shared exponent can be stored once in a node above both weights; each weight is recovered exactly as the product along its path. (c) The same tree computes w1x1 + w2x2 without forming either weight: each leaf becomes shifted copies of its own input (≫ k shifts by k binary positions, i.e. multiplies by 2−k), and the shared exponent is applied once, to the sum, as a shift by three positions. Three additions replace two multiplications and one addition.

Figure 3: The running example: a deeper state tree for one column j of a matrix with eight rows. Each internal node holds one bit that halves everything below it or leaves it unchanged; each leaf holds a sign and a magnitude, possibly zero. The value of an entry is the product of the states on its path (red), times a row scale and a column base, Equation (1). Apart from ρiβj , every factor is a power of two or zero. The column stores 7 node bits (6 if the root bit is folded into βj) and 8 five-state leaves, about 3.2 bits per weight.

In the format, a block of 16 rows and 64 columns, the shape the kernel feeds to the tensor cores, is one record of 16 × 97 = 1,552 bytes.

papers.tldr: TWIG represents neural-network weights as paths of shared discrete decisions, unifying compression and enabling efficient fixed-weight circuits and discrete optimization.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) in neural networks is a promising learning approach for updating the knowledge of deployed systems based on new data encountered at run time, that have not been learned during the offline training phase. To enable their power/energy-efficient CL processing, neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) concept with sparse event-based operations have recently been introduced. However, state-of-the-art NCL methods typically employ the memory-hungry data/experience replay, coupled with costly global learning rule (i.e., backpropagation-based surrogate gradient). To address these limitations, we propose ENCL, a novel methodology that enables efficient NCL by employing a lightweight local learning rule and sub-network freezing strategy. ENCL leverages the temporally- and spatially-local learning rule to perform efficient credit assignment for training new tasks, alleviating the expensive cost of global learning rule. ENCL also employs a sub-network freezing strategy based on the given tasks to avoid the needs for network architecture expansion, hence further improving the efficiency and scalability of the NCL training process. To efficiently support this, we train each task with a small number of epochs as well as adjusted learning rate and timestep. Experiment results on task-incremental learning (TIL) scenario show that, our ENCL consistently achieves strong performance across different datasets as compared to state-of-the-art works. Specifically, ENCL achieves competitive accuracy comparable to that of the state-of-the-art data/experience replay, while reducing memory cost by up to 88%, NCL training time by up to 51%, average power consumption by up to 40%, and energy consumption by up to 65% across different benchmarking datasets (i.e., Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100).
authors: Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Shuochen Zhou, Hassan Raza, Muhammad Shafique
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of experience replay and global backpropagation-based learning in neuromorphic continual learning.
Uses temporally and spatially local learning for efficient credit assignment when learning new tasks.
Freezes task-associated sub-networks to avoid network expansion and improve scalability.
In task-incremental experiments across Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100, it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art replay methods.
Reports reductions of up to 88% in memory, 51% in training time, 40% in average power, and 65% in energy consumption.

papers.abstract: In traditional Gaussian process (GP) regression, the inputs are typically assumed to be known, and uncertainty enters only through the measurements. When scalar fields are mapped using GP regression with measurements obtained from a mobile sensor, the inputs correspond to the estimated pose of the mobile sensor. The goal in this letter is to understand how a recorded GP, trained on erroneous inputs (e.g., pose estimates from dead-reckoning), can be corrected in a numerically efficient way when better estimates of the inputs become available. In the developed bias-aware GP (Ba-GP) framework, the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient is used to propagate estimated input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections. The resulting additive covariance structure is then exploited to develop numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms. A simulation study and an indoor light-intensity mapping experiment show that Ba-GP improves predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration relative to noisy-input GP baselines, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to full GP retraining.
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Tochukwu E. Ogri, Trivikram Satharasi, Kyle Volle, Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
bullets: Addresses GP regression with input errors caused by uncertain mobile-sensor poses.
Uses the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient to propagate input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections.
Exploits the resulting additive covariance structure for numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms.
Simulation and indoor light-mapping experiments show improved predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration over noisy-input GP baselines.
Achieves an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost than full GP retraining.

papers.abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.
authors: Ya Gao, Zhengtao Zou, Pekka Marttinen
bullets: The study reframes on-policy versus off-policy distillation as two hierarchical choices: history generation and action-prefix generation.
Student-generated histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone signal.
Following the student at both levels usually performs worst, but fully on-policy data helps when mixed with other configurations.
Mixtures with the same teacher/student proportions can perform differently depending on how the two levels are paired.
A schedule that starts with fully teacher-generated contexts and gradually introduces fully on-policy contexts outperforms a static mixture in the studied settings.

papers.abstract: Large neural networks are increasingly deployed with 1-4 bit weights and 16- or 32-bit activations, yet their dot products still use one multiplier per element. We show that a length-n dot product with k-bit weight codes can be computed with n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and 2^k multiplications. Each weight code is used directly as an address offset that selects one of 2^k accumulators; each activation is added into the selected accumulator; and the accumulated sums are decoded and multiplied only once, at the end, in a fused decode-and-multiply step. The decoded weight vector is never formed. The refactoring is exact for integer arithmetic, works with integer or floating-point operands and with arbitrary, including nonlinear, decoders, and extends to group-wise scales and to matrix and tensor products. The multiplier count falls by n/2^k, while total arithmetic energy improves by a smaller, bounded factor that we quantify with a cost model. We describe a scatter-accumulate processing element (SA-PE) that replaces the MAC unit in a weight-stationary systolic array, with a load/stream/reduce/drain schedule in which a small, time-shareable multiplier runs only 2^k times per tile. Because decoded weights are not stored, local weight memory shrinks by up to w_d/k for w_d-bit decoded weights. An RTL implementation synthesized for FPGA and compared with a matched MAC array shows that an unshared SA-PE is larger than a MAC PE, and that the saving appears when the reduction multiplier is shared across PEs. Software models confirm exact integer equivalence and floating-point error no worse than the conventional pipeline. We do not claim the underlying identity is new, and we discuss related work on weight sharing and lookup-based kernels.
authors: Jonathan Tapson
bullets: Uses each k-bit weight code to route activations into one of 2^k accumulators, avoiding explicit weight decoding.
Requires n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and multiplications for a length-n dot product.
Extends to nonlinear decoders, group-wise scales, and matrix or tensor products without storing decoded weights.
Reduces multiplier count by n/2^k and can shrink local weight memory by up to w_d/k, though energy gains are smaller and bounded.
FPGA results show benefits when the reduction multiplier is shared across processing elements; exact integer equivalence and no worse floating-point error are reported.

papers.title: Decode Late, Multiply Once: Rethinking the Dot Product for Quantized Weights

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.
authors: Keqi Deng, Ruchao Fan, Jinyu Li
bullets: Addresses the training-time bottleneck of dense attention, which limits practical speedups from sparse methods.
Uses gradient-aware block sparsification to rank query blocks by attention-output gradient norms and skip negligible updates.
Adapts sparsity with a per-head, per-step gradient-mass budget while importance sampling preserves dense gradients in expectation.
Integrates skipping into the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, avoiding loads and computation for skipped blocks.
Maintains downstream performance while delivering up to 5.7× attention-backward and 1.7× end-to-end training speedups.

In the backward pass, each query block is kept with a probability set by its output-gradient norm: skipped tiles are never loaded, and kept blocks are reweighted so that the gradient stays unbiased. As the bars illustrate, a small budget on gradient mass translates into a much larger saving in computation.
