papers.abstract: We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel-space generative modeling into feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel-space flow matching, enabling end-to-end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel-space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE-based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two-stage pipelines. To preserve feed-forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression-based approaches in challenging sparse-view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. Meanwhile, it maintains sub-second inference and remains competitive with substantially heavier pretrained generative models. Our project page is available at https://ranrhuang.github.io/pixgr/.
authors: Ranran Huang, Wenjing Bian, Weixun Luo, Ye Mao, Krystian Mikolajczyk
bullets: Targets sparse-view 3D reconstruction, especially widely spaced observations and view extrapolation.
Encodes context views once into a scene latent that conditions generation from noisy target views.
Uses pixel-space flow matching and differentiable rendering for end-to-end reconstruction supervision.
Avoids VAE-based latent compression and associated error propagation in two-stage pipelines.
Achieves sub-second inference, outperforming regression methods while remaining competitive with heavier generative models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of feed-forward reconstruction and generative pipelines. (a) Deterministic reconstruction cannot model scene uncertainty. Existing generative approaches address this limitation through (b) generation then reconstruction or (c) reconstruction then generation, but suffer from error propagation between stages, VAE-based information loss, and high computational costs. (d) PixG3R instead integrates lightweight pixel-space generation directly into 3D Gaussian reconstruction, enabling end-to-end optimization with direct pixel-space generative supervision.

Figure 2: PixGR Overview. Multi-view posed context images are encoded once into a scene latent representation. Target viewpoints are sampled and encoded as ray maps, which are combined with noisy target images. A lightweight generative decoder processes the concatenated scene latent and target tokens to predict a shared set of pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians supporting both context and target views. The decoder adopts a DiT-style architecture with global self-attention, followed by a linear Gaussian prediction head. Differentiable rendering of the predicted Gaussians produces denoised target views, enabling direct supervision through pixel-space generative objectives.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on extrapolated novel views. Regression-based methods fail in unseen regions, while generative baselines may produce artifacts and distortions, and lead to geometric misalignment (e.g., the sofa in Row 1) and detail loss (e.g., missing texture on the dustbin and the missing street lamp in Row 3). In contrast, PixGR produces geometrically consistent renderings while preserving fine details.

papers.abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
authors: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
bullets: Addresses swarm assembly without requiring a predefined list of attachment sites during deployment.
Combines neural cellular automata with site selection and collision-aware control.
Introduces decentralized discovery by sharing local NCA states among robots already in the formation.
Uses sparse-retention fine-tuning and false-positive loss to adapt NCA growth to gradual physical assembly.
Simulations scale to several hundred robots, while Crazyflie experiments validate the integrated pipeline using externally tracked, robot-relative observations.

Fig. 1. Swarm Morphogenesis time evolution. At each step tk , Advertisers maintain local NCA state around their occupied symbolic cells, assemble a 5× 5 neighborhood patch from observed attached neighbors, apply an NCA update, and advertise neighbouring unoccupied foreground cells as candidate attachment sites. Joiners can then occupy these advertised cells and become Advertisers, so the set of attached cells grows progressively toward the desired morphology.

papers.abstract: Traffic safety videos provide rich evidence for understanding interactions between pedestrians and vehicles, but synthetic-to-real evaluation makes this setting challenging because models must learn from simulated scenes and generalize to real-world traffic. In this work, we present StateBridge, a traffic video-language framework designed to operate under this synthetic-only training protocol. Our approach uses phase-aware clip construction, pedestrian and vehicle track summaries, and structured prompts to ground vision-language models in stable traffic evidence rather than appearance alone. We fine-tune public vision-language models on synthetic captioning and visual question answering examples, then combine their outputs through fact-locked caption fusion and evidence-diverse VQA consensus to improve consistency across actor roles, behavioral phases, and question types. StateBridge achieves an official S2 score of 55.4679 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2 using only synthetic training data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structured evidence transfer for traffic safety captioning and visual question answering.
authors: Blessing Agyei Kyem, Richard Dzinyela, Joshua Kofi Asamoah, Eugene Denteh, Andrews Danyo, Solomon Owusu-Ansah, Dickson Gyimah Asiedu, Armstrong Aboah

Fine-tunes public vision-language models on synthetic captioning and VQA examples.
Uses fact-locked caption fusion and evidence-diverse VQA consensus for more consistent answers.
Achieves an official S2 score of 55.4679 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.
authors: Tianxiang Xia, Kai Lion, Niao He, Michael Muehlebach, Melanie Zeilinger, Hao Ma
bullets: Motivated by the need to run large models locally despite limited memory, compute, unreliable connectivity, and privacy constraints.
Addresses the gap between parameter compression and real inference speed caused by indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparsity.
Jointly learns model weights, low-rank representations, and hardware-compatible structured sparse patterns during training.
Combines budget-aware compression with dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to accelerate inference across multiple memory budgets.
Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 across pretraining and distillation report improved perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs over evaluated baselines on multiple platforms.

papers.abstract: Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge. However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized. As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit. We propose TaxoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym-hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. TaxoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, TaxoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0-2% accuracy vs. 91-100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy.
authors: Xinyu Guo, Minglai Yang, Clayton T. Morrison, Eduardo Blanco, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the lack of taxonomic consistency and edit-scope control in conventional SAEs.
Uses a stack of SAEs aligned to taxonomy levels and a taxonomic alignment loss linking concepts to their hyponyms.
Evaluated on biographical-relation and animal factual-QA taxonomies.
Improves hypernym readout by up to 31.3 points and swap-control success by 25.5 points.
Supports readout of unseen concepts through hypernyms, improving accuracy by up to 37.9 points; suppression largely affects only the targeted concept.

papers.abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan, Nikolaus Correll, Alessandro Roncone
bullets: Whole-body proximity sensors provide useful inductive biases for reflexive collision avoidance.
Lossy, low-resolution sensing outperformed high-resolution coverage as a learning bias.
Anticipating future contact location and timing unexpectedly reduced sample efficiency.
Eight sensor representations were evaluated in reinforcement-learning simulations with over 200 humanoid robots.
The study focuses on end-to-end dodgeball behavior under intentionally constrained resources.

papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time series foundation models (TSFMs) accept a future path for a control variable and return a forecast, inviting what-if queries. The query is interventional; the models are trained on observational data. We determine whether their answers are the conditional slope $\partial E[Y|X]$ or the interventional effect $\partial E[Y|do(X)]$, at three levels. Theory: a Bayes-optimal observational predictor answers interventional queries associationally unless the adjustment set is available and used; for in-context least squares we derive the resulting confounding gap -- a model's effect estimate under an observational minus under a randomized context -- in closed form, a parameter-free reference line. Behaviour: on a preregistered grid with exact counterfactual ground truth, Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS and TimesFM-2.5 all track this line ($R^2$ 0.90-1.00) and respond more confounded than regression itself (slopes 1.3-1.8), on linear and nonlinear structural models. Pairs of models with identical observational laws prove this is not an identifiability limit: when the effect is identifiable, least squares recovers 100% of the true effect difference, Chronos-2 75%, TiRex-2 34%. Representation: linear probes decode the data-generating regime (94-96%) and the true effect ($R^2$ 0.7-0.9) from embeddings that the forecasts ignore. On two physical systems with randomized actuators, pretrained models under-respond by 2-5x and ignore in-window confounding. Minutes of interventional post-training on 3,000 synthetic series cut the gap by up to 83% and transfer outside the training prior. Its forecasting cost is a replay-distribution effect: replaying the model's own pretraining prior cuts it from +47% to +10% MASE, and with low-rank adaptation yields a recipe meeting the preregistered criterion over three seeds (52-61% gap reduction at +1-3% cost) while improving the DoTime benchmark.
authors: Zong-Han Bai
bullets: Theory predicts that observationally trained predictors answer what-if queries associationally unless they use an appropriate adjustment set.
Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS, and TimesFM-2.5 closely follow the predicted confounding pattern across linear and nonlinear systems.
The models’ embeddings contain information about the causal regime and true effects that their forecasts fail to use; randomized physical-system tests show 2–5× under-response.
Minutes of interventional post-training reduce the causal gap by up to 83%; low-rank adaptation achieves 52–61% reduction at 1–3% extra cost and improves DoTime.
Scope: findings concern covariate-aware TSFMs evaluated on synthetic structural models and two physical systems with randomized actuators.

papers.title: Forecasting Associations, Not Interventions: A Preregistered Causal Audit of Covariate-Aware Time Series Foundation Models

papers.abstract: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.
authors: Anais Jeger, Harry Holt, Lennart Puck
bullets: Motivation: Swarm-scale radioisotope heating is impractical for surviving the lunar night, which can cool the surface to 95 K.
Method: Train one policy for 20 robots using evolution-strategy reinforcement learning and a single end-of-night reward based on the five coldest robots’ mean temperature.
Emergent behavior: Robots aggregate into a sheltered core and circulate between the core and exposed rim, despite no explicit spacing, position, exposure, or motion objectives.
Result: The swarm’s survival threshold is 155.6 ± 1.3 pcm-h—37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound.
Scope: The behavior requires neither shared spatial references nor robot-to-robot contact and transfers from 20 to 40 robots without retraining.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Twenty simulated robots during the 354h lunar night, from one rollout of the learned policy. Ring color is each robot’s sky exposure χ on the scale of Fig. 3. Top: the scattered start at hour 0. Every robot is red: with no neighbor close enough to block it, each one radiates to the full sky. Bottom: hour 73, after the swarm has gathered. The interior is blue, shielded by the bodies around it, and only the rim stays warm-colored; all twenty are alive.

Fig. 4. Transfer to larger swarms. Change in survival requirement relative to N = 20, the size at which all five policies were trained; they were evaluated at N = 30 and N = 40 without retraining. Squares are the mean across policies with bars spanning best and worst; faint points are the individual policies. The grey region is the change available from the equalization bound.

Fig. 2 shows the full system. The optimization term consists of the terminal temperature of the coldest quintile of robots. For N = 20, this corresponds to K = 5. We use the coldest quintile rather than the swarm average so that the objective is dominated by the robots closest to failure, while remaining less sensitive to a single outlier. We use a sparse reward which is returned only once, at the end of the lunar night, and no reward shaping takes place during the episode. We leave out any terms which could influence our emergence claim, such as position, spacing, sky exposure, circulation, huddling, or motion. The only motivating factor is therefore to improve survival.

papers.abstract: Synthetic rewrites, where a language model rewrites a natural document e.g. into a target style, are now a standard ingredient of pretraining corpora. However, critical aspects of their use remain poorly understood, such as how much compute should be spent rewriting training data and whether a model trained on rewrites can outperform the rewriter. We study these two questions by proposing a rewriting scaling law that predicts loss from model size, training tokens, the fraction of training tokens that are rewrites, and the number of epochs over the natural data, charging the compute spent generating rewrites. We fit this scaling law in two settings. In the compute-limited setting, natural data is plentiful and rewrites come from a third-party rewriter trained with more compute than our largest run. We find that the estimated optimal rewrite fraction increases with compute, from under $10\%$ at $3\times10^{18}$ FLOPs to $32\%$ at $10^{22}$ FLOPs. Our scaling forecast extrapolates $33\times$ in FLOPs to train a 22B-parameter model, whose final loss is within $1.1\%$ of our prediction. This model achieves a better BPB than its rewriter on several web domains at one-tenth the rewriter's training compute. In the data-limited setting, we assume we only have a fixed seed set of natural data and that our rewriter is a model of the same size as the target, pretrained on that seed set. Again, we find the optimal rewrite fraction increases with the compute budget. We also demonstrate that a model trained on rewrites of its own pretraining data, generated by a rewriter of the same size, beats the best run on natural data alone at every model size up to 3B. Our results show that synthetic rewriting can be studied through the scaling law lens: that optimal methodological choices are predictable and scaling does not necessarily break down beyond the rewriter's capabilities.
authors: Nicholas Roberts, Ahmed Ahmed, Suhas Kotha, Percy Liang, Yu Wang, Alex Renda, Nitya Mani
bullets: Studies the tradeoff between rewrite-generation compute, model size, training tokens, rewrite fraction, and data epochs.
Fits the law in compute-limited and data-limited settings, accounting for the cost of generating rewrites.
In the compute-limited setting, the optimal rewrite fraction rises from under 10% at 3×10¹⁸ FLOPs to 32% at 10²² FLOPs.
A 22B-parameter model’s loss was within 1.1% of the scaling forecast after a 33× FLOPs extrapolation.
Models trained on synthetic rewrites can outperform their rewriters and natural-data-only baselines, including across sizes up to 3B parameters.

papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.
authors: Siliang Zeng, Luca Viano, Chenliang Li, Jiaxiang Li, Volkan Cevher, Markus Wulfmeier, Stefano Ermon, Alfredo Garcia, Mingyi Hong
bullets: Covers supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO).

Provides practical implementation insights for researchers and practitioners.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32 master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices, including LeRobot's SmolVLA default and its $\pi_0$/$\pi_{0.5}$ guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent $\pi_{0.5}$ fine-tunes with a training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success over LeRobot's storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at a ten-times lower learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at its default rate. For SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10 actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the copy beats every run without it (p < 0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.
authors: Shubham Singh
bullets: bf16 rounding removes updates smaller than 1/512 of a weight when no fp32 master copy is used.

The proposed fix is to keep trainable weights in fp32 during training; for SmolVLA in LeRobot, this requires one line.

papers.abstract: Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high-dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real-world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end-effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation. We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning-based baseline without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate long-horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework. The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.
authors: Youyuan Long, Gokhan Solak, Arash Ajoudani
bullets: Addresses underactuated, delayed, high-dimensional DLO dynamics and multiple feasible motions under obstacles.
Formulates multimodal planning as Bayesian set optimization balancing control quality with behavioral diversity.
Uses incremental updates to maintain promising control modes efficiently, plus an execution dynamics model for fast-motion mismatch compensation.
Evaluated on rope tracking, obstacle avoidance, and disturbance rejection in simulation and hardware.
Generalizes to unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning; reduces longest-task tracking RMSE by 44.0% and planning time by 29–66% versus relevant baselines.

Candidate control sequences are sampled around the multimodal warm-start set and evaluated through parallel rollouts using the execution dynamics model, DLO dynamics model, and collision detection. Based on rollout costs and trajectory features, BM2PC performs an incremental multimodal update to maintain a diverse set of high-quality control modes. One mode is selected for execution, while the updated multimodal set is propagated to the next MPC iteration.

Fig. 4: Trajectory tracking results (Sim). Comparison of trajectory tracking performance of the proposed BM2PC method and the SPiD baseline on both smooth parametric trajectories (Sinusoid, Egg, and Lemniscate) and complex hand-drawn trajectories (SpongeBob, PatrickStar, and Flower) under different execution durations. The proposed method achieves accurate tracking across most trajectories, while SPiD fails to reproduce fine geometric details, particularly on complex trajectories with sharp turns and rapid local variations. Thus, SPiD is not shown in the longer cases (T>12s) to avoid clutter.
Fig. 9: A test-time example of the execution dynamics model.

Fig. 5: Obstacle Avoidance (Sim). Comparison of BM2PC, C-MPPI, and SVMPC on the obstacle avoidance task. The top row presents the rope-tip trajectories together with the tracking RMSE and average inference time. The bottom row shows key snapshots of BM2PC, illustrating mode collapse in unimodal regions (A,C) and multimodal emergence near the obstacle (B,D). The rope tip may pass above the obstacle without touching it, as seen in snapshots B and D.

Fig. 10: Real-world trajectory tracking results. Top: comparison of the desired trajectory and the tracked trajectories generated by BM2PC and SPiD for three trajectories. Bottom: time-lapse snapshots of the real robotic system during the sinusoidal and lemniscate tracking experiments by BM2PC.

Fig. 3: Execution dynamics model. A GRU-based history encoder processes recent measured and desired end-effector states to initialize a latent representation of the current execution dynamics. Conditioned on this latent state and the desired future trajectory, the rollout cell recursively predicts future EE motion. At each rollout step, an MLP predicts the executed acceleration, which is integrated by a physicsinformed (PI) head to obtain the next velocity and position.

Fig. 2: The DLO model. The rope is represented by N+1 mass points m j connected by linear spring–damper elements (ks j,c s j) and bending spring–damper elements (kb j ,c b j ). Gravity g and air damping cair are also included.

Fig. 11: Real-world obstacle avoidance results. The rope tracks a Lemniscate (×3) trajectory while a movable obstacle is randomly repositioned along the path to evaluate dynamic obstacle avoidance performance. The blue curve denotes the target trajectory, the orange curve represents the executed trajectory, and the red segments indicate perception failures caused by occlusions, environmental noise, or network instability. Time-lapse snapshots (a)–(h) illustrate the avoidance process under different obstacle configurations. Despite severe perception degradation, including frozen measurements and abrupt trajectory spikes, the controller successfully avoids the obstacle and rapidly returns the rope endpoint to the desired trajectory.

Fig. 7: Multimodal adaptation under sudden blocking. Comparison of representative trajectories from experiments with τ = 0.70 s. (a) Predicted control modes before blocking. (b) The second obstacle appears and blocks the executed plan. (c) Replanning after 25 ms. (d) Predicted modes after 225 ms. (e) Executed rope-tip trajectories. BM2PC switches to an alternative mode on the unblocked side, whereas the ablated variants fail to recover a feasible passage in this example.

Fig. 6: Disturbance Rejection (Sim). The rope tip is subjected to external disturbances at the blue points to evaluate the robustness of the controller. The corresponding rope-tip trajectories and key snapshots of the experiment are presented. BM2PC rapidly suppresses the induced oscillations and drives the rope tip back to the desired trajectory.

papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
authors: Yuval Kansal, Karen Ullrich, Polina Kirichenko, Ilia Kulikov, Niraj K. Jha, Mohammad Pezeshki, Mark Ibrahim
bullets: Addresses the limits of temporary in-context reflection and costly, interference-prone full fine-tuning.

Across GAIA, Claw-Eval, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, success rates improve by 8.9–17.0 percentage points.
Lessons reduce repeated mistakes, nearly double correction reliability, and transfer to new tasks without additional training.

papers.selection_reason: Self-directed distillation of mistakes into lightweight persistent adapters directly fits test-time and continual learning plus LLM agent-memory topics.
papers.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons

papers.abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: How do children learn the meanings of the simple, concrete words that form a majority of their early vocabulary? Statistical information about many word meanings can be recovered from the gradual accumulation of information about the co-occurrence of words with their referents, a proposal known as ``cross-situational learning''. Contrastive vision--language models allow this learning strategy to be tested on egocentric video data capturing children's early real-life experiences with visual and linguistic inputs. Initial successes of this method on small datasets provide a proof-of-concept, but vision models struggle to learn robust visual representations when trained on these same egocentric videos. How dependent is cross-situational word learning performance on the quality of the model's visual representations? And can cross-situational models scale to larger and more diverse datasets? To address these questions, we trained models on the BabyView corpus, including 2,441 hours of longitudinal egocentric video from 48 children. Models trained on this dataset learned object--label mappings, but performance was far higher when they used internet-pretrained visual representations as opposed to when visual representations were learned solely from the developmental video data. Further, the majority of the learning signal was carried by a small proportion of utterances that described a visible referent. Models learned lexical representations that showed recognizable human-like semantic structure, but model performance showed substantially different trajectories over training experiences than those observed in children. Cross-situational learning is a viable word learning strategy for early noun vocabulary, but constructing developmentally plausible models will require understanding how to learn high-quality visual representations from naturalistic data.
authors: Michael C. Frank, Alvin W. M. Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Victor Moreno, Grace Keene-Lee, Meesha R. Ryan, Tarun Sepuri, Jane Yang, Virginia A. Marchman, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Bria Long
bullets: Models trained on 2,441 hours of egocentric video from 48 children learned object–label mappings.
Internet-pretrained visual representations substantially outperformed representations learned only from the developmental videos.
Most learning came from utterances describing a currently visible referent.
The learned lexical representations developed recognizable human-like semantic structure.
Model learning trajectories differed substantially from those observed in children.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.
authors: Xiao Tan, Yixuan Wang, Zhexi Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting control logic to physical contact during manipulation.
Writes Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion using visual and F/T observations.
Analyzes force records and visual outcomes after execution to diagnose failures and revise control logic.
Requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation.
Across five real-robot tasks, improves grasp accuracy and task success while reducing contact loss versus a vision-only agent.

papers.abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
authors: Zihe Song, Wenting Zhao, Ye Liu, Yuanjie Zhu, Ke Xu, Shanghao Li, Philip S. Yu
bullets: Addresses latency from autoregressive decoding of repeated tool calls, beyond accuracy optimization.
Maintains bounded, per-user call stores online with verified write-back and LRU eviction.
Uses a side-effect gate to defer irreversible calls until speculative drafts are verified.
Across three open-weight models, it improves mean accepted tokens by 27% over frozen stores and reaches up to 1.74× wall-clock speedup.
Live memory drives nearly all gains; per-user scoping prevents measured cross-user leakage without improving acceptance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A frozen TOOLSPEC-style datastore vs. SPECMEM on a recurring call: user u checked Google’s stock the day before and now asks for Apple’s. Each arm drafts a candidate call for a draft-then-verify decoder over the fixed served model (acceptance = token longest-common-prefix). SPECMEM retrieves u’s own GOOG call, accepted up to the changed ticker (17 of 28 target tokens) with only the remainder decoded; the frozen TOOLSPEC-style store’s stale build-time entry accepts 9, the schema-only draft 7 (full-run MAT 19.96 vs. 15.70 and 5.92). Only the live store writes the verified target back, so its advantage grows across sessions.

Right: the advantage over the frozen store grows from ∼1% (session 1) to a peak of ∼37% (session 10; 34% at the final session 11) as novel per-user calls accumulate, an effect a single-session benchmark cannot expose.

papers.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
papers.tldr: SpecMem accelerates agentic tool calling by continuously updating per-user memories for speculative decoding while gating irreversible actions until verification.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.
authors: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu
bullets: Recasts VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse as a shared 10-candidate, term-centric benchmark covering nouns, verbs, and entities.
Adds confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to test grounding beyond direct caption–image matching.
Introduces GAR, a training-free approach that combines gloss/definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification.
Definition augmentation helps across all subsets; constraint-guided reasoning helps VWSD and especially VerSe but is less effective on WikiDiverse.
Combining both signals raises Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22 with Gemma3-12B and provides the best macro-average performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Illustrative overview of the proposed GAR framework. CGR aggregates the affirmative probabilities into an interpretable semantic score for reranking.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a unified multimodal grounding benchmark and training-free gloss-augmented reasoning framework for multimodal large language models.
papers.title: SAGE: Sense-Aligned Multimodal Grounding Evaluation with Gloss-Augmented Reasoning

papers.abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the correct path among multiple geometrically plausible work-zone routes.
Generates candidate paths geometrically, then fuses geometric scores with agreement to a VLM-predicted trajectory.
Trains the VLM to identify lane status and hazard side before making a passage decision, with rule-based intervention for control compliance.
On 2,306 ROADWork episodes, SAGE reduces average displacement error by 8.3%, final displacement error by 12.0%, and hard-constraint violations by 37% versus the geometric ranker.
The approach improves all tested generator-selector combinations and is competitive with or better than adapted driving VLMs on reported accuracy and safety measures.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.
authors: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang, Huichi Zhou, Haozheng Zhang, Qi Xiong, Ping Luo, Wenbo Ding, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen
bullets: Addresses the manual effort and limited scalability of constructing robot-learning scenes and tasks in simulation.
Uses a coding agent to decompose demonstrations, orchestrate specialized image and 3D generation tools, and refine an executable world program with verification feedback.
Employs a camera-pose-anchored representation separating static context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships.
Supports error diagnosis, correction, physically consistent interactions, and replay of recorded robot trajectories.
Experiments on DROID show visually faithful and geometrically consistent reconstructed worlds that preserve trajectory validity.

papers.abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich manipulation tasks to be trained directly on physical robots, but unsafe interactions during online learning remain a key barrier to practical deployment. We propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for reliability-aware safety intervention during real-world policy learning. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. During online learning, SEVI evaluates each task-policy action before execution; if the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides it with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and distribution-shifted conditions. Across task-learning and safety-critic baselines, SEVI achieves the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, the highest final task success, and the lowest unsafe-event counts. SEVI also reduces unsafe events by 13.4 to 57.1 percent relative to recovery-based safe RL while preserving low-latency execution-time filtering. The project page is available at: https://sevi-safe.github.io/
authors: Shaekh Mohammad Shithil, Lantao Liu
bullets: Targets unsafe online interactions that hinder deployment of real-world reinforcement learning.
Uses an Evidential Safety Critic to estimate future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in one forward pass.
Overrides actions predicted unsafe or insufficiently supported with an offline-trained recovery policy.
Evaluated on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and shifted conditions.
Reports the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, highest final task success, and 13.4–57.1% fewer unsafe events than recovery-based safe RL, with low-latency filtering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the SEVI framework. In offline training, failure and recovery demonstrations are used to train the Evidential Safety Critic and recovery policy. During the runtime pipeline, the ESC evaluates task-policy actions using predicted risk and epistemic uncertainty and switches to the recovery policy when needed. In online RL, RLPD updates the task policy using executed transitions from the RL buffer together with prior demonstrations from the demo buffer.

Fig. 1: Illustration of SEVI on the real-world USB insertion task. When the task policy attempts an unsafe insertion, SEVI detects elevated safety risk or epistemic uncertainty and triggers the recovery policy. The recovery policy steers the robot toward a safer region before returning control to the task policy for continued online RL training.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates the inference speed of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) by sampling from a faster, lower quality draft model. Traditionally, a fundamental characteristic of speculative decoding is that it is lossless with respect to the verifier distribution, guaranteeing speed without sacrificing quality. This differs from recently developed diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which are notably able to achieve substantial speedups by degrading the quality of their outputs with less diffusion effort. Because diffusion models are able to sample faster than autoregressive models by generating tokens in parallel, they are considered strong candidates for draft models in speculative diffusion. While it is widely understood that diffusion models can sacrifice quality for speed, speculative decoding itself can also be generalized to generate lossy samples faster using more lenient acceptance criteria with respect to the verifier distribution. Presented with the two parameters of diffusion effort and speculative decoding leniency, this paper explores the full achievable Pareto frontier via joint variations of these parameters. Our experiments show that jointly varying diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can extend the speed-quality Pareto frontier over single step diffusion drafting.
authors: Aaron Zorel, Guy Van den Broeck, Aditya Grover, Daniel Israel
bullets: Diffusion language models can serve as fast, parallel-generating draft models for speculative decoding.
Unlike traditional lossless speculative decoding, both diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can deliberately trade quality for speed.
The paper maps the achievable speed–quality Pareto frontier by jointly varying these two parameters.
Experiments show joint tuning extends the frontier beyond using single-step diffusion drafting alone.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Comparison of Pareto frontiers. For a single Qwen3 8B verifier, we benchmark several speculative diffusion methods. Each line corresponds to the achievable speed-quality frontier of a specific draft model. Dashed curves fix one diffusion step and vary leniency, while solid curves are varied over diffusion effort and acceptance lenience. For the SDAR models that support multi-step speculative diffusion, varying over the parameters jointly significantly extends the Pareto frontier.

Figure 1: A conceptual overview. Diffusion has a speed-quality tradeoff parameterized by diffusion effort K, while speculative decoding has a speed-quality tradeoff parameterized by acceptance leniency λ. This work argues that speculative diffusion exposes both tradeoffs and therefore reveals optimal configurations that could not be found by varying only a single parameter.

Figure 4: Examples of the Pareto frontier. We provide examples of speculative diffusion for both masked diffusion (left) and uniform diffusion (right). Each point signifies a configuration of acceptance leniency in verification and diffusion effort (K steps) in drafting. We observe the same qualitative trend that the speedquality Pareto frontier is occupied by many different settings of diffusion effort which require different levels of lenience.

Left: Visualization of the proof of Theorem 1 shows that the linear interpolated distribution p̃⋆ is the optimal solution to maximize drafter q and verifier p alignment while staying within a constraint on deviation from the verifier ϵ. The solution to this constrained optimization is p̃. Right: A motivating example shows that the speed-quality frontiers independently induced by diffusion effort and acceptance lenience in speculative decoding can occupy separate regions of the Pareto frontier. We compare diffusion only with AR speculative decoding with leniency.

papers.tldr: Speculative diffusion accelerates LLM inference by jointly tuning diffusion effort and verification leniency to improve the speed–quality tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .
authors: Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
bullets: Introduces an alternative conditional-computation mechanism that generalizes attention and naturally nests with MoE sparsity.
Outperforms conventional MoE transformers at equal compute and sparsity during language-model pretraining.
Adapts more effectively to longer contexts and new domains during continual pretraining.
Forgets less about previously learned domains while adapting to new ones.
Benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length increase.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Nested sparsity in NESTOR. (a) The NESTOR architecture. In each block, the column router sends the token xj to Kc = 2 of the C = 4 columns. Each column has M layers, each with its own attention and its own E = 4 experts, of which a per-layer expert router selects Ke = 2. The token uses only the colored parameters. (b) The causal attention map computed by each column for S = 8 tokens, shown in terms of the whole sequence: column c computes attention only among the tokens Uc routed to it.

Figure 2: Held-out loss scaling laws for NESTOR, MoE, and dense models. Each law is fitted as L(F) = A F−α + L∞, where F is the training FLOPs. NESTOR reaches the lowest hold-out loss at every scale. The horizontal ticks mark the projected compute that the MoE and dense baselines need to match NESTOR.

Figure 5: The linear model and the two predictors, for C = 2 coarse labels (blue, green) and E = 3 fine labels. (a) One sample: the coarse label determines the relevant tokens, the pattern W⋆ c , and the row space of A⋆ c ; the fine label determines the map B⋆ ce. (b) The flat predictor (MoE transformer): the shared attention scores every token, and each expert has its own row space, fit from its own samples. (c) The nested predictor (NESTOR): the attention of a column scores only the tokens with its label, and its row space is fit once from the samples of all of its experts. The free parameters are counted below each panel.

Figure 3: Domain adaptation and forgetting relative to the MoE transformer. Top: reduction in held-out loss on the target corpus. Bottom: increase in held-out loss on the pretraining corpus. Both are measured relative to each model before adaptation and shown as a percentage of the MoE transformer’s value.

Figure 4: Long context extension by continued pretraining. We show the held-out loss at each context length from 4k to 64k at all scales, relative to the MoE transformer of the same scale. Top: the dense transformer. Bottom: NESTOR at equal FLOPs with new documents, at equal FLOPs with the documents of the equal-token run repeated over the run, and at equal tokens. The open markers at 4k are the pretrained checkpoints.

Figure 14: Routing statistics of the trained 500M models across depth, one column of panels per router family. Top: effective number of choices of the aggregate assignment distribution on each held-out corpus (thin lines) and on their equal-token mixture (heavy line). Middle: share of the layer’s choices that are never selected or selected well below the uniform load. Bottom: mean per-token entropy of the router’s softmax as a fraction of log E, which measures how concentrated the router’s distribution is for each token, as opposed to how balanced the load is. In the last block of NESTOR, every column is selected (shaded).

Figure 8: Ablation of the placement of the experts of NESTOR, at the 200M scale. We vary the stored parameters of three designs, with the columns, the schedule of active columns, the attention residual, the training recipe and the 10B-token budget of Section 3 held fixed, so that every model has the same active FLOPs: the design of NESTOR, Es = 8 shared experts with Ks = 2 and E ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32} experts per column with Ke = 2; a shared bank only, Es ∈ {12, 24, 48} with Ks = 3 and no experts in the columns, which is the MLP of the MoE baseline with column-routed attention; and experts in the columns only, E ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16} with Ke = 1 and no shared experts. The dashed line is the capacity law L(N) = c + aN−0.698 of the MoE baseline, fitted to its runs with 16, 24 and 48 experts (diamonds), and each design is fitted with the same exponent, solid over its measured span and dashed beyond it. Where two seeds were run, they are joined by a whisker. NESTOR is 0.018–0.031 nats below the law at every size. With experts in the columns only, the loss is below the law at small sizes and closer to the law at larger sizes. With a shared bank only, the loss is on the law from 24 to 48 experts. The shared bank with 96 experts is omitted: its routing collapsed, and 54 of its 96 experts per layer were selected by under 1% of the tokens.

Figure 9: Ablation of the attention residual of NESTOR at 100M, 200M, 500M, and 1B, on the axes of Figure 2. We compare the column attention residual (Col. AttnRes), the merged attention residual (AttnRes), which is that of Kimi Team (2026) with the changes of Appendix B, and no attention residual. The rest of the model is unchanged. Each series is fitted by L(F) = A F−α + L∞, and a horizontal tick marks the projected compute at which each variant reaches the loss of Col. AttnRes. Removing the attention residual increases the loss by 0.073–0.086 nats at every scale, which corresponds to 1.5–2× the compute. The two attention residuals have the same loss up to 500M and differ at 1B.

Figure 6: The schedule of active columns. Left: held-out loss of the ten schedules of Table 2 against the layer-weighted mean of Kc. The constant schedules are joined by a line; the run at Kc = 2 is above the plotted range. The grey circles are the gradual ramps of the configuration search, the dashed line is the dense transformer, and the band is the range of the two seeds of the MoE transformer. Right: groups of schedules that differ only in the order of their layers. Within a group, the schedules have the same multiset of layers and hence the same FLOPs and stored parameters, so the differences within a group are due to the order alone. The shaded band is the mean of the two seeds of NESTOR plus or minus 0.010 nats, the difference between seeds at this scale. Where two seeds were run, they are joined by a whisker.

Figure 7: Pretraining with sliding window baselines. Figure 2 without the dense transformer and with three sliding window baselines, described in Appendix C.2: the MoE transformer with sliding window attention in place of the column attention of NESTOR: at the depth of NESTOR, with windows that give the same number of attention scores as NESTOR in each layer (triangles); at the depth of the MoE, with the same windows (inverted triangles); and at the depth of the MoE, with one uniform window and periodic full attention layers (pentagons). Top: held-out loss against training compute, with the fitted laws and the compute multiples of Figure 2. Bottom: the same losses minus the fitted law of the MoE at the same training compute (the zero line), on a scale where differences of a few hundredths of a nat are visible; at 200M, a second seed is drawn as a whisker. The two windowed models at the depth of the MoE use fewer FLOPs per token than the MoE, so the MoE law is evaluated at their smaller compute, and their values in the bottom panel are lower than the differences between their losses and the losses of the MoE.

Figure 13: Long context extension with a sliding window baseline, one global layer in six. As Figure 11, with a different baseline (triangles): the MoE transformer with sliding window attention of window 4096 in five of every six layers and global attention in the sixth. Its FLOPs per token are 0.89–0.94× those of the MoE transformer at 8k and 0.34–0.43× at 64k, so at equal FLOPs it is trained on 1.15–1.49B tokens at 64k, against 0.60–0.62B for NESTOR. The 64k extension corpus has 1.2B tokens; at 100M, 200M, and 500M, 17%, 20%, and 2% of the tokens of the 64k run are therefore seen a second time. The vertical range of the bottom row is larger than in Figure 11.

Figure 10: Forward FLOPs per token against the context length. Top: the forward FLOPs per token of NESTOR and of the baselines at all scales, with the accounting of Appendix C.1. The baseline curve is that of the MoE transformer. The dense transformer has the same FLOPs at 100M and 500M; at 200M and 1B, because of the rounding of the MoE expert widths, the two differ by less than 0.2% over the plotted lengths. Bottom: the FLOPs per token of NESTOR relative to the MoE transformer. The markers are the context lengths of Figure 4, and the same formula is plotted up to 1M tokens as dashed curves. The projections and MLPs of NESTOR cost 4–8% more than those of the baselines, and its attention costs 0.75–0.81× as much. The share of attention in the total grows with S, so the relative cost of NESTOR decreases from 0.98–0.99× at 4k to 0.80–0.84× at 64k, and tends to the attention ratio as S→ ∞ (dotted).

Figure 11: Long context extension with a sliding window baseline. The panels of Figure 4 with one more baseline in the bottom row (triangles): the MoE transformer with sliding window attention in as many layers as needed to match the FLOPs per token of NESTOR, extended at equal FLOPs with new documents. It starts from the 4k checkpoint of the MoE transformer, so both have the same open marker at 4k.

Figure 12: Long context extension with a sliding window baseline, one global layer in two. As Figure 11, with a different baseline (triangles): the MoE transformer with sliding window attention of window 4096 in every other layer, starting from the first, and global attention elsewhere. papers.abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning robot behaviors aligned with human intent. However, its scalability is fundamentally limited by the need to collect expensive human preference labels for every new task. In this work, we present PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL on unseen target tasks without requiring any human feedback. The core idea is to learn a task-invariant latent preference space from a small amount of offline preference data on source tasks, where transferable preference structures are disentangled from task-specific variations. This learned manifold allows PrefO2O to transfer preference structures and reward priors to new tasks under distribution shift, while confidence-weighted optimal transport alignment generates reliable pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation. Extensive experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that PrefO2O substantially outperforms existing preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds PbRL methods trained with real human feedback, while generalizing across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings as well as across different robot embodiments.
authors: Ruiqi Wang, Dezhong Zhao, Xuesu Xiao, Erdem Biyik, Byung-Cheol Min, Guohua Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability problem of collecting human preference labels for every new task.
Learns a task-invariant latent preference space that separates transferable preferences from task-specific variations.
Uses confidence-weighted optimal transport to align new tasks and generate pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation.
Evaluated on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks across multi-to-one, one-to-one, and cross-embodiment transfer settings.
Reportedly outperforms preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds methods trained with real human feedback.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PrefO2O. The offline phase jointly learns a trajectory encoder, a preference VAE, and a meta reward model from source-task preference data. In the online phase, the pretrained encoder and reward model warm-start target-task PbRL, and the frozen preference VAE serves as a stable reference for OT-based alignment. Source labels are propagated to target trajectory pairs through the transport matrix, producing pseudo-preference labels with OOD-aware confidence weights for online reward learning and policy optimization.

Fig. 3. Learning curves of all methods on six tasks under two transfer protocols. The left panel shows intra-embodiment transfer, while the right panel shows cross-embodiment transfer. Learning curves for Sweep Into and Walker Walk are provided in Appendix B.

Fig. 7. t-SNE visualization of preference representations with Window Close as the target task, comparing the raw space against the learned latent preference space under intra-embodiment (left) and cross-embodiment (right) transfer. Each point denotes either a raw trajectory-pair difference or its corresponding latent preference vector epref. The upper row colors points by task domain and the lower row by preference label Υ. The learned latent space exhibits strong cross-task mixing and clear separation across preference labels, indicating a task-invariant yet preference-discriminative structure that the raw space lacks.

Fig. 1. Conceptual illustration of PrefO2O. Offline preference data from multiple source tasks are used to learn a task-invariant latent preference space that captures shared preference structures while absorbing task-specific variations. When deployed on an unseen target task, this learned space enables both transferable reward priors and OOD-aware pseudo-preference supervision for zero-shot online PbRL without target-task human feedback.

Fig. 8. Attribute alignment along the learned preference axis with Window Close as the target task, evaluated under intra-embodiment (top) and crossembodiment (bottom) transfer. Each point denotes a latent preference vector epref, colored by preference label Υ. The horizontal axis is the preference-axis projection score, obtained by projecting epref onto the direction between the centroids of samples with Υ = 0 and Υ = 1. The vertical axis reports the attribute value difference for three task-relevant behavioral attributes: approach progress, path directness, and motion smoothness. The dark curve shows the attribute trend along the preference axis, computed as the binned mean attribute value. The Spearman correlation coefficient ρ in each panel quantifies the monotonic association between the preference-axis projection score and the corresponding attribute value difference. The attributes increase consistently along the learned preference axis, indicating that the latent preference space captures a structured behavioral manifold aligned with preference-relevant properties.

Fig. 9. Case study of OT-based preference alignment in the learned latent space, with Sweep Into as the target task. Left: a chord diagram where outer bars denote individual preference pairs grouped by source task, colored by preference label Υ; each chord connects a target pair to a source pair, with width proportional to the transport mass T ∗ ij . Every target pair draws correspondences from all source tasks, but with markedly different mass, showing that alignment is driven by preference structure rather than task identity. Right: for two representative target pairs (Sweep Into #4 and #53), the source pair receiving the highest transport mass, visualized as trajectory rollouts. Despite belonging to entirely different tasks with distinct object interactions, the matched source and target pairs share the same underlying behavioral quality contrast, confirming that the learned latent space aligns preferences along transferable behavioral features rather than task-specific motions.

Fig. 5. Results of one-to-one transfer with intra- and cross-embodiment settings. Different colors indicate different single source tasks used for transfer. The dashed line reports the default multi-to-one performance as a reference.
Fig. 6. Results of ablation study on four target tasks under default intra-embodiment, multi-to-one transfer settings.
Fig. 4. Pseudo-label accuracy (%) across three benchmarks. Bars show the mean over five random seeds; error bars indicate one standard deviation.
Fig. 10. PrefO2O successfully completes real-world Cube Stacking and Pick-and-Place tasks on a Kinova Jaco robot.
Fig. 11. Learning curves on Sweep Into from MetaWorld and Walker Walk from DeepMind Control Suite under the same-embodiment transfer protocol.

papers.abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.
authors: Sangeeta Warrier, Anush Sankaran, Ryen White

papers.abstract: Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow-matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI-GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter-matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best-of-10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly. Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/)
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Luzhe Sun, Yiqing Xu, Matthew R. Walter

Applies geometric selection and refinement to reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation.
Best-of-10 selection reaches 72.4% physical stability with 0.970 silhouette IoU; PI-GNN generalizes better than a parameter-matched MLP.
