papers.abstract: Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)
authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Richard Cheng, Sergey Zakharov, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Targets costly, error-prone manual segmentation of robot demonstrations and avoids feeding raw multiview video into language models.
Learns Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs) to compactly encode recurring, temporally localized kinematic patterns.
Uses subtask annotations to supervise an open language model over SMT sequences.
Outperforms baseline segmentation methods in F1 against human labels and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion.
Also supports task-progress tracking on an unseen robot and detection of action reversal.

figures.caption: Figure 2: KiRoSe Pipeline. Given a robot kinematic stream and the task instruction “fold the paper box,” KiRoSe encodes motion using a transition-supervised encoder, then temporally pools and quantizes its features into Sparse Motion Tokens with a learned codebook. The language model reads these tokens, time markers, and the instruction to output action descriptions with start and end times, such as “pick up the object,” “place in the box,” and “adjust.” Transition annotations provide training supervision, while the motion tokenizer remains frozen during language-model adaptation.

Figure 5: Qualitative reversal probe on AgiBot (zero-shot). One subtask per episode is played backwards in place (red frames; stamps give original recording time). Curves show the signed progress rate (green: rising, red: falling); dashed: same model on the original video. ReWiND keeps counting up while the task is undone; KiRoSe’s progress falls; Table 4 reports statistic result.

Figure 7: Segmentation examples on held-out YAM tasks (ABC-130K). The zero-shot video model tends to emit a few coarse segments that restate the instruction (“fold and stack blue towel”, “attempt insert plug”), whereas KiRoSe recovers the repeated grasp–place, flatten–fold, and insert cycles of the reference from kinematics alone. KiRoSe’s Boundary F1 at ±1 s exceeds the video baseline on all five episodes (0.44–0.72 versus 0.07–0.38).

Figure 3: Evaluation Dataset. Top: example tasks and annotated action timelines, with colors indicating action categories. Bottom: representative 40-second traces of linear speed, angular speed, and opening rate for the left (black) and right (orange) arms or hands. The datasets differ in task semantics, temporal structure, and motion characteristics.

Figure 9: Segmentation examples on Ego-Exo4D human-hand trajectories (zero-shot). Keyframes are from the wearer’s Aria camera (top 20% cropped). Overlays show the hand joints that the conversion of Appendix D uses, projected from the 3D annotations into the image with an approximate equidistant fisheye model: the wrist (dot), which supplies linear velocity; the wrist-toknuckle fan, which defines the palm frame and angular velocity; and the dotted thumb–index line, whose length supplies the aperture. Frames without an overlay for a hand have no valid 3D track at that instant. Although KiRoSe never sees human data and hands have no gripper, it matches or exceeds the video baseline on all five episodes; over all 114 trajectories with video, KiRoSe reaches 0.375 Boundary F1 at ±1 s versus 0.255, and the gain depends on the motion tokens (Appendix D).

Annotations are dense and follow the arms’ kinematic events: alternating grasp and place cycles when organizing bottles, open, scoop, and close phases when filling the litter box, and explicit mistake intervals (hatched) when a grasp fails.

Figure 1: Encoding Kinematic Events into Sparse Motion Tokens. Across diverse manipulation tasks and objects, continuous robot motion decomposes into recurring, temporally localized patterns termed kinematic events (e.g., bimanual lift, handover, pick, place). Despite visual and spatial variations, end-effector trajectories within the same motion primitive share structural kinematic signatures. KiRoSe compresses kinematic events into a short, ordered sequence of N discrete Sparse Motion Tokens (colored blocks; shaded chronologically).

(a) Four tasks, one single-frame pose each: the palm frame of each hand (red along the palm, green across, blue normal) and the thumb–index pinch (purple) that serves as the gripper, projected from 3D into the Aria image with an approximate equidistant fisheye model. Frames are shown only where all 14 joints the conversion uses agree with a manual 3D label within 2 cm. (b) The resulting channels for a COVID-test run next to a YAM episode of the same length; dotted lines are annotated boundaries. Wrist speed and aperture rate rise at keystep boundaries much as robot speed and gripper rate do at subtask boundaries. (c) Annotation projection: keystep starts that fall inside a tracked run become that run’s boundaries, in run time.

Figure 12: How each robot channel is built for a robot and for a human hand. Rows are the channels of the shared representation (middle column). Figure 10: Dilated temporal convolutions in the kinematic encoder. (a) Each residual block applies a kernel-5 convolution whose dilation doubles from block to block; tracing one output of the fourth block back to the input shows that the same five taps per layer cover 61 input samples. Padding is symmetric, so every feature sees both past and future motion. (b) With seven blocks (dilations 1, . . . , 64), the receptive field grows to 1 + 4 ∑6 i=0 2 i = 509 samples, or 17 s at 30 Hz. papers.abstract: Estimating a camera pose from 3D-2D correspondences - Perspective-n-Point - is one of the most fundamental problems in computer vision. Existing methods either solve a minimal problem or replace the objective with an easier one. Surprisingly, no scalable certifiable solver for the actual Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) exists. We propose PnP*, the first practical solver that guarantees efficient computation and returns a certifiable globally optimal solution. We prove that the underlying convex relaxation is exact under moderate noise, which to our knowledge is the first stability guarantee for any relaxation for the MLE of PnP. Furthermore, we reduce the relaxation by exploiting chordal sparsity pattern and quotient ring reduction such that the relaxation is tractable and scalable. The stability and scalability results are verified numerically, as PnP* returns a provably correct camera pose at over 10 Hz.
authors: Bang-Shien Chen, Caitrin E. Eaton, David M. Rosen
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable certifiable solvers for the true PnP maximum-likelihood objective.
Uses a convex relaxation with a proof of exactness under moderate noise.
Exploits chordal sparsity and quotient-ring reduction to make the relaxation tractable and scalable.
Numerical experiments verify stability and scalability, with certified solutions reported at over 10 Hz.

papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.
authors: Hariharan Devarajan, Neeraj Rajesh, Aniruddha Marathe, Nikoli Dryden, Kin Ng, Michela Taufer
bullets: Addresses the reliance on manually authored skills and curated memory, which causes agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions.
Uses a predictor–validator–corrector loop: tools and skills propose solutions, executions validate them, and outcomes refine a persistent capability store.
Learned capabilities solve recurring tasks on the first attempt in 93–95% of cases across evaluated models.
Each task produces 7.6–30.8 durable capabilities without user instruction; once capabilities exist, creation drops below two per task.
Warm-start execution uses 0.38–0.40 million tokens per task, and Phronix improves correctness and task-solving rates on evaluated workflows and models.

papers.abstract: Federated unlearning (FU) aims to remove a designated target client's influence from a trained model without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. Existing methods largely treat unlearning as a post-hoc, stateless operation, overlooking that client influence is path-dependent: contributions made during training, particularly during critical learning periods (CLPs), can have disproportionate and persistent effects. Moreover, knowledge overlap and intermittent client availability make relying on all retained clients inefficient and impractical. We introduce PDF, a path-dependent client-selection framework based on the insight that retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning. During training, PDF maintains lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories summarizing each client's accumulated update direction and global-model alignment. Upon an unlearning request, these histories identify and rank retained clients that are globally informative yet weakly coupled to the target, enabling retraining-based unlearning with only the top-$k$ clients over a small number of rounds. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID settings show that PDF achieves effective forgetting and strong retained utility with substantially fewer retained clients. In particular, PDF achieves $0\%$ forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC on non-IID CIFAR-10, improves retained accuracy by up to $6.91$ percentage points over the strongest competing FU baseline on CIFAR-100, and reduces communication by approximately $69\%$ and computation by $57$--$61\%$ relative to Retrain.
authors: Thanh Linh Nguyen, Quoc-Viet Pham
bullets: Client influence is path-dependent, especially during critical learning periods, so retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning.
PDF tracks lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories of each client’s update direction and alignment with the global model.
When unlearning is requested, it ranks clients that are globally informative but weakly coupled to the target and retrains using only the top-k clients.
Across FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 in IID and non-IID settings, PDF preserves retained utility while using substantially fewer clients.
On non-IID CIFAR-10 it reaches 0% forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC; relative to Retrain, it cuts communication by about 69% and computation by 57–61%.

papers.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhiding Yu, Sifei Liu, Danfei Xu, Ben Levin, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan
bullets: Supports outcome rewards for deployment monitoring, process rewards for RL post-training, and timestamped captions for pretraining data curation.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on WGO-Bench, RoboReward, and Robometer.
Competes with GPT-6 Astra on internal benchmarks while costing roughly 125× less than API-based alternatives.
Processes 200,000 hours of robotics data daily across 512 GB300 GPUs.
Open-sourcing enables custom robotics datasets and applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.

papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.
authors: Jeanne Salle, Hardik Bhatnagar, Matthias Bethge, Sahar Abdelnabi, Maksym Andriushchenko
bullets: Context compaction is evaluated systematically in a fixed OpenCode scaffold across five strategies, three frontier models, and three long-horizon benchmarks.
For models with 1M-token contexts, changing the compaction threshold does not measurably affect performance; the smallest-context model degrades at lower thresholds on some tasks.
Default self-summarization performs best overall; more aggressive content removal can reduce some models’ performance substantially while leaving others unchanged.

Compaction summaries increasingly omit constraints: the first summary drops roughly one-third of ProgramBench anticheating rules on average, and procedural instructions are lost far more often than build specifications in real sessions.
The benchmarks are described as “compaction-friendly” because objectives and progress remain recoverable on disk; unrepeated constraints are most vulnerable.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Compaction keeps what the agent can re-read from disk and drops some of the rules it cannot. Left: overview of a ProgramBench run. The task prompt states the goal and anti-cheating rules: no copying or vendoring the reference, no internet access, and an original implementation that does not derive from or wrap the reference. At each compaction the agent replaces its context with a summary. The goal and the agent’s progress survive, because the agent can re-read its files, the rules exist only in the context, so a rule the summary discards is lost. On average, around one of the three rules is missing after the first compaction and around two after the tenth. Right: (1) for the 1M context models, task scores barely change when compaction is forced at thresholds from 160K to 380K tokens; (2) rules are dropped more often as compactions accumulate on ProgramBench, and on real user sessions from SWE-chat, compaction drops process instructions (“how to work”) and scope exclusions (“don’t touch X”) far more often than feature requirements (“what to build”).

All models are run at the same absolute compaction thresholds. Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over runs.

(a) On ProgramBench, the task’s anti-cheating rules disappear from the summaries progressively over a run. (b) On real user-agent sessions, process instructions and scope exclusions are dropped much more than feature requirements.

Figure 7: Failure rate by compaction strategy. Fraction of runs in which the agent failed to produce a valid result, for ProgramBench and PostTrainBench, per model. For each task, the failure rate is the number of failures divided by the number of attempts; bars corresponds to the mean over tasks, so every task has equal weight (ProgramBench: Canop/broot and jarun/nnn; PostTrainBench: GPQA, GSM8K and BFCL, each on two base models). Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Runs were launched until enough succeeded, so the number of attempts per task differs across tasks and conditions. Pooling all attempts would weight each task by how often it was retried, and since harder tasks fail more and are rerun more, this would inflate the weight of exactly the tasks that fail most. We therefore compute each rate per task and average, so that every task contributes equally and strategies are compared on the same task mix. Tasks with few attempts will thus have noisier rates, which the bootstrap intervals reflect. All runs were obtained at a fixed compaction thresholds (160K tokens before triggering compaction).

papers.selection_reason: Studies context compaction for LLM agents and constraint loss; relevant to agent memory and long-horizon context management.

papers.tldr: Current long-horizon agent benchmarks often tolerate lossy context compaction, but compaction can silently discard unrecoverable task constraints.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) can jointly process a broad range of modalities, such as text, audio, and video, enabling stronger multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities, but often at substantial inference cost. We observe that the benefit of additional modalities varies across queries, indicating that a fixed modality configuration can be inefficient. Motivated by this, we study query-wise modality selection, which keeps the underlying Omni-LLM fixed while adaptively selecting which modalities to provide for each query. We formulate the problem as an accuracy-cost optimization problem and develop a cost-sensitive learning approach for modality selection. We evaluate our approach on WorldSense using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under three inference-cost measures: input tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Across both models, query-wise modality selection consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off and can even outperform the standard setting in which all available modalities are provided to the Omni-LLM. For Qwen2.5-Omni, our cost-sensitive approach matches or exceeds this full-modality accuracy while requiring only approximately 41% of the input tokens, 39% of the latency, and 61% of the monetary cost.
authors: Shuqi Liu, Yuzhou Cao, Luke Ong
bullets: Additional modalities are not equally useful for every query, making fixed all-modality inference inefficient.
The method adaptively selects query-specific modalities while keeping the underlying Omni-LLM unchanged.
It formulates selection as an accuracy–cost optimization problem and uses cost-sensitive learning.
Evaluated with Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni on WorldSense across token, latency, and monetary costs.
For Qwen2.5-Omni, it matches or exceeds full-modality accuracy at about 41% of input tokens, 39% of latency, and 61% of monetary cost.

papers.abstract: Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera-control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross-view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine-grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross-view-consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross-view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross-view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm-ai-research.github.io/SyncVid-Webpage.
authors: Farhad G. Zanjani, Animesh Karnewar, Fatih Porikli, Amirhossein Habibian
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating temporally and cross-view coherent videos from a single reference video, especially for dynamic geometry.
Lifts the source video into a canonical 4D representation and rasterizes geometry-aware noise into target camera views.
Introduces cross-view-consistent whitening to reduce local correlations while preserving correspondence across views.
Uses the structured noise as the prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model without architectural modifications.
Experiments report improved perceptual quality and cross-view consistency, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SyncVid. Given a source video, SyncVid (1) lifts the observations into a canonical 4D point representation; (2) samples a Gaussian noise vector for each 3D primitive in the scene; and (3), after specifying novel camera trajectories, rasterizes and whitens the shared 3D noise into the corresponding views. These synchronized priors guide video diffusion to produce temporally and cross-view consistent videos from multiple cameras.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on a Multi-ViewBench example with an Arc-right trajectory.

Figure 2: View-consistent whitening Noise vectors z𝑖 are attached to 3D primitives and the cubemap; rasterization therefore provides cross-view correspondence, while overlapping footprints induce local correlation. We reduce this correlation with a per-pixel orthonormal transformation Q𝑝 derived from the rasterized canonical anchor position X𝑝 using random Fourier features and reduced QR (dashed box). Because Q𝑝 depends on X𝑝 rather than screen coordinates, pixels observing the same surface point share the transformation across views and over time. The resulting noise pattern (right) is approximately i.i.d. Gaussian within each frame while remaining cross-view synchronized.

papers.abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
authors: Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of relying directly on representations shaped by generic vision pretraining.

Jointly trains navigation with a JEPA-style latent “dream” that predicts the next scene representation before each action.
Reports new state-of-the-art results across VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and point-goal benchmarks, with gains transferring to a physical robot.
The learned latent predicts future depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy without direct occupancy supervision; its scope is navigation-focused and evaluated on the stated benchmarks and robot setting.

papers.abstract: Existing 3D talking avatar methods mainly rely on parametric face models including 3DMM or FLAME, whose compact motion representations limit their ability to synthesize extreme expressions and to model accessories such as headwear. We introduce AudioLift, a two-stage framework that uses generated multi-view videos as the intermediate representation for audio-driven avatar generation without parametric face models or per-instance optimization. Our framework combines a synchronized multi-view video generation stage with an inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction stage to recover coherent full-head geometry from a single portrait image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AudioLift produces 3D talking avatars capable of capturing more extreme facial expressions than existing methods, with improved geometric completeness and strong multi-view consistency across the full $360^\circ$ viewing range.
authors: Zhuoyuan Jiang, Weijie Lyu, Xiaoyuan Wang, Tiancheng Shen, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the limited expression range and poor accessory modeling of 3DMM/FLAME-based avatars.
Uses a two-stage pipeline: synchronized multi-view video generation followed by inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction.
Requires neither parametric face models nor per-instance optimization.
Produces more extreme facial expressions, more complete geometry, and strong consistency across 360° views.
Scope: results are reported for audio-driven single-image avatar generation; specific datasets and quantitative results are not given.

papers.abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.
authors: Zixian Gao, Lixin Xiu, Penghao Luo, Xiangcheng Cao, Ziqi Cai, Zhen Li, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang

Scans all cameras at low resolution each second, uses a hold-or-switch policy, then views the selected camera at high resolution before speaking.
Maintains only aired visuals, commentary, and recent context while allowing other views to expire, keeping processing cost bounded over arbitrarily long streams.
Introduces a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with per-hero cameras, director choices, and caster commentary.
Outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors, including GPT-5; its commentary wins 29.2% of Proact-VL comparisons against GPT-4o.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict human sentiments by integrating signals from different modalities such as text, video, and audio. However, raw multimodal sequences often suffer from semantic inconsistency--exhibiting redundancy or conflicts within and across modalities--which hinders robust understanding and increases computational cost. To this end, we introduce ConsMSA, which explicitly formalizes semantic distribution consistency across both $\textit{intra}$- and $\textit{inter}$-modality, providing a consistency-aware mechanism for robust and efficient multimodal sentiment prediction. Specifically, ConsMSA projects multimodal token features into a shared sentiment space to compute an Intra- and Inter-modality Consistency Score ($I^2CS$). By coupling this score with predictive relevance, we formulate consistency-aware importance signals that are utilized: (i) as a consistency regularizer to align latent distributions during training, (ii) to derive semantic-aware weights for adaptive multimodal token reweighting, and (iii) as a practical criterion to prune redundant or conflicting tokens. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate that ConsMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust under aggressive token compression--retaining only 10% of tokens yields comparable accuracy. These results establish semantic distribution consistency as a promising foundation for synergizing predictive robustness with computational efficiency.
authors: Pan Wang, Lipeng Ke, Huajun Ying, Pritish Mohapatra, Rohan Sarkar, Suresh Lakhani, Sankar Venkataraman, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses semantic inconsistency, redundancy, and conflicts in text, video, and audio sequences.
Projects multimodal tokens into a shared sentiment space to calculate intra- and inter-modality consistency scores.
Uses consistency-aware signals for distribution regularization, adaptive token weighting, and token pruning.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance and comparable accuracy when retaining 10% of tokens.

The optimized tokens are finally concatenated in the Fusion Module for the final prediction. The system is optimized via a joint loss to achieve a robust balance between task accuracy (Ltask), semantic consistency (LI2CS), and modality-specific losses (LMS).

papers.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.
authors: Xiaoran Chen, Binghui Li, Liwei Wang, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Under isotropic gradient noise, Muon provides no acceleration beyond learning-rate rescaling.
For heterogeneous task frequencies, Muon changes task-frequency dependence from linear to square-root scaling.
The analysis derives an exact two-task balancing threshold and extends to multiple tasks based on coverage and gradient reliability.
Muon avoids rotation-induced negative transfer identified in SignSGD, while momentum reduces sampling noise and tracks changing gradients.
Controlled experiments support the theory, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study suggests promise for fast-slow momentum.

papers.abstract: This article introduces Latin Modern BERT (LAMB), an encoder for the Latin language based on the ModernBERT architecture, pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a novel morphologically informed masking regimen. We also present two corpora for the Latin language. Acervus contains 24B BERT WordPiece tokens, including over 760K samples from heavily damaged OCR transcriptions, repaired by a ByT5 model trained for Latin text repair. The second dataset, Corpus Trinum, contains a mixture of over 100M strong and weak Latin language semantic triplets. Corpus Trinum is the first Latin semantic triplet dataset, opening the door for Latin language models to be adapted to general sentence semantic similarity tasks. We construct an experimental grid using five tasks and seventeen subtasks, applying a variety of finetuning configurations and subword aggregation techniques for 15 pretrained encoders, 6 LAMB training checkpoints, and an ablation model designed to quantify the impact of different masking regimens. Using this benchmark, we rank Latin encoders and find that LAMB outperforms all other evaluated models on 16 of 17 subtasks, coming within 0.8 percentage points of state of the art on the seventeenth. We provide additional analyses relating Latin encoder performance to tokenizer behavior, syntactic structure, finetuning configuration, pretraining state, subword aggregation, and variation in source texts and domains. In these, we identify unique acquisition dynamics for Latin open class words during terminal decay phases, and establish that for some task categories, finetuning configuration selection can have a greater effect on downstream scores than additional pretraining tokens.
authors: Aidan McCarthy
bullets: Pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a morphologically informed masking strategy.
Introduces Acervus, a 24B-token corpus incorporating repaired OCR text, and Corpus Trinum, a 100M+ semantic-triplet dataset.
Evaluated across five tasks and 17 subtasks, with varied checkpoints, finetuning settings, and subword aggregation methods.
Outperforms all other evaluated encoders on 16 of 17 subtasks and approaches state of the art on the remaining task.
Analyses examine tokenizer behavior, syntax, pretraining, finetuning, subword aggregation, and domain variation.

papers.abstract: We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median angles of about $36^\circ$ and $42^\circ$, respectively, at the smallest scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized Gram discrepancy by roughly 70\% on Reacher and 47\% on Cube. Geometry measured in pixels and embeddings varies more across scales than the chosen physical-state geometry. On held-out directions, environment Grams achieve median embedding response errors of 17\% and 28\%, compared with 26\% and 38\% for an isotropic reference with the same trace. LeWM's errors are higher at this scale. These findings support scale-specific evaluation of action sensitivity; its effect on control remains an open question.
authors: Vasil Vasilev, Siddharth Nayak
bullets: Action-sensitive directions differ from the simulator by median angles of about 36° on Reacher and 42° on OGBench Cube at the smallest scale.
Larger perturbations reduce normalized Gram discrepancies by roughly 70% on Reacher and 47% on Cube.
Pixel- and embedding-based geometries vary more across scales than physical-state geometry.
Environment-derived Grams yield lower held-out embedding-response errors than an equal-trace isotropic reference, while LeWM errors are higher at this scale.
Whether these geometric mismatches affect control performance remains open.

papers.abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
authors: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
bullets: Evaluates omni-modal guardrails across safety, utility, and reliability.
Covers over 183k samples from 35+ sources across text, image, audio, video, and cross-modal inputs.
Benchmarks 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails under a unified safety-risk taxonomy.
Finds that OLLMs can moderate content effectively without guardrail-specific tuning, but guardrails struggle with concealed harmful intent and sophisticated jailbreaks.
Reveals limited cross-modal safety understanding, including safety hallucination and over-reliance on textual patterns.

papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.
authors: Bingyu Bai, Cheng Zhang, Erhu Feng
bullets: Addresses how instruction and environment changes can invalidate previously successful GUI execution traces.
Represents reusable traces with UI-state/action graphs plus text for task intent, procedure structure, and variable slots.
Uses a record-template-replay process to validate each transition against the current instruction and live UI state.
Reduces LLM inference token consumption by about 80% on average across five agents on AndroidWorld, with most achieving at least 1.5× speedup.
Real-device tests on Android and HarmonyOS reuse 70.7–79.8% of actions while delivering over 2× speedup in most configurations.

papers.abstract: Indoor radio map estimation (RME) is essential for wireless applications such as coverage planning, localization, and network deployment. However, most existing methods follow a supervised learning paradigm that requires costly labeled data and task-specific model training. Moreover, indoor environments involve privacy-sensitive information, such as building layouts and structures, that often cannot be centralized. To address these challenges, we make the first attempt to formulate indoor RME as a collaborative in-context learning (ICL) problem. We propose Poly-Ripple, a framework in which multiple clients perform ICL using large autoregressive vision models (LAVMs) without model updates. Each client is prompted by its private demonstrations and predicts the radio map for the same scene query. To capture the causal structure of wireless propagation outward from the transmitter (Tx), we adopt ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling. We further introduce importance-aware aggregation to exploit heterogeneous contextual knowledge distributed across clients under the context length constraint. We provide theoretical analysis and conduct extensive experiments on a public indoor RME benchmark. The experimental results show that Poly-Ripple consistently outperforms representative ICL baselines, while aligning with our theoretical analysis.
authors: Yuanzhe Peng, Jie Xu
bullets: Reframes indoor radio map estimation as a collaborative in-context learning task, reducing reliance on centralized labeled data and task-specific training.
Uses large autoregressive vision models without model updates; each client predicts a shared scene’s radio map from private demonstrations.
Applies ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling to reflect wireless propagation outward from the transmitter.
Introduces importance-aware aggregation to combine heterogeneous client context under limited context length.
Theory and experiments on a public benchmark show consistent improvements over representative in-context learning baselines.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
authors: Elyas Rashno, Farhana Zulkernine
bullets: Frozen perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical signals and post cited evidence to a shared board.
An integration agent combines observations with retrieved examples, while a critic may request one revision.
Deterministic verification checks citation validity and whether final emotion claims are entailed by the evidence.
Failures are attributed to components and failure types, then converted into validated targeted prompt patches.
On MER2025, targeted adaptation improves F-score by 0.6–2.2 points across four MLLMs, including 52.3→54.5 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

papers.abstract: We present a surrogate-accelerated Bayesian history-matching framework, demonstrated on a realistic synthetic model ($N=100{,}188$ cells). The forward map $\mathcal{G}$ is replaced by a Fourier neural operator $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ trained in a closed loop, $\hat{x}_{n+1}=\mathcal{G}_\theta(u,\hat{x}_n)$, with the discrete black-oil residual $R(x_{n+1},x_n)$ as a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) penalty, truncated backpropagation and noise injection. We assimilate production data and 4-D seismic using adaptive regularised ensemble Kalman inversion (aREKI), and synthesise $\Delta V_p$ inside the rollout via a closed-form Gassmann transform of the surrogate, under a two-stage schedule (aREKI on production, then an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation, ES-MDA, on both). To temper the ill-posedness, we invert $(\log K,\phi)$ not in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$, where $N_e\ll 2N$ leaves a rank-deficient covariance and a null space the data never inform, but on a chart $u=\Psi(\tilde m)$, $\tilde m\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d\ll 2N$, given by a Parseval-exact truncated cosine transform or a variational auto-encoder decoder. The ensemble then spans its own search space; the directions the data cannot constrain are cut to those the chart can express, and every member decodes to a geologically plausible field. For the rollout we prove an exposure bound $W_1\le\sum_j L^{\,n-1-j}\mathbb{E}e_j$, a physics-penalty contraction $\|D_x\mathcal{G}_\theta\|\le\alpha 0.999$ on pressure and saturation and rolls out in $0.579$ s, a $\sim2500\times$ speed-up, bringing an $N_e=190$-member, $N_a=10$-iteration joint inversion within one GPU-hour.
authors: Clement Etienam, David Blom, Hari Pattathil, Tsubasa Onishi, Harpreet Sethi, Lalson Vincent, Suraj Pawar, Kishan Ramesh Kumar, Pandu Devarakota, Faruk O. Alpak
bullets: Replaces the reservoir forward simulator with an autoregressive Fourier neural operator trained using black-oil residual penalties, truncated backpropagation, and noise injection.
Assimilates production and 4-D seismic data through a two-stage aREKI and ES-MDA workflow, with seismic changes synthesized using a Gassmann transform.
Restricts inversion of permeability and porosity to low-dimensional cosine-transform or variational-autoencoder charts to reduce unidentifiable directions and promote plausible fields.
Provides an exposure-bound analysis and reports stable rollouts, a roughly 2500× speed-up, and completion of the stated ensemble inversion within one GPU-hour on the synthetic model.
Demonstration is limited to a realistic synthetic model with 100,188 cells.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Cartoon of the end-to-end workflow. A synthetic, fault-dissected reservoir model with unknown petrophysical properties (logK,φ) (left) is sampled by an ensemble of full-physics finite-volume runs; these train an autoregressive PINO–FNO surrogate that rolls out the black-oil state in closed loop; the surrogate’s own state is pushed through a closed-form Gassmann map to a 4-D seismic observable and through the Peaceman heads to production observables; and a two-stage ensemble Bayesian inversion (aREKI→ES-MDA) assimilates both to return a posterior reservoir model (dashed feedback). Each block corresponds to a stage of the pipeline and a subsection of this paper.

papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in astronomy, but choosing a suitable method for a scientific problem often requires expertise in both astronomy and ML. Large language models (LLMs) could help astronomers make such choices, yet this ability remains underexplored in existing benchmarks. We introduce Astro2Method, a benchmark of 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers (2024/01-2026/06), based on clear performance differences and complete (Easy) or partial (Hard) explanations from the authors. Across five LLMs, direct prompting achieves 87.50-92.55% accuracy on Easy questions but only 58.87-64.52% on Hard. Using historical papers, neither retrieval-augmented generation nor most agent methods with additional reasoning or retrieval (including ReAct, Self-Ask, and CRITIC) bring consistent improvement. Agents required to search the web improve accuracy mainly when they find the papers the questions are based on, with no consistent improvement otherwise. Providing the source paper's pipeline description with method names masked improves Hard accuracy, matching or exceeding web search. Together, these results suggest that relevant experimental information helps distinguish ML methods, but inferring it from related studies and domain knowledge remains challenging for LLMs in astronomy.
authors: Xingzhong Fan, Hangfeng He, Fatemeh Nargesian
bullets: Benchmarks ML-method selection with 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers.
Direct prompting reaches 87.50–92.55% accuracy on Easy questions versus 58.87–64.52% on Hard questions.
Retrieval-augmented generation and most agent approaches do not consistently improve performance.
Web-search agents help mainly when they locate the source papers; masked pipeline descriptions can match or exceed web search on Hard questions.
Relevant experimental information is important, but inferring it from related work and domain knowledge remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Movement primitives commonly represent robot mo- tions through basis functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics, we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables. The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bezier curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation). As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations. Simulation experiments demonstrate accurate joint recovery, refinement through modifications in model complexity and continuity, and improved robustness to variance in the demonstration set. Finally, we demonstrate online retiming and synchronization capabilities in a patient-turning task assisted by a robot, evaluated with a physical manikin.
authors: Boxuan Zhang
Ante Marić
Sylvain Calinon
bullets: Represents spatial paths and temporal progression using shared continuous Bezier-curve variables.
Adapts spatial and temporal model complexity independently, including demonstration-specific phase modulation.
Uses alternating optimization to recover path intervals from partial demonstrations.

A physical-manikin patient-turning task demonstrates online retiming and synchronization.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
authors: Razieh Rezaei
Ehsaneddin Asgary
Masoud Jalili Sabet
bullets: Addresses gaps in prior multimodal bias benchmarks, which cover limited categories or fail to make target group attributes visually clear.

Evaluates 23 open-source MLLMs in text-only, image-only, and image-with-context settings to isolate modality effects.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.
authors: Tam\'as D\'ozsa, Andrea Angino, Rolf Krause, Matthias Voigt

Demonstrates applications to support vector machines, deep ReLU networks, polynomial fitting, and PDE solution methods.
Numerical experiments illustrate the framework’s potential across these diverse problems.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $τ$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.

Introduces annotation pipelines and a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot text and oriented 3D bounding boxes.

Second, we construct 3D layouts by detecting and tracking subjects (Detectron2[44] + SAM2[33]), recovering human meshes (CameraHMR[31]), reconstructing scene depth and aligning meshes to a unified coordinate system (Pi3[42]), then encoding 3D boxes in NOCS and projecting them to 2D layout sequences. Third, we generate hierarchical captions (global/shot/subject) with Gemini, including consistent subject IDs across shots.

Figure 2. Overview of MeV. Creators first design the 3D scene and provide a hierarchical caption. We project the 3D layout into an NOCSbased encoding scheme and use it as guidance for ControlDiT. Meanwhile, we decompose the caption into global-, shot-, and subject-level descriptions, and fuse them via a Hierarchical Context Attention mechanism to enhance narrative consistency and subject coherence across shots.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison. We show frames from each shot generated by all compared methods. Our method not only strictly follows the prompt and maintains strong visual coherence, but also produces natural transitions between shots. In addition, our method closely follows the guidance provided by the 3D layout, especially in Shots 3 and 5, where it better realizes the subject’s layout and motion.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
authors: Jack Cai
Lijie Yang
Vasilis Kontonis
Dimitris Papailiopoulos
Shivam Garg
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache growth caused by long chain-of-thought decoding.

Uses in-block pause-token positions, layer-wise cache allocation based on entry value, and relatively large compression blocks.
On 446 competition problems with 32K-token generations, one-quarter of the generated cache matched an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length.
In vLLM, it reduced cache size 3.5× per sequence and improved saturated-H100 problem completion speed 3.2× versus full KV.

papers.selection_reason: Training learned pause tokens to compress long reasoning into a much smaller KV cache is a direct contribution to memory-efficient LLM inference and persistent memory.
papers.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
papers.tldr: AbridgeKV compresses long reasoning into learned pause-token KV entries, reducing cache use while preserving performance and speeding inference.

papers.abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
authors: Aayush Mishra
Arnau Padrés Masdemont
Victor Conchello Vendrell
Jordi Ros Giralt
Arash Behboodi
Fabio Valerio Massoli
bullets: Existing Ouro Looped LMs require KV-cache storage for every loop depth, forcing all loop computations despite supporting dynamic computation.
The proposed “best-available” KV caching strategy enables up to 30% lower FLOPs and KV memory without losing full-depth performance.
Training with awareness of this caching strategy further improves efficiency and performance.
A revised early-exit objective produces heterogeneous token depths based on token difficulty rather than uniform shallow processing.
Results are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pretrained from scratch.

figures.caption: Figure 2: (First row) Exit depth distribution of pre-trained Ouro models: predominantly depth 2/3 depending on the threshold τ , illustrating the lack of true dynamic exits due to local prior enforcement. Noticeably, depth 1 exits are non-existent. (Second row) Jump rate fractions. A high majority of tokens do not jump around and exit at similar depths as their neighbors. Even when they do, they typically only jump one depth up or down. Large jumps (|ei − ei−1| ≥ 2) rarely happen. These numbers undermine the claims of dynamic computation based on difficulty in Ouro models.

Figure 3: To enable early-exit, Ouro models are trained with a KL divergence term (w.r.t a uniform prior) over all tokens equally. This causes the same local pressure on all tokens regardless of difficulty, and makes the policy learn similar high entropy distributions. Our fix: enforce the KL to prior w.r.t the global expected exit distribution across tokens. On the right, we show that this simple fix creates confident (low-entropy), difficulty-aware exits per token while maintaining low KL with the prior (P: Poisson, G: Geometric, U: Uniform) overall. The exits are truly heterogeneous as evident by the large jump rates (|ei − ei−1| ≥ 2).

Figure 1: Ouro forces full-depth computation even after a token exits, as future tokens may need it. This makes early-exit practically useless. Ragged KV enables true early-exit by aliasing deeper blocks to the best-available cache. It avoids forced computation and saves memory+FLOPs during inference. Surprisingly, it works out-of-the-box for Ouro models! On the right, we compare fixeddepth (1-4 loops) with Ragged KV at different exit thresholds on BigBenchHard (details in §E.1). Ragged KV unlocks significantly higher performance at low average decode depths.

Figure 12: global prior enforcement produces visibly heterogeneous hard exits. True RaggedKV prefill at τ = 0.5 for the final 20B models (Poisson prior). Each column shows the first of five matched held-out 2,048-token sequences for one prior; the local and global rows within a column receive exactly the same tokens. Colored points are individual hard exit depths and the black curve is their 128-token rolling mean. A large jump is an adjacent pair with an absolute harddepth change of at least two, |ei − ei−1| ≥ 2]: 3→ 2 is not a large jump, while 3→ 1 and 1→ 4 are. global traces have large-jump rates of 19.2%, 20.9%, and 13.2% for Poisson, Geometric, and Uniform priors, respectively, versus 0.2%, 2.5%, and 1.9% for the paired local traces. And we can see that the low depth tokens in global are actually placed meaningfully according to difficulty (commas, spaces, semicolons, simple words that follow obviously, etc).
Figure 7: With a simple β-schedule, looped model pre-training collapses to a fixed-depth-1 like behavior. The model processes inputs in the first loop and then acts like identity in the next 3 loops.

papers.tldr: A practical KV-cache strategy and improved early-exit training make Looped LMs dynamically allocate computation, reducing costs while preserving full-depth performance.

papers.abstract: High-quality 3D reconstruction of lunar terrain from sparse rover images is indispensable for autonomous lunar exploration, but remains challenging because viewpoint overlap is insufficient, surface textures are weak, and data volume is limited. We propose MoonGS, the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored to lunar scenes. Given only two input images, MoonGS predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass and renders photorealistic novel views without any per-scene optimization. MoonGS (i) adopts an adaptable backbone design that seamlessly integrates advanced vision foundation models to extract robust depth features; (ii) integrates semantic priors in two manners: merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and adopting a semantic ranking loss that regularizes background depth; and (iii) employs an entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy to augment sparse observations by selecting the most informative distant viewpoints with negligible overhead. Experiments on the LuSNAR benchmark and our synthetic weak-texture MoonBlender dataset show that MoonGS surpasses state-of-the-art feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines by +4.9 dB PSNR, +0.29 SSIM, and 40\% lower LPIPS while maintaining sub-second inference. Furthermore, we validate the broad applicability of our framework by demonstrating that it effectively leverages state-of-the-art backbones, including VGGT, to significantly boost performance. Qualitative evaluations on Chang'e mission imagery also show the best visual quality among compared methods, indicating robustness on real lunar data. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/InRobots/MoonBlender.
authors: Yun Jiang
Bo Zheng
Yingying Zhang
Xueming Xiao
